q: During intake, a 62-year-old patient becomes pale and says they feel faint right after standing on the scale; what should the CMA do first before finishing vital signs or notifying the provider?
a: Assist the patient to a safe position (sit or supine) and assess airway/breathing/circulation while staying with them, because preventing a fall and stabilizing the patient is the immediate priority; a common mistake is trying to “just finish vitals” or walking away to get help before the patient is secured.

q: A patient with COPD history has RR 8/min and is difficult to arouse in the exam room; what should the CMA do first?
a: Call for immediate assistance/activate emergency response and assess airway/breathing per BLS, because this may be respiratory depression; the trap is trying to “let them rest” or finishing documentation first.

q: While preparing for an injection, you accidentally touch the needle to the countertop after removing the cap; what should you do next?
a: Discard the needle/syringe and restart with new sterile supplies because contamination breaks asepsis; the trap is wiping the needle with alcohol and proceeding.

q: A patient on contact precautions has a visitor sitting in the room; the provider asks you to bring in supplies from the clean supply room; what is the best infection-control approach?
a: Perform hand hygiene and don appropriate PPE before entering, and bring only necessary supplies to avoid contaminating clean stock; the trap is carrying a full tray of supplies in and returning unused items to clean storage.

q: During intake, an adult’s radial pulse is irregular and you count 72 for 15 seconds; what is the best next step?
a: Recount for a full 60 seconds and document irregularity, then notify the provider as directed, because short counts miss irregular rhythms; the trap is multiplying a 15-second count on an irregular pulse.

q: A CMA removes gloves after a wound dressing change and then answers the room phone; what should have been done instead?
a: Perform hand hygiene immediately after glove removal before touching shared equipment, because gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene; the trap is assuming glove use alone prevents transmission.

q: During CPR in the clinic, another staff member brings an AED and asks what to do next; what should the CMA instruct?
a: Turn on the AED, apply pads, and follow prompts while minimizing pauses in compressions, because early defibrillation with continuous CPR improves outcomes; the trap is stopping compressions too long while “setting up” the AED.

q: During intake, an adult patient says “I feel fine,” but you obtain BP 198/112 manually after an automated reading error; what should the CMA do next?
a: Recheck after 5 minutes with the patient seated, arm at heart level, then immediately alert the provider if still severely elevated because this is a high-risk value; the trap is documenting one bad machine reading or sending the patient back without confirmation/escalation.

q: A provider asks you to apply a sterile dressing to a laceration after suturing; what is the key difference in your technique compared with a routine bandage change?
a: Use sterile technique (sterile gloves/field and avoid touching the wound-contact surface) because post-suture wounds require asepsis; the trap is using clean gloves and letting the dressing touch nonsterile surfaces.

q: You administer a vaccine and the patient immediately develops hives and wheezing; what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate emergency response and stay with the patient while initiating clinic anaphylaxis protocol (e.g., bring epinephrine kit per standing orders), because airway compromise is life-threatening; the trap is sending the patient to the lobby or telling them to “wait it out.”

q: A patient says they are allergic to latex; you are preparing to administer a vaccine with a prefilled syringe; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop and check the product/packaging for latex components and notify the provider if any risk is present, because latex exposure can trigger reactions; the trap is proceeding because the allergy “isn’t to the vaccine.”

q: A patient begins to faint during a wound care visit and slides forward in the chair; what is the best immediate positioning action?
a: Lower the patient to a supine position with legs elevated if tolerated and protect the head, because this improves cerebral perfusion and prevents injury; the trap is trying to hold them upright in the chair.

q: During rooming, a 66-year-old reports dizziness when you stand him for height; seated BP is 88/54 with HR 118 and he looks pale, and the provider is still with another patient—what should the CMA do first?
a: Sit or lay the patient down with legs elevated and stay with him while calling for the provider/clinical help immediately, because this is symptomatic hypotension requiring rapid support and escalation (a common mistake is continuing intake or walking him to the scale, increasing fall/syncope risk).

q: In the waiting room an adult collapses and is unresponsive; a bystander says “I think they’re not breathing”; what should the CMA do first?
a: Assess responsiveness and breathing and immediately call for help/activate EMS and get the AED, because early CPR/AED saves lives; the trap is searching for a pulse for an extended time before starting action.

q: While taking vitals, a patient reports chest pressure and you measure SpO₂ 88% on room air with cold fingers; what should the CMA do first?
a: Assess accuracy by warming the hand/repositioning the probe and rechecking immediately while keeping the patient at rest, and if still low, alert the provider at once because true hypoxemia needs urgent evaluation; the trap is assuming artifact and ignoring the symptom.

q: You are about to take a patient’s blood pressure over a long-sleeve shirt because the clinic is behind; what is the best action?
a: Ask the patient to expose the upper arm and place the cuff on bare skin because clothing can falsely elevate readings; the trap is prioritizing speed over accuracy.

q: A patient rushes in dizzy and diaphoretic; while you start vitals you notice the radial pulse is very fast and irregular—what is the best first action?
a: Stop the routine intake and have the patient sit/lie down for safety while you get immediate help from the provider/clinical lead because symptoms with an irregular tachycardia can indicate instability; the trap is finishing the full history first.

q: After removing gloves, you plan to apply hand sanitizer but notice visible blood on your fingers; what should you do?
a: Wash with soap and water immediately because sanitizer is less effective on visibly soiled hands; the trap is relying on alcohol rub for all situations.

q: A patient becomes lightheaded during a capillary glucose check in the exam room; what position should you place them in first?
a: Place them supine with legs elevated (if tolerated) to improve perfusion and prevent a fall, then obtain help and reassess; the trap is keeping them seated on the table where they can faint.

q: During intake, a 68-year-old patient says they feel “lightheaded,” and their seated BP is 82/54 with HR 118; they insist they “just need water” and ask you to finish the rest of the vitals quickly—what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the intake, assist the patient to a safe position (supine with legs elevated if tolerated), recheck BP to confirm, and immediately alert the provider/activate the clinic’s emergency response as needed because symptomatic hypotension may indicate shock and the common mistake is leaving the patient upright or delaying escalation to complete routine vitals.

q: An adult has an apical pulse of 52 bpm and denies symptoms, but the chart shows they take a beta-blocker; what should the CMA do next?
a: Document the apical pulse and medication history and report the bradycardia to the provider for clinical correlation because meds can explain it but it still may affect treatment decisions; the trap is labeling it “normal” and not communicating.

q: A patient’s BP is 86/54 and they look pale after standing from the chair for weight; what is the best next step?
a: Assist them back to a seated or supine position and recheck BP/pulse, then notify the provider because hypotension with symptoms risks syncope and falls; the trap is having them “walk it off” or continuing the exam standing.

q: A provider asks you to give an IM injection; the patient states, “I’m allergic to that antibiotic,” but the order matches the chart allergy list you haven’t reviewed yet—what should you do first?
a: Stop and verify the allergy in the EHR and with the patient, then notify the provider before administering because allergy confirmation is a safety priority; the trap is proceeding because the provider already ordered it.

q: A coworker removes a mask by grabbing the front while leaving an isolation room; what should the CMA do to reduce contamination?
a: Remove PPE by handling only straps/ear loops and perform hand hygiene immediately because the front is considered contaminated; the trap is adjusting or touching the mask front and then touching surfaces.

q: You are about to administer an IM injection and the patient is tense and standing; what is the best action to reduce risk of injury?
a: Have the patient sit or lie down with the target muscle relaxed before the injection because muscle tension and standing increase pain and faint/fall risk; the trap is proceeding quickly while they remain standing.

q: You are preparing a sterile dressing change and realize you placed the sterile gauze on the exam table paper; what should you do next?
a: Discard it and open new sterile supplies because the field is contaminated once it touches a nonsterile surface; the trap is using it anyway because “the paper looks clean.”

q: During rooming, a 58-year-old patient says they feel “lightheaded,” and you obtain BP 86/54 and pulse 118 while they are seated; what should the CMA do FIRST before finishing the rest of the intake questions?
a: Assist the patient to a safe supine position with legs elevated and immediately notify the provider/activate help while reassessing vitals, because symptomatic hypotension with tachycardia can signal shock and the trap is continuing routine intake or walking the patient, increasing fall risk and delaying escalation.

q: You enter an exam room to clean after a patient with vomiting and diarrhea; what PPE is most appropriate before starting?
a: Don gloves and a gown (and add mask/eye protection if splash is possible) because contact precautions reduce exposure to body fluids; the trap is using only gloves or skipping PPE because the patient has left.

q: During a fingerstick, the lancet slips and punctures your glove; what is the best immediate action?
a: Encourage bleeding, wash the area with soap and water, then report per exposure protocol and complete incident documentation because prompt decontamination and reporting are time-sensitive; the trap is finishing the rooming process first.

q: Before administering an injection, the patient says, “That’s not my name,” when you call them from the waiting room; what should the CMA do next?
a: Pause and verify at least two identifiers (e.g., full name and DOB) against the chart and wristband/ID, then correct the chart flow before any medication is given because wrong-patient errors are preventable; the trap is relying on the room number or last name only.

q: You are cleaning a small blood spill in an exam room and a patient opens the door asking a scheduling question; what is the best response?
a: Ask them to wait outside and close the door while you complete spill cleanup with appropriate disinfectant and PPE because controlling the area prevents exposure and contamination; the trap is stopping mid-cleanup and talking while the hazard remains.

q: In the lobby, a visitor collapses and is unresponsive; you see normal breathing is absent—what should the CMA do first?
a: Begin CPR and have someone call 911 and bring the AED immediately because early compressions and defibrillation improve survival; the trap is searching for a pulse for an extended time or leaving the patient to find help yourself.

q: A patient returns from the waiting room coughing; you need to collect temperature and pulse oximetry; what PPE is most appropriate to put on first?
a: Perform hand hygiene then don a surgical mask (and eye protection if splash risk) because source control and droplet protection are key; the trap is skipping a mask because it’s “just vitals.”

q: A 6-year-old is anxious and crying during vitals; the automated cuff shows BP 142/90 but the child is moving and the cuff looks large; what is the best next step?
a: Reassess manually after calming the child and using the correct cuff size because inaccurate technique commonly causes falsely high readings; the trap is documenting the number as true hypertension without confirming.

q: A patient returns 10 minutes after a vaccine reporting hives and throat tightness; what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate emergency response (get the provider/bring emergency kit, call EMS per clinic protocol) and monitor airway/breathing because this suggests anaphylaxis requiring immediate intervention; the trap is offering water and asking them to “wait it out.”

q: While taking vitals on a patient with fever, you realize you forgot to perform hand hygiene before touching the patient’s wrist; what should you do next?
a: Stop, perform hand hygiene immediately, and then continue because breaking the chain of infection is priority; the trap is “finishing quickly” and washing only after the encounter.

q: During intake a 52-year-old reports dizziness; you obtain BP 86/54, HR 118, skin cool/clammy, and he says he “took all his BP pills early”; what should the CMA do first?
a: Sit/lay him supine with legs elevated and call for the provider/activate clinic emergency response because these are shock-like findings; the trap is continuing routine intake or letting him stand/walk to an exam room.

q: An adult’s radial pulse is irregular and you count 76 in 30 seconds; what is the correct next action before documenting?
a: Count for a full 60 seconds and report the irregular rhythm to the provider because short counts can miss variability; the trap is multiplying a 30-second count when the rhythm is irregular.

q: While drawing up medication, you notice the vial label and the order don’t match (similar drug names); what is the best action?
a: Pause, recheck the order, and clarify with the provider/pharmacy before preparing/administering because medication-rights safety prevents wrong-drug errors; the trap is assuming it’s a “new generic name.”

q: Immediately after an IM injection, the patient becomes pale, diaphoretic, and says they feel faint; what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist the patient to a safe position (supine or seated with support) and monitor airway/breathing while calling for help because vasovagal syncope can lead to falls; the trap is having them “walk it off.”

q: A patient needs orthostatic vital signs due to lightheadedness; what is the correct sequencing for obtaining them?
a: Measure after the patient rests supine, then sitting, then standing with timed intervals and safety support because sequence and timing affect accuracy and fall prevention; the trap is taking readings back-to-back without stabilization.

q: You are preparing to clean a minor laceration; the patient asks you to “just stitch it”; what is the appropriate CMA response?
a: Explain you can clean and dress the wound but a licensed provider must assess and suture because suturing is outside CMA scope; the trap is attempting closure to “save time.”

q: A provider orders a vaccine for a patient who states they had a severe allergic reaction to the same vaccine in the past; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and notify the provider before administering because potential contraindications require provider decision; the trap is proceeding because the order is in the chart.

q: You are about to give an IM vaccine and notice the needle packaging is damp and partially opened; what should you do?
a: Discard it and obtain a new sterile needle/syringe because sterility is compromised; the trap is using it “since the needle looks clean.”

q: After removing gloves, you notice a small tear in one glove and you had contact with the patient’s drainage; what should you do next?
a: Perform hand hygiene immediately and report/assess for exposure per clinic protocol because glove tears can allow contamination; the trap is assuming gloves fully protected you and skipping hand hygiene.

q: A wound dressing is stuck to a healing abrasion and the patient reports pain when you start to remove it; what is the best next step?
a: Moisten the dressing with sterile saline/warm water to loosen it before removal to avoid tissue damage; the trap is pulling quickly, which can reopen the wound.

q: In the lobby, a family member asks what vaccine the patient is receiving today while the patient is at the front desk completing paperwork; what should the CMA do?
a: Speak privately with the patient and obtain permission before sharing any details because this is protected health information; the trap is answering casually because they appear related.

q: During intake at an urgent care clinic, a 58-year-old patient says he feels lightheaded; you obtain a blood pressure of 82/50 and a pulse of 122, and he looks pale but is still talking—what should the CMA do first?
a: Have the patient sit or lie down safely and immediately alert the provider/activate the clinic’s emergency response while rechecking vitals; hypotension with tachycardia suggests possible shock/syncope risk, and a common trap is continuing routine intake or letting the patient stand/walk to the exam room.

q: During intake you measure an SpO₂ of 88% on a patient with cold hands and dark nail polish who is talking in full sentences; what should you do next?
a: Recheck on a warmed finger/alternate site and ensure proper probe placement, then promptly notify the provider if still low because artifact is common but true hypoxemia is urgent; the trap is documenting 88% without confirming.

q: You find an adult patient in the hallway unresponsive and not breathing normally; what is the first action for a CMA in an outpatient clinic?
a: Activate emergency response (call for help/911 per clinic process) and begin CPR while someone retrieves the AED because early activation and compressions save lives; the trap is searching for a pulse for an extended time or leaving the patient to find equipment alone.

q: During intake, a seated adult’s BP reads 182/112; the patient says they “feel fine” and wants to leave quickly—what should the CMA do first?
a: Recheck the BP manually after 5 minutes of rest with proper cuff/arm positioning and then alert the provider if still elevated, because technique and situational factors can falsely elevate readings and the trap is documenting one high value without confirmation.

q: You enter an exam room and find the sharps container overfilled with needles protruding near the opening; what should you do first?
a: Close/secure the room area and replace the sharps container per safety procedure (or notify the designated staff immediately) because overfilled containers increase needlestick risk; the trap is pushing contents down to “make room.”

q: While cleaning a room after a procedure, you see dried blood on the exam table paper and a small smear on the countertop; what is the best action?
a: Don gloves and disinfect with an EPA-registered disinfectant using proper contact time because blood requires standard precautions and correct dwell time; the trap is wiping quickly with alcohol and moving on.

q: A patient arrives for an injection but you cannot verify identity because the chart has two similar names and the patient says “I’m here all the time”; what should the CMA do?
a: Use two identifiers (e.g., full name and date of birth) and match to the order before administering because identity errors are high-risk; the trap is relying on recognition or room number.

q: A patient becomes dizzy when you stand them to get a weight after fasting labs; what should you do next?
a: Assist the patient back to a seated or supine position and obtain vitals before continuing, because fall prevention is the priority and the trap is trying to “finish quickly” while the patient is unstable.

q: An adult’s radial pulse is irregular when you check vitals for an ECG visit—what should you do next?
a: Count the apical pulse for a full minute and report the irregularity per clinic protocol, because irregular rhythms require apical confirmation and the trap is charting a short radial count that underestimates the true rate.

q: While measuring respirations, the patient starts talking and laughing with you—what is the best action to obtain an accurate rate?
a: Continue counting unobtrusively while appearing to still take the pulse, because awareness alters breathing and the trap is telling the patient you’re counting respirations.

q: During intake at an urgent care clinic, a 64-year-old with diabetes reports dizziness; you obtain vitals and note BP 86/54, pulse 118, RR 22, and the patient becomes pale while seated upright—what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist the patient to a supine position with legs elevated and immediately alert the provider/activate emergency response because these findings suggest possible shock/poor perfusion; the common mistake is continuing the intake or having the patient stand, increasing fall risk and delaying care.

q: You obtain an oral temperature of 101.8°F on a patient scheduled for an in-office steroid injection—what is the best next step?
a: Pause the procedure and notify the provider after confirming the reading (e.g., repeat/verify method), because fever may change treatment timing and the trap is proceeding with an injection despite a potentially infectious process.

q: You are preparing to enter a room for a patient with a draining wound and visible soiling on the bedding—what PPE is the minimum you should don?
a: Gloves at minimum (and add gown/eye protection if splash risk), because standard precautions apply to all body fluids and the trap is using no PPE because it’s “just a dressing change.”

q: A provider asks you to “quickly recap” a used needle before walking it to the sharps container—what is the CMA’s best response?
a: Do not recap; engage the safety device and dispose of it immediately in a sharps container, because recapping is a common cause of needlesticks and the trap is thinking careful recapping is safer than immediate disposal.

q: You finish cleaning an exam table after a patient with diarrhea; what must happen for the disinfectant to work properly?
a: Leave the surface visibly wet for the product’s required contact time, because wiping it dry too soon reduces kill time and the trap is equating “looks clean” with “disinfected.”

q: You’re about to administer a vaccine when the patient says, “I’m allergic to latex and I got hives from a shot years ago”—what should you do first?
a: Stop and clarify the reaction and vaccine history, check product components/packaging, and notify the provider before administering, because allergy screening is part of safe medication administration and the trap is giving the shot because it’s “routine.”

q: You have prepared an IM injection but realize the patient’s name on the syringe label doesn’t match the patient in the room—what is the best action?
a: Do not administer; stop and resolve the identification/labeling discrepancy and prepare a correctly labeled dose, because wrong-patient medication errors are high harm and the trap is assuming the schedule is correct.

q: A patient is due for an IM vaccine but is taking a blood thinner and has a large bruise at a prior injection site—what should the CMA do best before giving the shot?
a: Notify the provider and choose an appropriate site/technique (e.g., firm pressure afterward) per guidance, because anticoagulation increases hematoma risk and the trap is using the bruised area or skipping follow-up instructions.

q: While giving a subcutaneous injection, you feel unexpected resistance and the patient reports sharp burning pain—what should you do next?
a: Stop the injection, withdraw the needle, apply gentle pressure, and report to the provider, because continuing may worsen tissue injury and the trap is “pushing through” to finish the dose.

q: For a patient who feels faint during a fingerstick glucose check, what position is best to place them in first?
a: Supine with legs elevated if possible, because it supports cerebral perfusion and prevents falls, and the trap is keeping them seated “to finish the test.”

q: During a dressing change, you accidentally touch the sterile gauze pad with your ungloved hand—what is the correct next step?
a: Discard the contaminated gauze and obtain a new sterile pad before continuing, because sterility is broken once touched and the trap is using it anyway since it “looks clean.”

q: You are asked to remove sutures from a laceration; the wound edges are slightly separated with yellow drainage—what should you do next?
a: Do not remove the sutures; cover the area and notify the provider immediately, because dehiscence/infection needs evaluation and the trap is proceeding because the order said “suture removal.”

q: The provider orders IM ketorolac; the vial label reads 30 mg/mL and the order is for 15 mg—what volume should the CMA prepare, and what safety step should happen next?
a: Draw up 0.5 mL and have the dose verified per clinic policy before administration, because dose-volume conversion errors are common and the trap is drawing 1 mL because it “looks standard.”

q: After intake, a teen presents for a sports physical with a parent; the teen quietly asks you not to share a sensitive concern with the parent—what should the CMA do best?
a: Explain you’ll protect privacy within clinic policy and state law and involve the provider to discuss confidentiality and consent boundaries, because minors’ privacy rules vary and the trap is promising absolute secrecy or automatically telling the parent.

q: A 6-year-old is anxious and squirming while you attempt an oral temperature; what is the best next step to obtain a safe, accurate vital sign?
a: Switch to a tympanic or temporal method per clinic policy and ensure correct probe placement because movement increases oral reading error and injury risk; the trap is forcing the oral method and recording an unreliable value.

q: A patient arrives for a routine visit wearing a puffy coat and talking on the phone; what should the CMA do before measuring blood pressure for accuracy?
a: Have the patient sit quietly with feet flat, arm supported at heart level, and remove bulky clothing from the arm because improper positioning and clothing falsely elevate readings; the trap is taking BP over a sleeve while the patient is talking.

q: You turn on the AED and it says “analyzing—do not touch the patient,” but another staff member is still holding the patient’s shoulder—what should you do?
a: Instruct everyone to clear and ensure no one is touching the patient before analysis/shock, because contact can interfere with analysis and risk shock to rescuers and the trap is ignoring the warning to “save time.”

q: A patient suddenly becomes unresponsive in the waiting room; what should the CMA do first?
a: Assess responsiveness and breathing and activate emergency response (call for help/EMS and get the AED) while starting CPR if not breathing normally, because time to CPR/AED is critical and the trap is searching for the chart or provider first.

q: While obtaining vitals, a patient says they feel faint as you stand them to measure weight; what is the best immediate action?
a: Assist them back to a seated or supine position and assess responsiveness before continuing because preventing a fall is priority; the trap is insisting they finish the weight to “complete vitals.”

q: You recheck a pulse oximetry reading of 88% on a patient with cold hands but no distress; what should the CMA do next?
a: Warm the hand/reposition the probe and verify waveform, then reassess and notify the provider if it remains low because poor perfusion causes false lows; the trap is documenting 88% as true hypoxemia without troubleshooting.

q: During intake, a 58-year-old reports dizziness and you obtain BP 84/52 and pulse 124; the provider is running behind—what should the CMA do first?
a: Keep the patient seated or supine and immediately alert the provider/activate clinic emergency protocol because hypotension with tachycardia suggests possible shock; the trap is continuing the intake or sending the patient to the waiting room.

q: You place a patient in supine for an exam and they become short of breath; what should the CMA do first?
a: Raise the head of the exam table to Fowler’s position and reassess because positioning can quickly improve breathing; the trap is leaving them flat while you “go get the provider.”

q: A patient with a known latex allergy is scheduled for an injection and the only gloves in the room are powdered latex; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and obtain non-latex gloves/supplies before proceeding because avoiding exposure prevents an allergic reaction; the trap is “being careful” but using latex anyway.

q: A patient with a draining wound arrives without a dressing and sits in the waiting area; what should the CMA do first to reduce transmission risk?
a: Provide a clean dressing/covering and move them to an exam room as soon as possible because source control interrupts the chain of infection; the trap is leaving the wound uncovered while you finish check-in.

q: You are preparing to administer an IM vaccine and the patient asks to use the restroom first; what should the CMA do with the drawn-up syringe?
a: Discard it and prepare a new dose when the patient returns because unattended prepared medication risks mix-ups and contamination; the trap is setting the labeled syringe on the counter “just for a minute.”

q: Right before an injection, the patient states they had a severe reaction to a similar medication years ago but “can’t remember which one”; what is the best next step?
a: Hold the medication and notify the provider to verify allergy history before administration because preventing anaphylaxis is priority; the trap is proceeding because the allergy list in the chart looks incomplete.

q: After cleaning an exam room, you notice dried blood on the counter near where supplies are stored; what is the best action?
a: Don appropriate PPE and disinfect with an EPA-registered disinfectant using proper contact time because blood requires standard precautions and correct dwell time; the trap is wiping quickly with alcohol and immediately setting clean supplies there.

q: A coworker removes gloves after a fingerstick but skips hand hygiene because “I wore gloves”; what should the CMA do?
a: Perform hand hygiene and remind/educate that gloves do not replace hand hygiene because contamination can occur during glove removal; the trap is assuming glove use alone prevents transmission.

q: The provider orders 0.5 mL of a medication, but the vial concentration and your calculation indicate the drawn volume would be 5 mL; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and clarify the order with the provider before preparing/administering because the dose appears unsafe/unreasonable; the trap is assuming a large volume is correct and giving it anyway.

q: While changing a dressing, you accidentally touch the sterile gauze to the patient’s clothing; what should the CMA do?
a: Discard the contaminated gauze and replace it with a new sterile dressing because sterility is broken once it touches a nonsterile surface; the trap is using it anyway because “it still looks clean.”

q: A patient arrives for suture removal but the wound edges are red, warm, and draining; what should the CMA do next?
a: Do not remove sutures independently and promptly notify the provider because signs suggest infection/dehiscence risk and requires clinical evaluation; the trap is proceeding with removal because it’s “scheduled.”

q: In the lobby, a patient suddenly collapses and is unresponsive; what is the CMA’s first action?
a: Check responsiveness and breathing and activate emergency response (call 911/bring AED per clinic protocol) because rapid recognition and activation precede CPR/AED use; the trap is immediately searching for a pulse and delaying action.

q: You are about to give a subcutaneous injection and notice the medication label looks similar to another drug stored beside it; what should the CMA do to follow medication rights?
a: Compare the medication label to the order and patient identifiers again (right drug/right dose/right route/right time/right patient) before administering because look-alike packaging causes errors; the trap is relying on where it was stored as “proof.”

q: You apply an AED and it announces “shock advised” while another staff member is still touching the patient; what should the CMA do next?
a: Loudly state “clear,” ensure no one is touching the patient, then deliver the shock because contact during shock risks injury and reduces effectiveness; the trap is pressing shock quickly without visually confirming everyone is clear.

q: During intake, a 58-year-old reports “crushing chest pressure” and you obtain BP 88/54, pulse 124, RR 24, SpO₂ 90% on room air; what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate the clinic’s emergency response (call for help/EMS per protocol) and keep the patient seated/resting while alerting the provider because these are unstable vitals suggestive of shock/cardiac emergency; the trap is continuing the full intake or having the patient walk to an exam room.

q: A patient becomes pale and sweaty immediately after a vaccination and says, “I’m going to pass out”; what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist them to a supine position with legs elevated and stay with them while calling for help because vasovagal syncope can lead to injury; the trap is walking them to the lobby for water.

q: The provider requests help positioning a patient for a rectal exam in an outpatient room; what position should the CMA use?
a: Assist the patient into Sims’ (left lateral) position for best access and comfort because it aligns anatomy and preserves modesty; the trap is using supine, which is less appropriate and increases discomfort.

q: A patient arrives coughing with fever and asks to sit in the crowded waiting area while you “finish the chart”—what should the CMA do next?
a: Provide a mask, perform hand hygiene, and promptly separate/room the patient (or place at distance) using standard precautions because early source control breaks transmission; the trap is delaying PPE/actions until after registration.

q: A provider orders PT/INR, CMP, and CBC, and the CMA has light blue, gold, and lavender tubes ready; what is the correct order of draw?
a: Draw light blue first, then gold, then lavender, because coagulation testing must be collected before serum/EDTA tubes and a common trap is drawing lavender early which can contaminate and alter clotting results.

q: After removing gloves used for a wound dressing change, your hands look clean and you’re about to type in the EHR—what is the correct action?
a: Perform hand hygiene immediately after glove removal because gloves are not a substitute and contamination can occur during doffing; the trap is touching the keyboard/phone first and spreading pathogens.

q: You are preparing an IM vaccine and the patient states they have a history of anaphylaxis to a prior dose; the order is already in the chart—what should the CMA do?
a: Stop and verify with the provider before administering because a reported severe allergy is a safety stop despite an existing order; the trap is proceeding because “the provider ordered it” or because the patient is due today.

q: While drawing up medication for an injection, you notice the vial’s label concentration does not match what you expected from the order (e.g., different mg/mL) but you haven’t injected yet—what is the best next step?
a: Pause and re-clarify the order/concentration with the provider/pharmacy reference and re-calculate before giving the dose because concentration mismatches are a common cause of dosing errors; the trap is “making it work” by guessing or adjusting after the injection.

q: While preparing to draw blood, the CMA notices the requisition says “fasting lipid panel,” but the patient mentions they had breakfast 30 minutes ago; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and clarify with the ordering provider or follow clinic protocol to reschedule/annotate before drawing, because collecting a non-fasting specimen can invalidate results and a common trap is drawing anyway and “just noting it later.”

q: You are rooming a patient and recheck an initial BP of 168/102; the repeat after 5 minutes is 166/100, and the patient denies symptoms—what is the best next step?
a: Notify the provider and document both readings, method, and arm used because persistent severe hypertension needs provider evaluation even without symptoms; the trap is charting only the “better” number or giving lifestyle counseling as if that resolves the immediate finding.

q: A patient becomes unresponsive and pulseless in the exam room while the provider is with another patient—what should the CMA do first?
a: Start CPR immediately and have someone call 911 and bring the AED because early compressions and rapid defibrillation are the priority in cardiac arrest; the trap is searching for vitals/history first or waiting for the provider to arrive.

q: A patient takes a daily anticoagulant and continues oozing after the draw despite brief pressure; what is the best action?
a: Apply firm pressure longer and use a pressure dressing as needed, then reassess before discharge, because anticoagulants increase bleeding risk and a common trap is sending them out with minimal pressure once the tube is filled.

q: A CMA draws blood and realizes they forgot to cleanse the site with antiseptic first; what is the best next step?
a: Discard the specimen and perform a new venipuncture with proper skin antisepsis, because contamination risk is increased and a common trap is sending the sample anyway since “it looks fine.”

q: The patient’s name on the tube label is “Jon Smyth,” but the patient states their legal name is “John Smith”; what should the CMA do before sending the specimen?
a: Stop and resolve identification using two identifiers and relabel per protocol in the patient’s presence, because mislabeled specimens are rejected and a common trap is “fixing it later” away from the patient.

q: After venipuncture, the puncture site begins to swell and bruise rapidly; what should the CMA do next?
a: Release the tourniquet, withdraw the needle, and apply firm pressure with the arm straight, because this suggests a hematoma and a common trap is bending the elbow, which can worsen bleeding and bruising.

q: After collecting a lavender-top tube for CBC, the CMA sets it on the counter and sees small clots later; what should have been done immediately after collection?
a: Gently invert the tube the recommended number of times right away, because anticoagulant tubes must be mixed to prevent clotting and a common trap is shaking vigorously, which can hemolyze the sample.

q: During phlebotomy, the CMA cannot palpate a vein well and considers using the same arm with an IV infusion running; what should the CMA do?
a: Choose an alternate site/arm and avoid drawing above an active IV when possible, because IV fluids can dilute or contaminate the specimen and a common trap is using the easiest visible vein despite accuracy issues.

q: A patient becomes pale and says they feel faint during a blood draw; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the draw, remove the tourniquet and needle, and assist the patient to a safe position (supine or head-down as appropriate), because preventing a fall is priority and a common trap is trying to “finish the tube” before addressing syncope.

q: During venipuncture, blood stops flowing into an evacuated tube after initially filling; what should the CMA do first?
a: Reposition the needle slightly and check tube engagement before re-sticking, because the bevel may be against the vein wall and a common trap is immediately removing the needle and attempting multiple sticks unnecessarily.

q: A provider asks the CMA to interpret an EKG as “normal” for a patient complaint of chest pressure; what is the appropriate response?
a: State that interpretation is provider responsibility and promptly ensure the EKG is obtained and given to the provider for review, because CMAs do not diagnose and a common trap is offering reassurance based on limited training.

q: During EKG setup, the CMA places the limb electrodes on the wrists and ankles and gets a lot of motion artifact as the patient shifts; what is the best adjustment?
a: Place limb electrodes on the torso (per facility practice) to reduce motion artifact while maintaining correct lead orientation, because distal placement increases movement interference and a common trap is repeatedly reprinting without correcting placement.

q: A urine specimen for culture is brought to the front desk unlabeled, and the patient has already left; what should the CMA do?
a: Reject the specimen and request a recollect with proper labeling, because unlabeled specimens cannot be verified and a common trap is labeling it based on the appointment schedule.

q: The CMA completes venipuncture and notices the tourniquet has been on for over 2 minutes while searching for a vein; what is the best next step before another attempt?
a: Release the tourniquet and allow circulation to normalize before reapplying for a new attempt, because prolonged stasis can alter results and a common trap is keeping it on while continuing to troubleshoot.

q: The CMA is preparing a 12-lead EKG and the patient is shivering and talking on the phone; the tracing shows jagged baseline; what should the CMA do first?
a: Address artifact by warming and positioning the patient and asking them to remain still/stop talking before repeating the tracing, because muscle movement mimics abnormal rhythms and a common trap is printing and sending a poor-quality strip.

q: A provider requests blood cultures and a CMP from the same venipuncture; what should the CMA do first to reduce contamination risk?
a: Collect blood cultures first using strict aseptic technique before other tubes, because preventing skin flora contamination is critical and a common trap is drawing routine tubes first and then “adding cultures.”

q: A patient’s EKG shows a flat line in one lead, but the patient is alert and talking; what should the CMA do next?
a: Check that electrode and lead wire connection and replace the electrode if needed, because this is most likely a loose lead artifact and a common trap is treating it as true asystole without troubleshooting.

q: While obtaining a capillary fingerstick glucose, the CMA squeezes the fingertip repeatedly to get more blood; what should the CMA do instead?
a: Wipe away the first drop and allow free-flowing blood with minimal pressure, because excessive squeezing can dilute with tissue fluid and a common trap is “milking” the finger to speed collection.

q: A provider orders a fasting lipid panel, but the patient admits they ate breakfast an hour ago and asks you to “just draw it now”; what should the CMA do?
a: Clarify and follow clinic protocol—typically reschedule or notify the provider before drawing because the result may be inaccurate; the trap is drawing without documenting/communicating the non-fasting status.

q: A CLIA-waived rapid strep test is negative, but the control indicator did not change as expected; what should the CMA do?
a: Do not report the result and repeat the test with a new kit and proper QC, because an invalid control means the test is unreliable and a common trap is documenting “negative” anyway due to symptoms.

q: You are about to draw blood and the patient says they fainted during their last blood draw; what is the best preparation before you start?
a: Have the patient lie down (or recline) and ensure safety measures (call light, observation) because prior syncope increases risk; the trap is proceeding with the patient seated and unattended.

q: During an outpatient venipuncture, the patient says “I feel dizzy” and becomes pale while you’re filling the first tube; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the draw, remove the tourniquet and needle, and assist the patient to a safe position (recline/legs elevated) because preventing syncope injury is priority; the trap is trying to “just finish the tubes” before addressing symptoms.

q: After drawing a lavender-top tube for a CBC, you notice you forgot to label it and another patient has just been roomed; what is the best next step?
a: Do not guess—discard and recollect with proper labeling at the patient’s side because unlabeled specimens are unacceptable for patient safety; the trap is labeling later from memory.

q: While collecting a basic metabolic panel, you vigorously shake the green-top tube to “mix it faster”; what should you do next when you notice foaming?
a: Notify the lab/your supervisor and recollect if needed because vigorous shaking can hemolyze the sample and alter results; the trap is sending it anyway hoping it “runs fine.”

q: You have an order for blood cultures, PT/INR, CMP, and CBC in the same visit; what is the correct collection sequence the CMA should follow?
a: Collect blood cultures first, then light blue (citrate), then serum/SST, then lavender (EDTA) because order of draw prevents additive carryover; the trap is drawing CBC before PT and contaminating coag studies.

q: At the start of the day, the CMA runs glucometer quality control and the control value is out of range; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop patient testing, troubleshoot per manufacturer instructions (new strip lot, control solution, calibration/cleaning) and document, because out-of-range QC invalidates patient results and a common trap is testing patients first and “fixing QC later.”

q: During a venipuncture for a CMP and CBC, you draw the tubes in the wrong order and fill the lavender (EDTA) before the serum separator tube; what should the CMA do next to best protect specimen integrity?
a: Stop and recollect using the correct order of draw with new tubes and a new venipuncture site if possible, because EDTA carryover can falsely alter chemistry results (common trap: just sending the specimens anyway or swapping labels, which does not fix contamination).

q: An SST tube is drawn for a chemistry panel, but it was placed in the rack and never inverted; what is the best next step?
a: Gently invert it the recommended number of times as soon as noticed and document/communicate if delayed because proper mixing affects clot activation/serum quality; the trap is shaking it hard to “catch up.”

q: You placed limb leads for an EKG and the machine flags “lead reversal suspected”; what should the CMA do next?
a: Pause and verify correct lead placement/color coding and re-run the EKG because reversed leads can mimic cardiac pathology; the trap is sending the tracing to the provider without correcting placement.

q: While setting up a 12-lead EKG, the patient’s chest is sweaty and electrodes keep lifting; what is the best action?
a: Clean and dry the skin (and lightly abrade if allowed) before reapplying electrodes because poor contact causes artifact; the trap is pressing harder or adding tape without skin prep.

q: You’re collecting a urine specimen for culture and the patient hands you a cup that was filled at home this morning; what should you do next?
a: Request a new specimen collected per instructions (clean-catch, timely transport) because old urine can alter bacterial growth results; the trap is accepting it to avoid inconveniencing the patient.

q: You need a capillary glucose and the patient’s fingers are cold after being outside; what should you do before puncturing?
a: Warm the site and let the arm hang down to improve capillary flow because squeezing/cold fingers can dilute the sample; the trap is “milking” the finger to get enough blood.

q: A patient on dialysis has a prominent AV fistula in the left arm and offers that arm because it’s “easier”; what should the CMA do?
a: Use the other arm (or consult for an alternative site) because venipuncture over an AV fistula can damage access; the trap is using it since it looks like a good vein.

q: An EKG prints with a shaky baseline in all leads, and you notice the patient is talking and shivering; what should the CMA do first?
a: Coach the patient to lie still, relax, and warm them if needed before repeating because muscle movement causes artifact; the trap is immediately repositioning all electrodes without addressing motion.

q: A patient asks you to interpret their EKG saying, “Is this a heart attack?” right after you print it; what is the best response?
a: Tell them you can’t interpret results and promptly notify the provider that the EKG is ready because interpretation is outside CMA scope; the trap is reassuring or speculating based on the printout.

q: You run a waived urine dipstick and the bottle indicates it must be read at specific times, but the clinic gets busy; what is the best practice?
a: Use a timer and read each parameter at the specified interval because timing errors cause false results; the trap is “reading it all at once” after a delay and documenting anyway.

q: During venipuncture a patient says, “I feel dizzy,” becomes pale, and starts sliding down the chair while you are filling the second tube; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, apply pressure, and position the patient safely (supine with legs elevated if possible) because preventing injury from syncope is the priority; the common trap is trying to “finish the tubes” before addressing the reaction.

q: A coworker hands you opened POCT reagent strips that were left uncapped on the counter; what should you do before using them on a patient?
a: Do not use them—discard and open a properly stored container because exposure can degrade reagents and skew results; the trap is using them to avoid waste.

q: After a fingerstick hemoglobin POCT, you realize the device’s daily QC was not documented today; what should the CMA do next?
a: Hold reporting the patient result until QC is completed/verified and notify the appropriate staff because CLIA-waived testing still requires QC to ensure accuracy; the trap is entering the value in the chart and “doing QC later.”

q: During an outpatient EKG, the patient reports new chest pressure and looks diaphoretic; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the test and alert the provider/activate emergency response per clinic protocol because new concerning symptoms require immediate escalation; the trap is finishing the tracing “for documentation” before calling for help.

q: You are performing a CLIA-waived rapid strep test and the control line fails to appear; what should the CMA do next?
a: Treat it as an invalid test, repeat with a new device/sample per instructions, and document QC issues because results can’t be reported without a valid control; the trap is reporting “negative” because no test line appeared.

q: You are collecting blood cultures, a light blue tube, and a serum tube from one venipuncture; what is the correct order of draw?
a: Blood cultures first, then light blue, then serum (red/gold) because culture contamination and citrate tube additive carryover can alter results; a common trap is drawing the blue tube after serum “because it clots.”

q: While preparing to draw blood, the patient says they are on warfarin and “always bleed a lot”; after removing the needle, what is the best action?
a: Hold firm pressure longer than usual and confirm bleeding has stopped before bandaging because anticoagulants increase bleeding risk; the trap is using the standard brief pressure time and letting the patient leave still oozing.

q: You are about to perform a venipuncture and notice the requisition has the correct patient name but the wrong date of birth compared with the patient’s ID; what should you do first?
a: Stop and resolve the identity discrepancy before collecting because mislabeled/misidentified specimens are a major safety event; the trap is drawing “now” and fixing paperwork later.

q: After drawing a lavender-top tube for CBC, you notice the tube was not mixed and small clots are forming; what is the best action?
a: Reject and recollect the specimen (following facility process) because clotted EDTA samples can falsely alter counts and cannot be fixed by shaking later; the trap is vigorously shaking to “break up” clots, which also causes hemolysis.

q: You drew a green-top tube for a CMP and accidentally left it on the counter for an hour before sending; the test requires plasma separation; what is the best next step?
a: Follow lab policy for delayed processing (often recollect) because prolonged contact with cells can change analytes like potassium/glucose; the trap is spinning “whenever you remember” and assuming results are still valid.

q: After a difficult venipuncture, the patient develops a rapidly growing bruise at the site; what should the CMA do next?
a: Release the tourniquet (if still on), withdraw the needle if present, and apply firm pressure/ice as directed because this indicates hematoma formation; the trap is continuing to probe or immediately bandaging without sustained pressure.

q: A patient’s hand is clenched and pumping during the draw to “make the vein pop,” and you are collecting potassium; what should the CMA instruct?
a: Ask the patient to relax the hand and avoid pumping because muscle activity can falsely elevate potassium; the trap is encouraging fist pumping to speed the draw.

q: A patient with a history of mastectomy on the right side needs routine labs; the left arm has an IV from a prior visit dressing still in place; what should the CMA do?
a: Use the left arm away from the old IV site if appropriate and avoid the mastectomy side because lymphatic disruption increases complication risk; the trap is choosing the mastectomy arm because the other arm “looks harder.”

q: A provider orders PT/INR and you fill a light blue tube only halfway because the vein stopped flowing; what should the CMA do next?
a: Recollect with a properly filled light blue tube because underfilling changes the blood-to-anticoagulant ratio and can falsely prolong clotting times; the trap is sending it anyway since “some blood is better than none.”

q: You need a clean-catch urine for culture and the patient hands you a cup filled to the top with no label; what is the best next step?
a: Verify patient identity, label the specimen immediately in the patient’s presence, and assess if collection was midstream/clean-catch—recollect if technique is incorrect because culture results are highly contamination-sensitive; the trap is labeling later at the desk or accepting a non-clean-catch for culture.

q: During venipuncture for a CMP and a CBC, the CMA draws the lavender EDTA tube first and then the green heparin tube and notices the lavender tube is underfilled; what is the best next action?
a: Stop and recollect the specimens using the correct order of draw (green before lavender) with properly filled tubes, because additive carryover and underfilling can alter results (a common mistake is sending the mislabeled/poor-quality draw “to see if the lab can run it”).

q: Before running CLIA-waived rapid strep tests, you notice the test kit box is expired by one month; the patient is already swabbed; what should you do?
a: Do not run the expired kit—obtain a non-expired kit or send a lab test per protocol because expired reagents can give false results; the trap is running it “since the swab is already collected.”

q: Halfway through an EKG you realize you placed the limb electrodes on the torso to save time, and the provider needs an accurate diagnostic tracing; what is the best action?
a: Stop and place electrodes in correct limb locations and repeat the EKG because torso placement can alter interpretation; the trap is printing and sending it anyway because “it’s close enough.”

q: You are obtaining a 12-lead EKG and the tracing shows heavy wandering baseline while the patient is talking and shivering; what should the CMA do first?
a: Instruct the patient to lie still and warm them (blanket) before repeating because muscle tremor and movement cause artifact; the trap is immediately repositioning leads repeatedly without addressing patient motion.

q: You perform a fingerstick glucose POCT and the reading is “HI” on a symptomatic patient; what is the CMA’s best next action?
a: Repeat per protocol to confirm (new strip, proper technique) and immediately report the critical/high result to the provider because “HI” can indicate dangerous hyperglycemia requiring prompt evaluation; the trap is only documenting it or trying to counsel the patient as if you can manage treatment.

q: While placing chest leads for a 12-lead EKG on a patient with dense chest hair, electrodes keep lifting and the tracing is noisy; what should the CMA do next?
a: Prep the skin (clip hair if allowed, clean/dry, mild abrasion) and replace electrodes because poor contact causes artifact; the trap is pressing harder or adding gel to failing electrodes without proper skin prep.

q: A provider orders a fasting lipid panel and the patient admits they drank coffee with cream an hour ago; what should the CMA do next?
a: Notify the provider/clinical lead and document the non-fasting status before collecting or rescheduling because dietary intake can invalidate fasting-dependent results; the trap is drawing anyway and hoping the lab “will adjust.”

q: After drawing several tubes, you realize you labeled them at the nurses’ station instead of in the room; what is the correct action?
a: Do not submit the specimens and follow the facility mislabeling policy (typically recollect) because labeling must occur in the patient’s presence using two identifiers; the trap is “fixing” labels from memory, which risks wrong-patient errors.

q: A patient asks for their printed lab results at checkout while the waiting room is crowded, and you can see names on other papers at the front desk; what should the CMA do first?
a: Move the conversation/documents to a private area and verify identity/authorization before releasing results because protecting PHI is required even in routine workflows; the trap is handing results over the counter where others can see or hear.

q: While collecting a PT/INR, you fill the light blue tube only halfway because the vein collapses; what is the best next step?
a: Discard and recollect a fully filled light blue tube to the required fill line because the blood-to-anticoagulant ratio must be exact; the trap is topping it off later or sending a short draw that yields false clotting times.

q: A fasting glucose is ordered, but the patient says they drank orange juice in the car; the provider is running behind—what should the CMA do next?
a: Notify the provider and document the intake before collecting because the result may be invalid and rescheduling may be needed; the trap is drawing anyway to “save time” and producing misleading data.

q: During venipuncture for a CBC and BMP, you accidentally draw the lavender tube first and then the green tube; what should you do next?
a: Stop and redraw using a new set of tubes in the correct order of draw because additive carryover can alter results; the trap is sending “good-looking” tubes anyway and causing inaccurate potassium/calcium values.

q: A provider orders blood cultures and a CBC; the patient is seated and ready—what should the CMA do first to reduce contamination?
a: Perform skin antisepsis per protocol and collect blood cultures before other tubes because cultures require strict asepsis and are drawn first to avoid contamination; the trap is drawing routine tubes first and then “going back” to cultures.

q: You draw a gold SST for a lipid panel and immediately place it in the centrifuge without letting it sit; what should you do next?
a: Stop and allow the SST to clot for the recommended time before centrifuging because premature spinning can create fibrin strands and incorrect results; the trap is assuming all serum tubes can be spun right away.

q: You complete an outpatient EKG and the machine interpretation flags “acute MI,” but the patient is stable and waiting; what should the CMA do next?
a: Immediately alert the provider and follow urgent escalation protocol because machine reads can indicate a time-sensitive emergency and the CMA should not interpret or dismiss it; the trap is assuming it’s “just artifact” and filing it for later review.

q: When obtaining a capillary fingerstick for glucose, you squeeze the fingertip repeatedly to get more blood; what should you do instead?
a: Use a gentle “milk” motion after wiping the first drop because excessive squeezing dilutes the specimen with tissue fluid and skews results; the trap is thinking more pressure equals a better sample.

q: A patient on the phlebotomy chair suddenly reports tingling shooting down the arm when you insert the needle; what should you do next?
a: Stop the draw and remove the needle immediately, then apply pressure and report per protocol because this may indicate nerve involvement; the trap is “repositioning” and risking nerve injury.

q: You cannot palpate a vein in the antecubital area and the patient suggests using the same arm with an IV line running; what should the CMA do?
a: Choose an alternate site/arm or seek assistance rather than drawing above an active IV because IV fluids can dilute specimens and alter results; the trap is using the IV arm “just this once” for convenience.

q: During an outpatient EKG, the tracing shows a wandering baseline and the patient is shivering in a cold room; what should the CMA do first?
a: Warm/cover the patient and ask them to relax and remain still, then repeat the tracing because muscle tremor commonly causes artifact; the trap is immediately troubleshooting the machine or repositioning all leads without addressing patient factors.

q: After collecting a lavender EDTA tube, the CMA sets it upright without mixing because the patient is impatient; what should be done?
a: Gently invert the tube the required number of times immediately because inadequate mixing can cause microclots and inaccurate CBC results; the trap is shaking vigorously, which can hemolyze the sample.

q: A urine culture is ordered and the patient hands you an unlabeled cup from the restroom sink; what is the best action?
a: Do not accept it and have the patient provide a new properly labeled specimen after confirming identifiers because sink-side specimens risk mix-ups and contamination; the trap is labeling it afterward based on who is “probably” in the room.

q: Mid-draw, the patient becomes pale and says they feel faint; what should the CMA do first?
a: Immediately remove the tourniquet and needle, apply pressure, and assist the patient to a safe position (reclined/supine) because preventing injury from syncope is priority; the trap is trying to “finish the tube” before addressing safety.

q: After venipuncture, a hematoma begins swelling at the site while blood is still flowing; what is the best next step?
a: Release the tourniquet, withdraw the needle, and apply firm pressure because continued bleeding into tissue worsens the hematoma; the trap is redirecting the needle or continuing the draw.

q: An EKG printout shows a flatline in one lead but normal complexes in the others; what is the best next step?
a: Check that specific electrode/lead wire connection and skin contact, then repeat the EKG because a loose lead commonly causes a single-lead failure; the trap is reporting as asystole or a clinical emergency without verifying artifact.

q: A CLIA-waived urine dipstick bottle was left uncapped overnight and a provider requests immediate testing; what is the best action?
a: Discard and replace the strips (and run QC if required) because exposure to air/moisture degrades reagents and invalidates results; the trap is using them to avoid delay and documenting “normal” findings.

q: During venipuncture, blood stops flowing into a vacuum tube after a good initial flash and the patient’s arm is still—what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Reposition the needle slightly (pull back a millimeter or adjust angle) while keeping it stable because the bevel may be against the vein wall; the trap is “digging” or fishing, which increases hematoma risk.

q: A provider orders CBC, BMP, PT/INR, and a lactate; the CMA has a butterfly set and tubes on the tray—what order of draw should the CMA use?
a: Draw blood cultures first (if ordered), then light blue, then serum (red/gold), then green, then lavender, then gray because correct order prevents additive carryover (common trap: drawing lavender before light blue can falsely prolong coag results).

q: You are preparing for a 12-lead EKG on a patient with a hairy chest and oily skin; what should you do to improve electrode adherence?
a: Clean and dry the skin and clip hair as needed before applying electrodes because poor contact causes artifact and repeat testing; the trap is placing electrodes over hair/oil and blaming the machine for noise.

q: While performing a 12-lead EKG, the patient asks, “Does this mean I’m having a heart attack?” after seeing the monitor; how should the CMA respond?
a: Explain that the EKG records heart electrical activity and the provider will interpret the results, and promptly relay symptoms/concerns if present because interpretation is outside CMA scope; the trap is reassuring or diagnosing based on the tracing.

q: A patient’s point-of-care hemoglobin result seems inconsistent with their prior value, but the patient feels fine; what should the CMA do next?
a: Repeat the test following proper technique and QC checks and report the discrepancy per protocol because POCT errors (sample/strip/device) are common; the trap is charting the unexpected value without verification or acting as if it is a diagnosis.

q: Your clinic’s CLIA-waived strep test control result is out of range at the start of the day; what should the CMA do next?
a: Do not test patients, troubleshoot per manufacturer instructions (new reagents/controls, storage checks), and notify the supervisor if unresolved because reporting patient results with failed QC is unsafe; the trap is running patients anyway “since it usually works.”

q: Immediately after a blood draw, a patient becomes pale and says, “I feel dizzy,” with eyes rolling upward—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, activate safety, and assist the patient to a safe position (supine with legs elevated if possible) because preventing injury is priority; the trap is trying to finish filling the tube.

q: After drawing a lavender-top tube for CBC, the CMA is about to place it in the rack—what should the CMA do to the tube FIRST?
a: Gently invert the tube the recommended number of times immediately because EDTA must mix to prevent clotting; the trap is vigorous shaking, which can hemolyze the sample.

q: While collecting a CMP and CBC, the CMA realizes the SST tube was filled only halfway and already inverted once—what is the BEST action?
a: Discard and recollect the SST to the proper fill because incorrect blood-to-additive ratio can alter results; the trap is “topping off” from another tube, which is contamination and not allowed.

q: A CMA collects a throat swab for rapid strep at POCT but sets it down unlabeled because the EHR printer jammed—what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Do not test it; re-collect with proper patient identification and labeling because unlabeled specimens are rejected for safety; the trap is labeling from memory after the fact.

q: A provider orders a timed 2-hour postprandial glucose and the patient arrives early asking to be drawn now—what should the CMA do?
a: Verify the exact timing from the patient’s meal start/end and schedule the draw for the ordered time because timed tests require accuracy; the trap is drawing early “to help the schedule,” which invalidates the result.

q: A patient’s requisition says fasting lipid panel, but the patient reports eating breakfast an hour ago; the waiting room is full—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Pause the draw and notify the provider or follow clinic protocol to reschedule because a non-fasting specimen can invalidate results; the trap is collecting anyway and “noting it” after, which may waste a redraw.

q: A urine specimen for culture sits at room temperature on the counter for over an hour before transport—what should the CMA do?
a: Refrigerate promptly and follow lab policy for acceptability or recollect if required because bacterial overgrowth can alter culture results; the trap is sending it unrefrigerated and hoping the lab “fixes it.”

q: A patient’s arm develops swelling and bruising during venipuncture—what is the CMA’s BEST next step?
a: Release the tourniquet, withdraw the needle, and apply firm pressure for at least several minutes because this is likely a hematoma; the trap is continuing to draw or immediately applying a bandage without pressure.

q: A CLIA-waived rapid influenza test kit was left out past its room-temperature stability time, but controls “usually pass”—what should the CMA do?
a: Discard the compromised kit and use an in-date, properly stored kit because storage errors can produce false results; the trap is running the test anyway because it “might be fine.”

q: The CMA completes a 12-lead EKG but sees a wandering baseline in multiple leads while the patient is shivering—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Warm and relax the patient (blanket, reduce muscle tension) and repeat the tracing because muscle artifact commonly causes baseline wander; the trap is repositioning all electrodes without addressing tremor.

q: During EKG setup, the CMA notices the patient has a hairy chest and electrodes keep lifting—what is the BEST next step?
a: Clean and dry the skin and clip/shave small patches as needed for electrode contact because poor adhesion causes artifact; the trap is pressing harder or adding gel without improving skin prep.

q: An EKG prints “leads off” and Lead II is flat, but the patient denies symptoms—what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Check cable connections and electrode placement/adhesion for the affected lead and rerun the EKG because this is usually a technical issue; the trap is documenting it as an abnormal rhythm.

q: While placing precordial leads, the CMA is unsure of V1 and V2 landmarks and the provider is waiting—what should the CMA do BEST?
a: Pause and re-identify landmarks (4th intercostal space at right and left sternal border) before recording because incorrect placement can mimic pathology; the trap is guessing to save time, creating a misleading EKG.

q: While performing a fingerstick glucose, the CMA prepares to puncture the center of the fingertip for “more blood”—what is the BEST correction?
a: Use the lateral side of the fingertip and wipe away the first drop because it improves blood flow and reduces tissue-fluid contamination; the trap is squeezing hard, which can falsely lower results.

q: A patient says they took aspirin today and “bleed easily,” and after venipuncture the site continues oozing—what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Maintain direct pressure longer and reassess before bandaging because prolonged bleeding requires extended pressure; the trap is applying a small adhesive bandage quickly and sending the patient out.

q: A patient with a mastectomy on the right side and an active IV on the left needs routine labs—what should the CMA do BEST?
a: Notify the provider and follow clinic guidance to select the safest alternative site (often avoiding the mastectomy side and not drawing above an IV) because both sides have risks; the trap is drawing from the IV arm “below the IV” without authorization.

q: A urine pregnancy POCT is negative, but the patient insists she is pregnant and reports a missed period and nausea—what should the CMA do BEST within scope?
a: Report the result to the provider and document timing/collection details because early pregnancy or dilute urine can cause false negatives; the trap is reassuring the patient definitively or advising treatment based on the POCT alone.

q: A provider orders PT/INR, CMP, and CBC; the CMA has light blue, red/gold, and lavender tubes ready—what is the correct order of draw?
a: Draw light blue first, then serum tube (red/gold), then lavender because coagulation tubes must be collected before tubes that can contaminate with additives; a common trap is drawing lavender before blue and skewing clotting results.

q: During venipuncture for a CBC and CMP, the patient says, “I’m going to pass out,” becomes pale, and slumps in the chair—what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, and assist the patient into a safe position (recline with legs elevated) because syncope is an immediate safety risk; a common trap is trying to “finish the last tube” and causing a fall injury.

q: Immediately after removing the needle, a hematoma begins to form at the venipuncture site—what should the CMA do next?
a: Apply firm direct pressure and elevate the arm, then document and select a different site for any redraw because continued bleeding causes tissue damage; a common trap is placing a bandage only and letting the patient leave.

q: A patient with small veins has a slow blood flow with a butterfly set and the CMA switches collection tubes mid-draw—what should the CMA do to prevent inaccurate coag results when a light blue tube is among the orders?
a: Use a discard tube before filling the light blue tube because butterfly tubing contains air that can underfill the citrate tube; a common trap is skipping the discard and ending up with a short draw.

q: During a fasting CMP and CBC draw, the CMA accidentally collects the light blue citrate tube after the lavender EDTA tube and notices a small amount of lavender additive may have backflowed into the blue tube; what is the best next step before sending specimens to the lab?
a: Discard and recollect the light blue tube using the correct order of draw (blood cultures, light blue, serum, green, lavender, gray) because EDTA contamination can alter coagulation results, and the common mistake is “sending it anyway” since it was only a small backflow.

q: After collecting a light blue tube for PT/INR, the CMA notices the tube is only half full—what is the best next action?
a: Recollect the specimen with a properly filled light blue tube because an underfilled citrate tube alters the blood-to-additive ratio and invalidates results; a common trap is sending it anyway “so the lab can decide.”

q: The CMA draws blood from the arm with an IV infusing normal saline because the other arm is difficult—what is the best action?
a: Avoid drawing above/near an active IV and use the other arm or notify the provider for guidance because IV fluid can dilute the specimen; a common trap is assuming “saline won’t affect labs.”

q: While running a 12-lead EKG, the tracing shows a wavy baseline and the patient is shivering from a cold room—what should the CMA do next?
a: Warm the patient (blanket/adjust room) and ask them to lie still, then repeat the EKG because muscle tremor mimics artifact; a common trap is documenting it as an abnormal rhythm without troubleshooting.

q: A patient arrives for an EKG and asks if the test will “tell me if I’m having a heart attack right now”—what is the most appropriate CMA response?
a: Explain that the EKG records the heart’s electrical activity and the provider will interpret results, because the CMA should not diagnose; a common trap is reassuring or interpreting ST changes to the patient.

q: The CMA draws a CBC in a lavender tube and sets it down without mixing; 10 minutes later they remember—what is the best action?
a: Gently invert the tube the recommended number of times and inspect for clots, recollecting if clotted because EDTA tubes require immediate mixing; a common trap is shaking vigorously, which can hemolyze the sample.

q: A urine culture is ordered, and the patient hands the CMA a specimen cup filled to the brim with no label—what is the best next step?
a: Label the specimen in the patient’s presence using two identifiers and confirm it was collected midstream clean-catch, because unlabeled/uncertain specimens must not be processed; a common trap is labeling it later from memory.

q: During a CLIA-waived fingerstick glucose check, the meter displays “QC FAIL” but the patient is waiting for results so the provider can adjust the plan; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and do not report a patient result, repeat quality control with the correct control solution/expiration and technique (and troubleshoot or remove the meter from use if it still fails) because failed QC means results are unreliable—a common trap is rerunning the patient sample anyway to “save time.”

q: A throat swab for rapid strep and culture is collected, but the courier pickup is delayed—how should the CMA handle the specimen?
a: Place the swab in the correct transport medium and store/transport per test requirements promptly because improper storage can reduce organism viability; a common trap is leaving it on the counter “until pickup.”

q: The EKG printout shows “lead off” and a flat line in one lead—what is the best immediate action?
a: Check electrode placement and cable connections for that lead and reattach/replace the electrode because a disconnected lead produces false readings; a common trap is sending the strip as-is to the provider.

q: While drawing a fasting lipid panel, the patient repeatedly opens and closes their fist to “help the blood come out”—what should the CMA do?
a: Ask the patient to relax the hand and avoid fist pumping because it can falsely elevate certain analytes (e.g., potassium, lactate); a common trap is coaching vigorous pumping to speed the draw.

q: A CLIA-waived urine pregnancy test shows a faint second line within the allowed read time—what should the CMA do next?
a: Treat it as positive and follow clinic protocol for reporting/documentation because any visible test line within the time window is positive; a common trap is calling it negative because it’s faint.

q: At the start of the day, QC for a CLIA-waived rapid strep test is out of range—what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop patient testing, troubleshoot per manufacturer instructions (new kit, controls, storage), and notify the supervisor if unresolved because out-of-range QC means patient results are unreliable; a common trap is repeating the patient test and ignoring QC failure.

q: After collecting a CMP, the CMA realizes the tube was labeled with the correct patient name but the wrong date of birth—what is the best next action?
a: Do not alter the label; recollect and label correctly in the patient’s presence because mismatched identifiers can cause wrong-patient results; a common trap is crossing out and rewriting identifiers on the tube.

q: A patient on warfarin arrives for a scheduled PT/INR draw but says they took an extra dose by mistake last night and feels dizzy—what should the CMA do first?
