a: Ensure no one is touching the patient, loudly clear the area, then deliver the shock and resume CPR immediately; the trap is pausing to recheck a pulse, which delays defibrillation and compressions.

q: While obtaining an oral temperature, you realize the patient just drank hot coffee 2 minutes ago; what should the CMA do?
a: Wait about 15 minutes (or use an alternate route per clinic protocol) and document the method, because taking it immediately can give a falsely elevated reading and mislead clinical decisions.

q: In a busy lobby, a patient loudly asks, “Why am I here for my STI results?” and other patients look over; what should the CMA do first?
a: Move the conversation to a private area and speak quietly, because maintaining confidentiality is required and discussing sensitive results in public is a common HIPAA lapse.

q: You enter an exam room and see used gauze with dried blood on the counter from the previous visit; what is the CMA’s best next action before rooming the next patient?
a: Don gloves and disinfect the surfaces with an approved disinfectant following contact time, because standard precautions apply even when blood looks dry and “quick wipe” is a common trap.

q: A patient with a frequent cough is roomed for a sore throat and you anticipate close contact for a throat swab; what PPE is most appropriate?
a: Wear a surgical mask and eye protection (plus gloves), because droplets and splashes are plausible during swabbing and skipping eye protection is a common oversight.

q: You are preparing a sterile dressing change and realize the sterile field was set up but you reached over it to grab tape; what is the best next step?
a: Discard the contaminated setup and reestablish a new sterile field, because reaching over the field breaks sterility and trying to “work around it” is a common contamination trap.

q: While drawing up medication for an injection, you notice the vial’s rubber stopper looks intact but the medication is cloudy when it should be clear; what should the CMA do?
a: Do not administer it and obtain a new vial per protocol (and notify the supervisor), because abnormal appearance suggests contamination or degradation and “it’s within date” is a common false reassurance.

q: You are about to give an IM vaccine and notice the patient’s chart has two patients with the same last name and similar DOBs; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop and confirm identity using two identifiers (e.g., full name and DOB) against the order and label, because wrong-patient administration is a high-risk error and “it’s probably fine” is the trap.

q: The provider orders 0.5 mL of a medication, but the syringe you grabbed is a 3 mL syringe with wide markings and you’re unsure of precision; what should the CMA do next?
a: Use an appropriately sized syringe (e.g., 1 mL) to measure accurately, because dosing errors often occur from using the wrong syringe and guessing at markings.

q: You prepare to administer a vaccine and the patient says they feel lightheaded with shots; what positioning is best before giving the injection?
a: Have the patient seated or supine with support, because syncope and falls are common after injections and standing is a frequent safety mistake.

q: Right before an injection, the patient says, “I’m allergic to latex,” and you already opened supplies; what is the best action?
a: Stop and replace with latex-free equipment and alert the provider if needed, because proceeding can trigger a reaction and “the needle is latex-free” doesn’t address gloves/bandages.

q: After removing gloves, you plan to answer the phone “just for a second” before washing your hands; what should you do instead?
a: Perform hand hygiene immediately after glove removal, because gloves are not a substitute for handwashing and touching shared equipment is a common way pathogens spread.

q: You are positioning a patient for an abdominal exam and they say they are short of breath when lying flat; what is the best positioning adjustment?
a: Raise the head of the table (semi-Fowler’s) and notify the provider as needed, because forcing supine can worsen breathing and patient comfort/safety comes first.

q: During CPR in the clinic, an AED arrives and another staff member says, “Keep compressions going while I analyze”; what should the CMA do?
a: Stop compressions during AED rhythm analysis and ensure no one touches the patient, because movement can interfere with analysis and touching the patient risks safety during shock delivery.

q: During intake, an adult’s BP reads 188/112 and they say they feel “fine” and want to proceed with their sports physical; what should the CMA do first?
a: Recheck the BP manually after 5 minutes of rest with the correct cuff size and arm at heart level, because an initial high reading may be technique-related and the trap is immediately “clearing” the patient without confirming a potentially urgent value.

q: During a wound dressing change, the patient winces and says the pain is suddenly much worse than earlier; what should the CMA do next?
a: Pause the procedure, assess for bleeding/changes, and notify the provider, because new or escalating pain can signal a complication and continuing is a common mistake.

q: A provider asks you to administer an IM injection, but you notice the medication label doesn’t match the order (different concentration); what should the CMA do first?
a: Hold the medication and clarify with the provider/pharmacist per clinic policy before preparing the dose, because giving it “as usual” is a common trap that leads to wrong-dose errors.

q: While taking an oral temperature, the patient says they just drank hot coffee in the waiting room; what should the CMA do next?
a: Wait about 15 minutes and retake (or use a tympanic/temporal method per clinic practice), because recent hot liquids falsely elevate oral readings and the trap is documenting an inaccurate fever.

q: A patient stands up from the exam table after vitals and becomes pale and dizzy; what is the CMA’s best next action?
a: Assist them back to a safe position (sit or supine) and check BP/pulse, because preventing a fall is the immediate priority and the trap is continuing the visit or sending them to the lobby.

q: In the waiting area, a patient suddenly collapses and is unresponsive; what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate emergency response (call for help/911 per protocol) and start CPR if no pulse/breathing, because early activation and compressions save lives and searching for the chart is a common delay.

q: A 6-year-old’s respirations are irregular and the child is crying during counting; how should the CMA obtain the most accurate respiratory rate?
a: Count respirations unobtrusively for a full minute after the child calms (or while pretending to take the pulse), because crying skews the rate and the trap is announcing you’re counting breaths and worsening distress.

q: An older adult’s pulse is irregular on initial check; what should the CMA do next before reporting it?
a: Count the apical pulse for a full minute, because irregular rhythms require longer assessment and the trap is charting a 15-second estimate that can miss clinically significant irregularity.

q: After removing gloves, the CMA notices a small tear on one fingertip that may have contacted the patient’s skin; what should the CMA do first?
a: Perform hand hygiene immediately and assess for any exposure to blood/body fluids, because hand hygiene is required even after glove removal and the trap is assuming gloves alone prevent contamination.

q: A patient arrives for a wound check and the dressing is saturated with drainage; how should the CMA handle the used dressing during removal?
a: Remove and discard it directly into an appropriate biohazard container without placing it on the counter, because contaminated materials spread organisms and the trap is setting it down “just for a second.”

q: A provider requests sterile dressing supplies but the outside of a sterile package is wet from the sink area; what should the CMA do?
a: Discard the package and obtain a new sterile set, because moisture wicks microorganisms through packaging and the trap is opening it anyway because the inside “looks clean.”

q: You enter the room to room a patient with a frequent cough and visible nasal drainage; what PPE should the CMA apply first?
a: Perform hand hygiene and don a surgical mask (then eye protection if splash risk), because respiratory source control reduces transmission and the trap is skipping the mask because it’s “just a cold.”

q: A patient in a wheelchair is due for orthostatic vitals but cannot safely stand; what is the CMA’s best action?
a: Notify the provider and document that standing measurements could not be safely obtained, because patient safety and accurate reporting come first and the trap is forcing standing and risking a fall.

q: The CMA is preparing to irrigate a wound and expects splashing; what is the best PPE choice?
a: Gloves plus gown and eye/face protection (goggles/face shield), because irrigation creates splash risk and the trap is wearing only gloves and contaminating clothing or mucous membranes.

q: Immediately after an IM injection, the patient reports tingling and sharp pain radiating down the arm; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop the injection (if still injecting), assess, and notify the provider promptly, because this may indicate nerve irritation/injury and the trap is telling the patient it’s “normal” and sending them out.

q: A patient scheduled for a vaccine says they feel lightheaded when they see needles and previously fainted; what should the CMA do before giving the injection?
a: Seat or place the patient in a supine position and ensure a safe environment, because preventing syncope-related injury is priority and the trap is vaccinating them standing at the counter.

q: The provider orders a subcutaneous medication, but the CMA is preparing a 1.5-inch needle because it’s what’s available; what should the CMA do?
a: Obtain the correct needle/syringe for the ordered route before administering, because wrong equipment increases tissue injury and absorption changes and the trap is “making it work” to save time.

q: While cleaning an exam room, the CMA finds a used needle left on the tray; what should the CMA do next?
a: Place it immediately into a sharps container without recapping, because sharps disposal prevents needlestick injuries and the trap is recapping “to be safe,” which increases injury risk.

q: During a dressing change, the CMA cleans a surgical incision from the dirtiest area outward to “get the worst part first”; what should be done instead?
a: Clean from the cleanest area to the dirtiest using a new gauze each stroke, because this prevents dragging microbes into the incision and the trap is starting where drainage is heaviest.

q: In the waiting room, a patient suddenly collapses and is unresponsive; what is the CMA’s first action?
a: Check responsiveness and call for help/activate emergency response (have someone call 911 and bring the AED), because rapid activation and AED access saves time and the trap is running for supplies before initiating the response.

q: The provider orders an IM injection; the patient says they are allergic to latex and you notice the syringe tip cap packaging indicates latex; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop and obtain latex-free supplies (and alert the provider if needed), because preventing an allergic reaction is critical and the trap is proceeding since the latex “won’t touch the patient.”

q: While rooming a patient for an annual physical, you measure a blood pressure of 186/112 mm Hg; the patient says they feel “fine” and asks to proceed with the visit—what should the CMA do next?
a: Recheck the BP after the patient rests quietly for about 5 minutes with proper cuff size/arm position, and if it remains severely elevated notify the provider immediately because this level can indicate a hypertensive urgency/emergency and the common trap is documenting it as “high” and moving on without confirmation and escalation.

q: During intake, a 58-year-old reports “pressure in my chest” and looks pale; you haven’t taken vitals yet and the provider is with another patient—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Activate the clinic’s emergency response (get help/notify provider immediately and prepare AED) because possible cardiac event takes priority over completing vitals; the trap is delaying escalation to “finish intake.”

q: You’re rooming a patient and need to palpate the abdomen; which position is BEST to place the patient in?
a: Supine with knees flexed (or pillow under knees) because it relaxes abdominal muscles for comfort and accuracy; the trap is leaving the patient sitting upright, which increases guarding.

q: A seated BP reads 182/110 on an adult who denies symptoms and says they “rush-stressed” to the appointment; what is the BEST next step before reporting it?
a: Recheck BP after 5 minutes of quiet rest with correct cuff size and arm at heart level because technique/anxiety can falsely elevate readings; the trap is reporting a single potentially inaccurate reading as confirmed.

q: During intake at an urgent care clinic, a 58-year-old reports sudden dizziness and looks pale; you obtain vital signs showing BP 84/52, pulse 118, RR 22, and they say they might faint—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Assist the patient to a supine position with legs elevated and immediately alert the provider/activate emergency response while reassessing vitals, because suspected shock/syncope requires rapid perfusion support and escalation; a common mistake is leaving them seated to finish paperwork or walking them to an exam room, increasing fall risk.

q: A patient becomes lightheaded and diaphoretic immediately after standing for a weight measurement; what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Assist the patient to a safe position (sit or lie down) and assess responsiveness because fall prevention and airway/breathing/circulation come before continuing measurements; the trap is trying to “finish the weight” while the patient is unstable.

q: A 6-year-old’s respirations are 34/min at rest with nasal flaring during intake; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Stop routine intake and notify the provider promptly while keeping the child upright because signs of respiratory distress require immediate escalation; the trap is waiting until all vitals are completed.

q: A patient is pulseless and not breathing and the AED arrives; what should the CMA do next?
a: Turn on the AED, apply pads, and follow prompts while minimizing interruptions in CPR, because early defibrillation is key and the trap is delaying pad placement to continue compressions without integrating the AED.

q: While taking a radial pulse, you note it is irregular and you count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4; what is the BEST action?
a: Count for a full 60 seconds and report/document irregularity because short counts are unreliable with irregular rhythms; the trap is using a standard shortcut that under/overestimates the rate.

q: You are preparing an IM injection and the medication label reads “10 mg/mL,” order is “5 mg IM”; what should the CMA do BEFORE preparing the syringe?
a: Calculate the volume (0.5 mL) and double-check the math/label against the order because dose-to-volume conversion errors cause overdoses; the trap is drawing up “5 mL” by confusing mg with mL.

q: A patient with a cough asks you to lower your mask so they can “hear you better” at check-in; what is the BEST response?
a: Keep your mask on and offer communication alternatives (speak clearly, move to a private area, use written instructions) because source control protects patients and staff; the trap is removing PPE for convenience.

q: In an exam room, you remove gloves after cleaning a small blood spill and then reach for the doorknob; what should you do NEXT?
a: Perform hand hygiene before leaving the room because contaminated glove removal can transfer pathogens to hands; the trap is assuming glove removal alone prevents spread.

q: During room turnover, the previous patient used the exam table and BP cuff; what should be cleaned FIRST to reduce cross-contamination?
a: Clean/disinfect high-touch items the next patient will contact (exam table surface, BP cuff, stethoscope) because these are common vectors; the trap is focusing on low-touch areas while missing patient-contact surfaces.

q: After drawing up medication for an injection, you accidentally touch the sterile needle to the countertop; what is the BEST next step?
a: Discard the contaminated needle/syringe appropriately and prepare a new dose using aseptic technique because sterility is broken; the trap is “wiping it off” with alcohol and using it anyway.

q: Right before administering a vaccine, the patient says, “I faint every time I get shots”; what should the CMA do BEST to prevent injury?
a: Have the patient seated or supine and observe after administration because syncope risk makes positioning a safety priority; the trap is giving the injection while the patient stands.

q: You’re told to place a patient with suspected shingles rash on the trunk into a room; what is the BEST infection-control action within CMA scope?
a: Apply standard precautions and ensure the rash is covered and the patient is roomed promptly while notifying the provider for isolation guidance because transmission risk is reduced by covering lesions; the trap is treating every rash as requiring sterile technique instead of appropriate precautions.

q: You are preparing to give an IM injection and realize you didn’t perform hand hygiene after removing your jacket; what should you do immediately BEFORE touching supplies?
a: Perform hand hygiene because it is required before any clean/aseptic task; the trap is thinking gloves alone replace hand hygiene.

q: A patient’s oral temperature reads 95.9°F after they were chewing ice in the waiting room 2 minutes ago—what is the best next step?
a: Wait the recommended interval (about 15 minutes) and retake the temperature (or use an alternate route per clinic policy) because recent cold intake falsely lowers oral readings; the trap is documenting a false hypothermia.

q: During intake, a 58-year-old reports dizziness and you obtain BP 86/52 with HR 122; the patient is pale but awake—what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist the patient to a supine position with legs elevated and notify the provider immediately because this suggests possible shock/hypotension; the trap is continuing the interview or rechecking multiple times while the patient deteriorates.

q: A patient arrives for suture removal but the wound edges look separated with yellow drainage; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Do not remove the sutures and notify the provider for evaluation because dehiscence/infection needs provider assessment; the trap is proceeding because “they’re due for removal.”

q: After giving an IM injection, you notice a small drop of blood and the patient asks you to massage the site vigorously; what should you do?
a: Apply gentle pressure with gauze and place a bandage if needed because vigorous massage can increase bleeding/bruising and alter absorption for some meds; the trap is massaging automatically for every injection.

q: In the lobby, an adult collapses and is unresponsive; a coworker is calling 911—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Start CPR and send someone to bring the AED immediately because early CPR/AED use improves survival; the trap is searching for a pulse for too long instead of beginning compressions when unresponsive and not breathing normally.

q: You prepared a subcutaneous injection, but the patient says they already received the same medication today at another clinic; what is the BEST next step?
a: Hold the injection and verify with the provider and documentation/records because preventing duplicate dosing is critical; the trap is administering anyway because “it’s ordered.”

q: While taking an adult’s blood pressure you hear intermittent “thumps” that disappear and then reappear as you deflate—what should you do to avoid an inaccurate reading?
a: Inflate 20–30 mmHg above the palpated systolic and deflate slowly, recording systolic at first sound and diastolic at disappearance because an auscultatory gap can cause underestimation; the trap is starting too low and missing true systolic.

q: While changing a simple dressing, you accidentally drop the sterile gauze onto the patient’s gown; what is the BEST action?
a: Discard it and use new sterile gauze because a dropped item is contaminated even if it “looks clean”; the trap is using it to avoid wasting supplies.

q: A sharps container is 3/4 full and a coworker tries to push down used needles to make space—what should the CMA do?
a: Stop them and replace/close the container at the fill line because pushing contents increases needlestick risk; the trap is compressing sharps to “save supplies.”

q: An adult arrives for a routine visit with RR 8/min and appears difficult to arouse—what is the CMA’s priority action?
a: Activate emergency response (call for help/911 per protocol) and begin basic life support assessment because this is a potentially life-threatening respiratory depression; the trap is trying to finish vitals or leaving the patient unattended.

q: A patient with a latex allergy needs a dressing change—what is the best way to prevent a reaction?
a: Use non-latex gloves and supplies and verify the allergy is clearly flagged before starting because exposure can occur through gloves and adhesive products; the trap is assuming “small contact won’t matter.”

q: You are about to obtain orthostatic vital signs on a patient who nearly fainted earlier—what is the safest sequencing?
a: Measure BP/HR after 5 minutes supine, then sitting, then standing while staying with the patient because position changes can trigger syncope; the trap is leaving them standing alone or skipping the supine baseline.

q: You remove gloves after cleaning a small blood spill on the counter—what must you do immediately next?
a: Perform hand hygiene because gloves are not a substitute and removal can contaminate hands; the trap is putting on new gloves or touching the chart before washing.

q: You realize you touched the outside of your clean gloves to a used tissue in the room while setting up for an injection—what is the best action?
a: Remove gloves, perform hand hygiene, and don new gloves because the gloves are contaminated; the trap is continuing because “the needle is still sterile.”

q: A patient with a productive cough is placed in an exam room and asks for water; before entering you plan to do vitals—what PPE is most appropriate?
a: Wear a surgical mask (and add gloves if anticipating contact with secretions) because droplet protection reduces transmission risk; the trap is using no mask because it’s “just vitals.”

q: A patient’s pulse is irregular and you count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4—what should you do next before documenting?
a: Recount the apical pulse for a full 60 seconds because irregular rhythms require a full minute for accuracy; the trap is using a shortened count that misrepresents the rate.

q: While preparing an IM injection, you accidentally touch the needle to the counter—what should you do?
a: Discard the needle in sharps and restart with a new sterile needle because sterility is broken; the trap is wiping the needle with alcohol and proceeding.

q: After an IM injection, a patient becomes lightheaded and diaphoretic while seated on the exam table—what should you do next?
a: Assist them to a safe position (supine or seated with support), monitor, and notify the provider because vasovagal syncope can lead to falls; the trap is having them stand to “walk it off.”

q: A patient returns from the restroom and you are about to clean an abrasion; you’ve washed your hands and donned gloves—what is the correct skin-prep direction?
a: Clean from the center of the wound outward using a new swab each pass because it moves contaminants away from the area of highest risk; the trap is wiping back and forth and dragging bacteria into the wound.

q: You are changing a simple wound dressing and the patient reaches toward the sterile gauze; what is the best immediate response?
a: Ask the patient to keep hands away and replace any supplies that were contaminated because patient contact breaks clean technique; the trap is using the same gauze since it “looks clean.”

q: A patient says, “I’m nervous—what are you injecting me with?” and you notice the syringe is unlabeled on your tray—what is the best action?
a: Do not administer it; discard and redraw/relabel after verifying the medication and dose because unlabeled syringes create high-risk errors; the trap is trying to “remember what it was.”

q: You are about to administer a medication injection and notice the EHR shows “penicillin allergy,” but the order is for an antibiotic injection—what should you do first?
a: Stop and clarify with the provider before giving the medication because allergy verification is part of safe administration; the trap is assuming it’s unrelated or relying on the patient “looking fine.”

q: The provider orders 0.5 mL of a vaccine; the vial label reads 1 mL single-dose and you draw up 0.5 mL—what is the correct next step?
a: Give only the ordered 0.5 mL and discard the remaining vaccine per single-dose guidance because leftover should not be saved; the trap is storing the remainder for another patient.

q: A provider requests help positioning a patient for a rectal exam—what position should the CMA assist with?
a: Place the patient in Sims’ (left lateral) position with the right knee flexed because it provides optimal access and comfort; the trap is using supine which limits exposure and stability.

q: During intake, a 54-year-old patient says he feels “fine,” but you obtain BP 198/112 with a regular pulse and no acute symptoms; what should the CMA do next?
a: Recheck BP manually after 5 minutes with the correct cuff and arm supported, then immediately report the confirmed critical reading to the provider because severe hypertension requires prompt escalation and the trap is charting a single automated value as “true” without confirmation.

q: A patient’s pulse is irregular on the vital signs machine, but the patient denies chest pain and is chatting normally; what should the CMA do next?
a: Auscultate the apical pulse for a full 60 seconds and report the irregularity to the provider because irregular rhythms can be missed or misread by machines and the trap is documenting a pulse rate without assessing rhythm.

q: During rooming, a patient reports shortness of breath and you measure SpO₂ at 88% on room air; what should you do next?
a: Recheck probe placement and confirm reading, then immediately notify the provider (and follow clinic emergency protocol if distress worsens) because hypoxemia is urgent and the trap is delaying by completing the rest of intake.

q: While rooming a 67-year-old, you get an oral temperature of 95.8°F after he just drank ice water in the lobby; what should you do first?
a: Wait 15 minutes and retake the temperature (or use a route not affected by oral intake per clinic protocol) because recent cold liquids can cause a falsely low oral temp and the trap is escalating “hypothermia” without validating technique.

q: A patient with dizziness stands to get on the scale and becomes pale and unsteady; what is the CMA’s best immediate action?
a: Assist the patient to sit or lie down safely and check vital signs before continuing intake because preventing a fall is the priority and the trap is “finishing vitals” while the patient is actively unstable.

q: In the lobby, a patient collapses and is unresponsive; you see normal-looking chest movement is absent—what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate emergency response and start CPR while someone retrieves the AED because early CPR/AED saves lives; the trap is searching for a pulse for too long or moving the patient unnecessarily before calling for help.

q: A 3-year-old is crying and kicking during vitals and the automated cuff shows BP 142/96; what is the best next step?
a: Calm and reposition the child and repeat the BP using the correct pediatric cuff and manual method if needed because movement/crying falsely elevates readings and the trap is reporting an artifact as hypertension.

q: You are about to enter a room and see the previous patient’s used gauze and an uncapped needle on the counter; what should you do first?
a: Do not enter/continue care until the sharps hazard is addressed—use proper puncture-resistant sharps disposal without recapping and alert the responsible staff because needlestick prevention is immediate and the trap is “just cleaning later.”

q: A patient arrives coughing and asks to sit in the crowded waiting area while you “quickly” take vitals; what is the CMA’s best first step?
a: Offer a mask and perform hand hygiene, then separate the patient from others as able and notify the team per respiratory hygiene etiquette because source control prevents spread and the trap is prioritizing speed over infection control.

q: The provider orders an IM vaccine and the patient says they fainted during their last shot; what is the best setup before giving the injection?
a: Seat or place the patient in a supported position (preferably seated with arm supported or supine if high risk) and have them remain seated after because syncope safety comes first and the trap is vaccinating them standing up.

q: After removing gloves, you plan to type vitals into the EHR and then sanitize your hands; what is the correct order?
a: Perform hand hygiene immediately after glove removal before touching the keyboard because gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene and the trap is contaminating shared equipment.

q: During rooming, an adult patient says they feel lightheaded as you inflate the BP cuff while they are standing and their face becomes pale; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the measurement and assist the patient to sit or lie down (legs elevated if possible), then reassess vitals and notify the provider because preventing a fall/syncope injury takes priority over finishing vitals, and the common mistake is trying to “get the reading” while the patient remains unstable.

q: While preparing a medication, you discover the syringe label doesn’t match the vial you just drew up from, and you are not sure which it is; what should the CMA do?
a: Discard the prepared syringe and restart using the “rights” with correct labeling because uncertainty is a medication error risk and the trap is guessing or asking later after it’s drawn up.

q: A provider verbally tells you to give 0.5 mL of a medication, but the written order in the chart says 0.05 mL; what should you do next?
a: Hold the medication and clarify the order with the provider before preparing/administering because dose discrepancies must be resolved and the trap is choosing the verbal order “because it’s faster.”

q: You are sterile-setting up for a minor procedure and your sterile glove brushes the edge of the counter; what should you do next?
a: Consider the glove contaminated and change it immediately because touching a nonsterile surface breaks sterility and the trap is “it barely touched” and continuing the setup.

q: A patient with a draining wound asks you to change their dressing; which PPE is most appropriate for the CMA to don first?
a: Don gloves and add a gown/eye protection if splashing is possible because Standard Precautions are based on anticipated exposure and the trap is under-protecting because “it’s a small wound.”

q: You are administering an IM injection and the patient suddenly reports dizziness and itching with facial flushing; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the injection/keep the patient safe in a supported position and activate the clinic’s emergency response (notify provider, prepare for anaphylaxis protocol) because this may be an allergic reaction and the trap is finishing the dose before responding.

q: You are the first to bring the AED to a collapsed patient, and the chest is wet from cleaning solution; what should you do next?
a: Quickly dry the chest and apply pads as shown, then follow AED prompts because moisture can interfere with pad adhesion/shock delivery and the trap is placing pads on wet skin and delaying analysis.

q: In the procedure room, a patient becomes unresponsive and you do not feel a pulse; what should the CMA do first in an outpatient clinic?
a: Activate emergency response (call for help/911 per protocol) and begin CPR immediately while someone retrieves the AED because early CPR/AED saves lives and the trap is searching for the chart or waiting for the provider.

q: While taking vitals, a patient becomes pale and says they feel faint while seated on the exam table; what is the best next action?
a: Assist the patient to a supine position with legs elevated and stay with them while calling for help because preventing a fall is priority and the trap is leaving to “get the nurse/provider” and the patient collapses.

q: During intake, a 58-year-old patient says they “feel fine,” but you obtain BP 198/112 and pulse 104; what should the CMA do first?
a: Recheck the BP manually after 5 minutes of rest and correct cuff size/arm position, then alert the provider promptly because a severely high reading needs timely escalation and the trap is charting a single possibly inaccurate reading without confirmation.

q: The provider asks you to position a patient for an exam of the rectum and prostate; what position should you prepare?
a: Assist the patient into Sims’ (left lateral) position with appropriate draping because it provides access while maintaining safety and privacy and the trap is using dorsal recumbent, which is less appropriate for this exam.

q: You take an oral temperature immediately after the patient chewed peppermint gum and it reads 99.9°F; what should you do next?
a: Wait about 15 minutes or use an appropriate alternate route/device per clinic practice and retake, because recent food/gum skews oral temps and the trap is reporting a falsely elevated fever.

q: A patient needs a wound dressing change, and you have clean gloves on; you realize you forgot the tape and gauze across the room; what is the best action?
a: Remove gloves, perform hand hygiene, gather supplies, then re-glove before touching the wound because leaving the patient area with contaminated gloves spreads pathogens and the trap is “just grabbing one thing quickly.”

q: The provider asks you to set up a sterile dressing change tray; what is the key action to maintain sterility during setup?
a: Keep sterile items above waist level and only touch sterile-to-sterile surfaces because reaching over or dropping below waist breaks sterility and the trap is assuming “clean hands” equals sterile technique.

q: A patient in a wheelchair needs a weight for medication dosing today; what is the safest approach?
a: Use a wheelchair scale or other assisted weighing method and document the method, because accurate weight impacts dosing and the trap is estimating or recording an old weight without verification.

q: After rooming a patient with a draining wound, you remove gloves and head to the next room; what is the correct next step?
a: Perform hand hygiene immediately after glove removal because gloves are not a substitute for handwashing and the trap is thinking “I wore gloves” so it’s safe to skip hand hygiene.

q: A sharps container is filled past the recommended line, and a coworker suggests “just push it down to make room”; what should you do?
a: Close and replace the container per safety protocol because overfilled sharps increase needlestick risk and the trap is compressing contents, which is unsafe and against sharps safety practices.

q: You are preparing to recheck BP on a patient who just walked in from the parking lot carrying bags; what should you do before measuring?
a: Have them sit quietly with feet flat and back supported for about 5 minutes and keep the arm supported at heart level, because activity/positioning can falsely elevate BP and the trap is measuring immediately and acting on an inflated value.

q: A patient with a persistent cough arrives without a mask and sits in the crowded waiting area; what should the CMA do first?
a: Provide a mask and move them to a separate area/exam room as soon as possible because source control reduces airborne/droplet spread and the trap is delaying until after check-in paperwork.

q: You have visible blood on your gloved hands after a fingerstick; how should you remove PPE to reduce contamination?
a: Remove gloves first, then perform hand hygiene, then remove any remaining PPE as appropriate because gloves are most contaminated and the trap is touching your face/phone or removing other PPE with bloody gloves.

q: A patient’s pulse feels irregular when you take it for 15 seconds; what should you do next before documenting?
a: Count the apical pulse for a full 60 seconds (and notify the provider per protocol) because irregular rhythms require a full count and the trap is multiplying a short count that misrepresents the true rate.

q: You are applying a dressing to a minor laceration; what is the correct sequence to reduce infection risk?
a: Perform hand hygiene, don clean gloves, cleanse the wound as directed, then apply the sterile dressing because cleaning before covering reduces contamination and the trap is placing a dressing over an uncleaned wound.

q: A patient is due for an injection, but the chart shows a documented latex allergy and the room has latex gloves on the counter; what should you do first?
a: Remove latex supplies and use latex-free gloves/equipment, confirming vaccine components as needed, because exposure can trigger a reaction and the trap is thinking “gloves won’t touch the patient” so it doesn’t matter.

q: You draw up an injectable medication and then realize the patient’s identity hasn’t been verified yet; what should you do next?
a: Pause and verify the patient using two identifiers before administering (and relabel/reprepare if there’s any doubt about mix-ups) because right patient is a core medication right and the trap is assuming the room assignment guarantees identity.

q: A patient needs a pelvic exam; how should you position them and what should you do to support safety and dignity?
a: Place them in lithotomy with proper draping and explain each step before assisting, because positioning and privacy reduce anxiety and improve cooperation and the trap is rushing positioning without draping or consent to proceed.

q: When giving an IM injection, you’re about to recap the needle “just to walk it to the sharps”; what should you do instead?
a: Do not recap; activate the safety device and discard immediately into a sharps container because recapping causes needlesticks and the trap is thinking a quick recap is safer for transport.

q: A patient reports dizziness immediately after a vaccination while standing at the checkout desk; what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist them to sit or lie down and monitor while calling for clinical help because syncope/fall prevention is immediate priority and the trap is offering water and letting them remain standing.

q: You accidentally stick yourself with a used lancet after a glucose test; what is the first action?
a: Wash the area immediately with soap and water and report the exposure per clinic protocol because prompt cleansing and reporting are time-sensitive and the trap is waiting until the end of the shift to “see if it’s a big deal.”

q: You are preparing an IM vaccine and notice the syringe label doesn’t match the order even though the vial looks similar; what is the best next step?
a: Stop and verify the medication against the order and the vial’s name/strength/expiration before proceeding because look-alike products cause errors and the trap is relying on appearance or a partially read label.

q: In the lobby, a visitor tells you a patient “just collapsed and isn’t breathing”; what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate emergency response (call for help/911 per clinic policy) and begin CPR/AED as soon as available because early activation and compressions save lives and the trap is searching for the provider first instead of starting lifesaving steps.

q: You enter the room wearing gloves only to remove a saturated wound dressing, and the patient begins coughing repeatedly—what PPE change is best?
a: Add a surgical mask with eye protection (and keep gloves) because splash/droplet exposure is possible during wound care with coughing; the trap is thinking gloves alone meet Standard Precautions when mucous membrane exposure risk increases.

q: You are about to administer a medication and notice the MAR lists 0.5 mL but the syringe is drawn to 0.8 mL—what should you do next?
a: Stop and resolve the discrepancy by rechecking the order and recalculating/remeasuring before giving anything because the “right dose” is a core safety check; the trap is assuming the prefilled syringe amount is correct and administering anyway.

q: The provider orders an IM injection, and the patient says they have a severe latex allergy—what should the CMA do before preparing supplies?
a: Verify all supplies (gloves, vial stoppers, syringe/needle packaging, bandage) are latex-free and alert the provider if alternatives are needed because preventing exposure is the priority; the trap is assuming nonsterile gloves are the only latex source.

q: During rooming, an adult patient’s BP is 186/112 and they report a new severe headache; they are here for a routine refill visit—what should the CMA do first?
a: Recheck BP manually after a brief rest and immediately alert the provider with symptoms and readings because this may be hypertensive crisis; the trap is documenting it and continuing intake as “white coat” without prompt escalation.

q: While obtaining vitals, a patient becomes pale and says they feel faint while standing on the scale—what is the best next action?
a: Assist them to a seated or supine position (legs elevated if tolerated) and stay with them, then obtain vitals and notify the provider because fall prevention comes before finishing measurements; the trap is insisting they “hold on” to complete height/weight.

q: After drawing up an IM vaccine, the patient suddenly asks to use the restroom and you step out holding the uncapped syringe—what is the safest action?
a: Discard the prepared syringe and prepare a new dose before administration because leaving with/transporting an uncapped or unattended prepared medication risks contamination and mix-ups; the trap is “saving the dose” to avoid waste.

q: You obtain an oral temperature of 101.8°F on a patient who just drank hot coffee in the waiting room—what should you do next?
a: Wait about 15 minutes and retake using an appropriate route/device (or use tympanic/temporal per clinic practice) because recent hot liquids can falsely elevate oral temps; the trap is charting the first reading as true fever without confirming.

q: During venipuncture for a CBC and BMP, the CMA fills the lavender tube first because it was closest on the tray; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Stop and redraw using the correct order of draw because drawing EDTA (lavender) before a serum/chemistry tube can contaminate the sample and alter results; the trap is “it’s already collected” but accuracy requires recollection.

q: A fasting lipid panel specimen sits on the counter for 45 minutes after collection because the clinic got busy; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Follow the test’s handling requirements and contact the lab/supervisor to determine if recollection is needed because delayed processing can compromise stability; the trap is assuming all blood is stable at room temperature.

q: In the lobby, a visitor says, “Is my sister done yet? She’s in room 3 for an STI test,” and they ask you for her results—what should the CMA do?
a: Decline to confirm information and direct the visitor to the patient or authorized contact process because HIPAA prohibits sharing even presence/test details without permission; the trap is giving “just a status update” because it seems harmless.

q: A provider orders PT/INR, CMP, and CBC; the CMA prepares light blue, gold SST, and lavender tubes—what is the correct order of draw?
a: Draw light blue first, then gold/SST, then lavender because coagulation tubes must be collected before additive tubes that can affect clotting tests; the trap is placing SST before citrate.

q: After drawing a lavender tube, the CMA shakes it vigorously to “mix it fast”; what is the best corrective action?
a: Gently invert the tube the recommended number of times to mix additive without hemolyzing the specimen; the trap is shaking, which can cause hemolysis and inaccurate labs.

q: A patient arrives for a minor procedure and asks to watch while you set up the sterile field, reaching toward the drape to “help”—what is the best response?
a: Politely ask them to keep hands away and reposition them for safety (and re-establish sterility if contamination occurs) because patient movement can contaminate the field; the trap is allowing “help” to save time and then proceeding after contamination.

q: A patient’s name on the label is correct but the date of birth is missing; the specimen is already in the transport bag—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Do not send the specimen; relabel correctly at the patient’s side using two identifiers because mislabeling is a patient-safety event; the trap is fixing labels away from the patient, which breaks identification integrity.

q: While collecting a light blue tube for PT/INR, the tube stops filling early and is only half full; what should the CMA do?
a: Discard and recollect a properly filled tube because citrate tubes require the correct blood-to-additive ratio for accurate coagulation results; the trap is “send it anyway” which can falsely prolong or shorten results.

q: A rapid strep test is CLIA-waived, but the CMA realizes the control was not run for a new kit lot; the patient is waiting—what is the best next step?
a: Run the required controls before reporting patient results because lot verification is part of quality assurance even for waived tests; the trap is thinking CLIA-waived means “no QC needed.”

q: A patient’s antecubital veins are hard to palpate and the CMA is tempted to “fish” with the needle; what should the CMA do BEST?
a: Stop and reassess (reposition arm, warm site, try a different vein or obtain assistance) because probing increases pain, hematoma risk, and nerve injury; the trap is repeated redirection to salvage a missed attempt.

q: The provider orders a blood culture, and the CMA has collected the tubes but has not cleaned the site with antiseptic yet; what should the CMA do?
a: Discard and restart with proper skin antisepsis before collection because cultures are highly contamination-sensitive; the trap is thinking you can “clean after” or rely on alcohol alone without proper technique.

q: A urine dipstick POCT was performed, but the bottle of reagent strips has been left uncapped on the counter for an hour; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Repeat the test with properly stored strips (and document the issue) because moisture/light exposure can invalidate reagent chemistry; the trap is accepting the first result because it “looked normal.”

q: The clinic’s CLIA-waived glucose meter displays “QC failed” before patient testing; what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Do not test patients and perform troubleshooting/QC per manufacturer instructions (repeat control, check strips, calibration, expiration) because failed QC means patient results are unreliable; the trap is proceeding to “save time.”

q: After venipuncture, a hematoma begins forming at the site while the tube is still filling; what is the CMA’s best next action?
a: Release the tourniquet, remove the needle, and apply firm pressure because continued blood flow into tissue worsens hematoma; the trap is keeping the needle in to complete the collection.

q: A patient on anticoagulant therapy has persistent oozing after the needle is removed; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Maintain firm pressure longer and reassess before bandaging, escalating per clinic protocol if bleeding won’t stop because anticoagulants increase bleeding risk; the trap is applying a bandage too soon and letting the patient leave.

q: During a draw, the patient says, “I feel dizzy,” becomes pale, and starts to slump in the chair; what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, apply pressure, and assist the patient into a safe position (reclined with legs elevated if possible) to prevent syncope injury; the trap is trying to “finish the tube” despite symptoms.

q: A patient’s EKG has a wandering baseline and the CMA notices the patient is talking and the bed is not locked; what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Instruct the patient to remain still and quiet and stabilize the environment (lock bed, ensure comfortable position) because movement causes artifact that can mimic dysrhythmias; the trap is assuming it’s a true rhythm change.

q: After placing chest leads for an EKG, the CMA realizes V1 and V2 were placed too high near the clavicles; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Reposition V1/V2 to the 4th intercostal space at the sternal borders and repeat the EKG because incorrect placement can mimic ischemia or axis changes; the trap is keeping the tracing because “it’s readable.”

q: The EKG printout shows consistent 60-cycle interference, and the CMA sees a nearby power cord draped over the lead wires; what should the CMA do BEST?
a: Separate/untangle lead wires from electrical cords and ensure good skin contact because electrical interference commonly causes this artifact; the trap is turning up filter settings instead of fixing the source.

q: While filling a light blue sodium citrate tube for PT/INR, blood flow stops and the tube is only half full; what should the CMA do next?
a: Discard that tube and recollect a fully filled light blue tube because underfilling changes the blood-to-additive ratio and invalidates results (trap: “topping off” from another tube or accepting it “since it clotted fine”).

q: A fecal occult blood POCT card is developed, but the sample window is smeared with too much stool and the result is hard to read; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Repeat the test with a proper thin smear and follow kit timing exactly because excess specimen can invalidate readability and accuracy; the trap is guessing the result or over-interpreting a compromised test.

q: While setting up a 12-lead EKG, the CMA places limb electrodes on the patient’s wrists and ankles, but the tracing shows heavy motion artifact from tremor; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Reposition limb electrodes to the torso (per facility practice) and have the patient relax/keep still to reduce artifact while maintaining correct lead orientation; the trap is repeating the EKG without addressing artifact source.

q: A provider asks the CMA to interpret the EKG as “normal” so the patient can leave; the tracing prints with an automated message “possible acute MI”; what should the CMA do?
a: Immediately notify the provider with the tracing and patient status because CMAs do not interpret/clear EKGs and possible critical findings require prompt escalation; the trap is reassuring the patient or documenting an interpretation.

q: A provider orders CBC, PT/INR, BMP, and a lactic acid, and you have one venipuncture attempt to get all tubes; what order of draw should you use?
a: Draw blood cultures first (if ordered), then light blue, then serum (red/gold), then green, then lavender, then gray because correct order prevents additive carryover (common trap: drawing lavender before light blue can falsely prolong coag results).

q: A patient’s wristband is missing, and they verbally confirm their name and date of birth; what is the best way to label the tubes?
a: Label at the patient’s side immediately after the draw using two identifiers matched to the order because bedside labeling reduces mislabeling errors (trap: labeling later at the workstation from memory).

q: A patient is fasting for labs and asks if they can sip coffee while you prepare the draw; what should the CMA do?
a: Ask what the provider ordered and instruct the patient to avoid anything but water until the draw is complete because coffee can break fasting requirements and alter results (trap: allowing “just a little” without verifying test prep).

q: The only specimen you receive for a potassium level is visibly hemolyzed (pink/red serum) after a difficult draw; what should the CMA do next?
a: Notify the lab/provider per clinic process and recollect if requested because hemolysis can falsely elevate potassium and compromise accuracy (trap: sending it anyway to “see what it says”).

q: A patient becomes pale and says, “I’m going to pass out,” while seated upright in the phlebotomy chair; what should you do first?
a: Stop the draw and assist the patient to a safe reclined position (legs elevated if possible) to prevent injury from syncope (trap: offering water or continuing the draw while they remain upright).

q: You’re preparing for venipuncture and the patient says they are on “blood thinners”; after removing the needle, how should you adjust aftercare?
a: Hold firm pressure longer than usual and ensure bleeding has stopped before bandaging because anticoagulants increase bleeding risk (trap: using the usual brief pressure time and letting them leave with continued oozing).

q: You drew a lavender tube for CBC and set it on the counter without mixing while you label other tubes; what should you do?
a: Gently invert the lavender tube the recommended number of times as soon as possible because EDTA tubes must be mixed to prevent microclots (trap: shaking vigorously, which can hemolyze, or assuming mixing isn’t needed).

q: You have difficulty advancing the needle and see no blood return; what should you do to avoid damaging the vein?
a: Withdraw the needle slightly and reassess angle/position, then stop and attempt a new site if unsuccessful because “digging” increases hematoma/nerve injury risk (trap: probing repeatedly under the skin).

q: After a venipuncture, you notice swelling and firmness at the site as blood is entering the tube; what is the CMA’s best immediate action?
a: Release the tourniquet, remove the needle, and apply firm pressure because this suggests a hematoma/infiltration and continuing worsens tissue injury (trap: finishing the draw to “get all tubes” despite swelling).

q: You place limb electrodes on the patient’s torso to reduce artifact, and the provider asks why the EKG looks different than prior studies; what is the best response/action?
a: Repeat the EKG with correct limb placement on wrists/ankles (or distal limbs per standard) because nonstandard placement can change axis and waveform comparisons (trap: leaving it because it “prints fine”).

q: You are performing an EKG and notice the machine displays “LEAD OFF” for V2; what is the next best step?
a: Check that the V2 electrode is adhered and the wire is securely snapped in, then repeat the acquisition because a disconnected lead produces incomplete/erroneous data (trap: printing and sending an incomplete tracing).

q: After printing an EKG, you see the patient’s name is misspelled and the DOB is wrong; what should you do?
a: Do not send it as-is—correct the patient identifiers and repeat/regen the report per device workflow because misidentified diagnostics are a major safety risk (trap: hand-correcting with pen and hoping it’s “good enough”).

q: A CLIA-waived urine pregnancy test shows the control line is absent; what should the CMA do next?
a: Treat it as an invalid test and repeat with a new device/specimen as appropriate because a missing control means the result can’t be trusted (trap: reporting “negative” because the test line is absent).

q: You run daily quality control on a POCT analyzer and the control is out of range; what is the best next action?
a: Stop patient testing, troubleshoot per manufacturer instructions (new control/strip, verify lot/expiration, clean device), and document/notify as required because reporting patient results without passing QC is unsafe (trap: rerunning patient samples and assuming it will “average out”).

q: Before running a fingerstick glucose on a clinic meter, you notice the test strips expired last week; what should you do?
a: Do not use expired strips—discard and obtain in-date strips because expiration affects accuracy and QC compliance (trap: using them “just for today” since the meter still reads).

q: A patient’s skin is oily and the EKG leads keep popping off; what should you do to get a clean tracing?
a: Clean and dry the skin (and gently abrade if allowed) before reapplying electrodes because good contact reduces artifact (trap: adding extra gel only or taping over poorly prepped skin).

q: During a 12-lead EKG, the tracing shows a wandering baseline and the patient is shivering; what should you do first?
a: Warm and relax the patient (blanket, adjust room temp) and ask them to stay still because muscle tremor causes artifact (trap: immediately repositioning all electrodes without addressing shivering).

q: After drawing a lavender-top tube, the CMA vigorously shakes it to mix and the specimen becomes frothy—what is the best action?
a: Recollect and gently invert the new tube the recommended number of times to prevent hemolysis; the trap is assuming “more mixing is better,” which can invalidate results.

q: A patient’s requisition says fasting lipid panel, but at check-in the patient reports drinking a sugary coffee 30 minutes ago—what should the CMA do next?
a: Notify the provider or follow clinic protocol to reschedule/clarify before drawing because non-fasting can alter results; the trap is drawing anyway and “letting the lab decide.”

q: A patient arrives with a urine specimen collected at home “this morning,” unlabeled and sitting in a warm car; what should you do?
a: Reject and request a new properly labeled, fresh specimen (or follow storage requirements) because time/temperature can alter urine chemistry and promote bacterial growth (trap: labeling it yourself and sending it to avoid delaying the visit).

q: The CMA prints labels for two patients and is about to label tubes at the counter after leaving the room—what is the best practice?
a: Label tubes in the patient’s presence immediately after collection using two identifiers because delayed labeling increases mislabeling risk; the trap is relying on “I’ll remember which tube is which.”

q: A provider orders PT/INR, CBC, and BMP, and the CMA has blue, lavender, and light green tubes ready—what is the correct order of draw?
a: Draw light blue, then light green, then lavender because coagulation tubes must be collected before EDTA tubes to prevent clotting-test interference; the trap is drawing CBC first “because it’s routine.”

q: While drawing a blue-top tube, you notice the vacuum stops early and the tube is only half full—what should the CMA do?
a: Redraw the blue-top to the required fill line because underfilling alters the blood-to-additive ratio and skews coag results; the trap is “topping off” from another tube or sending it anyway.

q: During venipuncture for a CBC and CMP, you collect the CMP in a lavender tube first and then remember the order of draw—what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and redraw using the correct order of draw because additive carryover can contaminate results; the common trap is “it’s already labeled so send it,” which risks inaccurate labs.

q: You are about to collect a throat swab for a CLIA-waived rapid strep test and the patient just used mouthwash; what should you do next?
a: Ask when they used it and, if recent, notify the provider/consider recollection timing per test instructions because mouthwash can reduce organism load and cause false negatives (trap: collecting immediately without considering pre-test interference).

q: A 12-lead EKG printout shows heavy baseline wander, and you notice the patient is shivering in a cold room—what is the best next step?
a: Warm/comfort the patient and repeat the EKG because muscle tremor commonly causes artifact; the trap is troubleshooting the machine first when the issue is patient-related.

q: A urine specimen for culture was collected, but it sat at room temperature on the counter for 2 hours before being processed—what should the CMA do?
a: Treat it as compromised and follow protocol to recollect or refrigerate with proper timing because bacterial overgrowth can alter culture results; the trap is sending it anyway to “avoid bothering the patient.”

q: Immediately after you remove the tourniquet and needle, the patient reports tingling shooting down the arm—what should the CMA do?
a: Stop, apply pressure, assess for persistent symptoms, and promptly report to the provider because nerve irritation/injury is possible; the trap is dismissing it as “normal soreness.”

q: While placing EKG limb leads, the patient’s wrists are covered in lotion and the electrodes keep lifting—what should the CMA do?
a: Clean and dry the skin (and lightly abrade if appropriate) then reapply electrodes because poor contact causes artifact; the trap is pressing harder or adding tape without prepping the skin.

q: During a routine venipuncture for CBC, BMP, and PT/INR, you draw the tubes in the wrong order and the light blue citrate tube is filled only halfway before the vein collapses; what should the CMA do next before sending specimens to the lab?
a: Stop and redraw the specimens with a new venipuncture using the correct order of draw and fully fill the light blue tube to its mark, because underfilling or drawing it after other additives can alter the blood-to-anticoagulant ratio and cause inaccurate coagulation results (a common mistake is “topping off” or submitting a short-draw citrate tube).

q: During venipuncture, a patient suddenly becomes pale, diaphoretic, and says they feel faint—what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, activate safety, and position the patient safely (recline with legs elevated if possible) because syncope can cause injury; the trap is trying to “finish the last tube.”

q: The first venipuncture attempt is unsuccessful and the patient is anxious and asking you to “just try again right away”—what should the CMA do next?
a: Ask for assistance or follow the clinic limit on attempts (often no more than two) because multiple sticks increase complications and patient distress; the trap is repeated attempts to “prove you can get it.”

q: A patient says they have a history of mastectomy with lymph node removal on the left, and you were preparing to draw from the left arm—what is the best action?
a: Use the other arm (or consult the provider if both sides are restricted) to reduce lymphedema/infection risk; the trap is thinking a small venipuncture “doesn’t count.”

q: The provider orders a CLIA-waived fingerstick glucose, but the control solution has not been run on the meter today—what should the CMA do next?
a: Run and document quality control before testing the patient because QC verifies accuracy and is required for reliable results; the trap is skipping QC “since the meter turned on fine.”

q: A CMA is collecting a blood specimen for PT/INR, CBC, and CMP using evacuated tubes; which tube should be drawn first?
a: Draw the light blue citrate tube first because coagulation testing is most sensitive to additive carryover; a common trap is drawing the purple EDTA first, which can falsely prolong clotting results.

q: During venipuncture, blood flow stops after the first tube and the tube is only partially filled; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Reposition the needle slightly (without probing) and ensure the tube is fully seated, because loss of vacuum/needle position is common; a trap is “milking” the arm, which increases hemolysis and alters results.

q: During a routine venipuncture for a CMP and CBC, the CMA accidentally fills the lavender EDTA tube first and then the light green heparin tube; the patient is stable and the draw is complete—what should the CMA do next to prevent an inaccurate CMP result?
a: Notify the provider/lab and recollect the CMP specimen in the correct order of draw because EDTA carryover can falsely alter chemistry values (common trap: sending both tubes anyway or just “mixing well” to fix the error).

q: During a 12-lead EKG, the machine flags “leads off” intermittently and the tracing is intermittent—what should the CMA check first?
a: Verify each electrode and lead wire connection at the patient before restarting because loose leads are the most common cause; the trap is assuming the printer or paper is the problem.

q: A patient brings in a home-collected stool sample with no label and says, “It’s mine; I dropped it off for the test”—what should the CMA do next?
a: Do not accept it as-is; obtain proper labeling with two identifiers and verify collection requirements (or recollect) because unlabeled specimens are a major identification error; the trap is labeling it later based on the patient’s word.

q: A patient asks the CMA, “Does this EKG mean I’m having a heart attack?” after you see abnormal-looking complexes—what is the best response?
a: Tell the patient you can’t interpret results, keep them calm, and immediately alert the provider because abnormal findings require prompt clinical evaluation; the trap is reassuring or diagnosing based on the tracing.

q: A urine dipstick bottle has been left open on the counter, and another CMA says it’s fine because “the strips still look normal”—what should the CMA do?
a: Discard per manufacturer guidance and open a new bottle because moisture/light exposure can cause false results; the trap is relying on appearance instead of storage requirements.

q: A urine pregnancy test (POCT) is negative but the control indicator did not appear; what is the CMA’s BEST next step?
a: Treat it as an invalid test, repeat per manufacturer instructions with QC as required, because missing controls mean results can’t be reported; a trap is documenting “negative” anyway.

q: A specimen label is printed but the CMA realizes it was placed on the tube before the draw and the patient stepped out to the restroom; what should the CMA do?
a: Discard the pre-labeled tube and recollect/label at bedside after re-identifying the patient, because unattended pre-labeling risks misidentification; a trap is “confirming later” from memory or the schedule.

q: A patient says they fainted during a previous blood draw and looks pale while seated upright on the exam table; what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Stop and place the patient supine (or reclined) before attempting the draw because preventing syncope-related injury is priority; a common trap is proceeding quickly “to get it over with.”

q: The patient’s arm becomes swollen and cool around the venipuncture site while blood is being drawn; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Stop the draw, release the tourniquet, remove the needle, and apply pressure because this suggests hematoma/infiltration; a trap is continuing to fill the tube, which worsens tissue damage.

q: A CMP and potassium are ordered, and the sample arrives in the lab with visible hemolysis; what is the most likely collection error the CMA should avoid next time?
a: Avoid vigorous shaking/forceful syringe transfer because hemolysis can falsely elevate potassium; a trap is assuming the result is “still usable” and not recollecting when required.

q: The clinic runs CLIA-waived glucose testing and the meter flags “QC overdue”; a patient is waiting for a reading; what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Perform the required quality control before patient testing because results are not reliable without QC compliance; a trap is running the patient sample “just this once” to save time.

q: After drawing a lavender-top tube for CBC, the CMA sets it down and continues charting; what is the BEST immediate action?
a: Gently invert the tube the required number of times right away to mix anticoagulant and prevent clotting; a common trap is shaking vigorously, which can hemolyze the specimen.

q: A provider requests blood cultures and a CBC from the same venipuncture; what should the CMA collect FIRST?
a: Collect blood cultures first using aseptic technique because contamination control is critical; a trap is drawing other tubes first, increasing the risk of skin flora contaminating cultures.

q: The provider asks the CMA to “interpret” an EKG that appears abnormal; what is the CMA’s appropriate response?
a: Immediately notify the provider of concerning findings and document that the EKG was performed, but do not interpret/diagnose because interpretation is outside CMA scope; a trap is telling the patient what it “means.”

q: A rapid strep POCT is performed, but the swab touched the tongue and cheeks before reaching the tonsillar area; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Discard that swab and recollect correctly because oral contamination can cause inaccurate results; a trap is running the test anyway to avoid an uncomfortable recollection.

q: A patient’s ECG limb leads are placed on the wrists/ankles and the tracing is very noisy as the patient talks and moves hands; what change is MOST helpful?
a: Reposition limb electrodes to the torso (if facility protocol allows) and instruct the patient to keep arms/legs still because motion artifact is common; a trap is increasing gain/filter settings to “hide” the noise.

q: While performing a 12-lead EKG, the tracing shows a wandering baseline and the patient is shivering; what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Warm/comfort the patient and ask them to lie still and relax muscles because tremor causes artifact; a trap is repeatedly reprinting without fixing the cause.

q: A 12-lead EKG prints with a flatline in lead I and an unusual pattern suggesting lead reversal; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Verify electrode placement and cable connections and repeat the EKG because misplacement commonly mimics abnormalities; a trap is alerting the provider with an unverified tracing.

q: A fasting lipid panel is ordered, but the patient states they drank a large coffee with cream 30 minutes ago; what should the CMA do?
a: Notify the provider and document the intake because the test may need rescheduling for accurate results; a trap is proceeding without disclosure and creating misleading lab values.

q: During EKG setup, the patient has oily lotion on the chest and multiple electrodes won’t stick; what should the CMA do BEST?
a: Clean and dry the skin (and lightly abrade if allowed) before applying electrodes because poor contact causes artifact; a trap is taping over loose electrodes without skin prep.

q: After centrifuging a serum tube, the CMA notices the cap popped slightly open during spinning; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Treat it as a potential exposure/compromised specimen, follow spill/exposure procedure, and recollect if needed because aerosol/leak risk and integrity are concerns; a trap is simply snapping the cap back and sending it.

q: A CBC is ordered and the patient has an IV running in the left arm; which site selection is BEST for venipuncture?
a: Use the opposite arm if possible because drawing above/near an IV can dilute or contaminate the specimen; a trap is drawing from the IV arm “below the IV” without guidance.

q: After a successful venipuncture, the patient asks to see their lab results on the computer screen while other patients are nearby at check-in; what should the CMA do?
a: Maintain privacy by moving the conversation to a private area or offering the patient portal process, because HIPAA requires limiting exposure of PHI; a trap is turning the monitor toward the patient in public view.

q: After drawing a light-blue tube for PT/INR, the CMA notices it is underfilled—what should the CMA do next?
a: Redraw the specimen to the proper fill line, because citrate tubes require a correct blood-to-additive ratio for accurate coagulation results; a common trap is “topping off” from another tube or accepting a short draw.

q: During venipuncture, blood stops flowing and the tube is only partially filled while the needle is still in the vein—what should the CMA do next?
a: Gently reposition the needle (slightly withdraw/adjust angle) and ensure the tube is fully seated before restarting, because the bevel may be against the vein wall; a common trap is “digging” aggressively or removing the needle without first checking tube engagement.

q: A patient has an IV infusing in the left forearm and requests blood be drawn from that arm “to be quick”—what is the best action?
a: Use the opposite arm or coordinate to pause the infusion per facility protocol before drawing, because IV fluids can dilute or contaminate results; a common trap is drawing below the IV site without guidance, which still risks altered values.

q: During a routine venipuncture with a butterfly set, you draw a light blue sodium citrate tube first and notice it is only about half full because blood flow slowed; what should the CMA do NEXT to ensure the specimen is acceptable for coagulation testing?
a: Discard that underfilled tube and recollect a new light blue tube filled to the indicated line (using a discard tube first if needed with a butterfly) because citrate tubes must be correctly filled to maintain the 9:1 blood-to-additive ratio; a common mistake is sending a short-draw tube, which can falsely prolong PT/INR/aPTT.

q: A provider order includes a CBC, BMP, PT/INR, and a lipid panel; the CMA prepares to draw from one venipuncture—what is the correct order of draw?
a: Draw light blue first, then red/gold (serum), then green (heparin), then lavender; this prevents additive carryover (common trap: drawing EDTA lavender before chemistry tubes, which can falsely elevate potassium/calcium results).

q: A patient stands up immediately after a blood draw and says they feel lightheaded—what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist the patient to sit or lie down with legs elevated and stay with them, because preventing a fall is the priority; a common trap is sending them to the lobby with juice before ensuring they are safe and stable.

q: A patient’s arm is bruising and swelling rapidly at the venipuncture site while the tube is filling—what should the CMA do first?
a: Release the tourniquet, withdraw the needle, and apply firm pressure, because this suggests a hematoma and continuing the draw worsens bleeding; a common trap is finishing the tube “since it’s almost done.”

q: The CMA labels tubes after leaving the exam room and realizes there were two patients with the same last name—what is the best action?
a: Stop processing and resolve identification immediately by confirming with two identifiers and recollecting if tube identity cannot be guaranteed, because mislabeling is a serious patient-safety event; a common trap is guessing based on room number or appointment time.

q: While preparing for an EKG, the CMA notes the patient’s chest is sweaty and the electrodes keep lifting—what should the CMA do next?
a: Dry/clean the skin (and clip excessive hair if needed per protocol) before reapplying electrodes, because poor contact causes artifact; a common trap is pressing harder or repeatedly replacing leads without skin prep.

q: A CMP result is rejected for hemolysis and the patient asks what went wrong—what is the CMA’s best response?
a: Explain that red blood cells broke during collection/handling and a redraw is needed, because hemolysis can alter key analytes; a common trap is blaming the patient or giving detailed medical interpretation outside CMA scope.

q: A patient states they “usually faint with needles” before venipuncture begins—what should the CMA do next?
a: Have the patient lie down or recline and ensure supervision throughout the draw, because anticipatory syncope increases fall risk; a common trap is proceeding with the patient seated upright to save time.

q: A urine specimen for culture is collected, but the lid touches the inside of the cup during closing—what should the CMA do?
a: Treat it as contaminated and recollect using clean-catch instructions, because culture results are highly sensitive to contamination; a common trap is sending it anyway and “hoping the lab can tell.”

q: An EKG tracing shows a wavy baseline that worsens when the patient talks and improves when they hold still—what should the CMA do first?
a: Instruct the patient to relax, remain still, and avoid talking, because muscle movement commonly causes artifact; a common trap is immediately recalibrating the machine without addressing patient motion.

q: The provider orders a blood culture and a CBC; the patient’s skin was cleaned with alcohol, but the CMA is about to palpate the site again—what should the CMA do?
a: Palpate before final antisepsis or re-clean if you must re-palpate, because touching after cleansing can reintroduce skin flora and contaminate cultures; a common trap is “quickly” touching the site and proceeding anyway.

q: During EKG setup, the patient says they have a do-not-resuscitate order and asks if the EKG changes it—what should the CMA do?
a: Explain the EKG is a diagnostic test and does not change advance directives, and notify the provider if questions persist, because scope includes reassurance and escalation—not legal counseling; a common trap is giving definitive legal advice.

q: The provider asks for a “repeat EKG now” because the first printout shows limb lead reversal suspected—what is the best action by the CMA?
a: Verify correct lead placement and repeat the EKG promptly, because misplacement can mimic ischemic patterns and mislead clinical decisions; a common trap is charting it as “abnormal” without checking lead setup.

q: A CMA documents a POCT urine pregnancy test as “positive” but forgot to record the kit lot number and expiration—what should the CMA do next?
a: Add the required QC documentation immediately (lot/expiration, controls if applicable) per CLIA/clinic policy, because traceability is part of valid testing; a common trap is leaving it undocumented since the result is already known.

q: A waived rapid strep test is negative, but the patient’s swab was left on the counter for an hour before processing—what is the best action?
a: Repeat the test with a new specimen per manufacturer time limits, because delayed processing can invalidate results; a common trap is reporting the negative as final despite compromised specimen integrity.

q: During venipuncture the tube fills slowly and the patient reports tingling shooting down the arm; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the draw immediately and remove the needle, then apply pressure and report per protocol because this can indicate nerve involvement (trap: “repositioning” the needle to improve flow can worsen injury).

q: After a fingerstick INR POCT, the CMA notices the patient’s finger continues to bleed under the bandage—what should the CMA do first?
a: Apply direct pressure and elevate the hand until bleeding stops, then reinforce dressing and notify the provider if persistent, because anticoagulated patients can bleed longer; a common trap is applying a small bandage and moving on without confirming hemostasis.

q: A CLIA-waived fingerstick glucose control test is out of range at the start of the day—what should the CMA do next?
