a: Don a surgical mask and eye protection (plus gloves) because droplet and splash protection is needed during close contact; the trap is wearing gloves only.

q: A patient is scheduled for an injection, but the chart shows two patients with the same name in the clinic today; what should the CMA do first?
a: Use two identifiers (e.g., full name and DOB) and match to the order before preparing/administering because misidentification is a high-risk error; the trap is going by room number or face recognition.

q: While preparing a medication, you notice the order reads 0.5 mL but the prefilled syringe is 0.25 mL and you’re unsure if they are equivalent; what is the best next step?
a: Hold the medication and clarify the order with the provider/pharmacist before administration because dose accuracy is required; the trap is “doubling it” or guessing conversions.

q: You are preparing an IM vaccine and the provider hands you a vial with a partially torn label; what should the CMA do before drawing up the medication?
a: Stop and obtain a properly labeled vial (or have the provider/pharmacy verify and replace) because you must confirm the right medication/strength; the trap is relying on memory or vial appearance.

q: You begin CPR and an AED arrives; the patient’s chest is wet from a spilled drink—what should the CMA do next before applying pads?
a: Quickly dry the chest and then apply pads and follow AED prompts because moisture can interfere with pad adhesion/shock delivery; the trap is delaying AED use to fully clean or reposition extensively.

q: You retake a blood pressure and get 168/102 in an asymptomatic patient who says they “forgot their BP pill today”—what should the CMA do next?
a: Recheck after 5 minutes of rest with correct cuff/position and then promptly report the confirmed reading to the provider, because the trap is documenting a single high value without verifying technique.

q: A patient arrives for suture removal and you notice the wound edges are separating with yellow drainage; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and notify the provider before removing sutures because this suggests dehiscence/infection and needs evaluation; the trap is removing sutures because the appointment is scheduled.

q: You are assisting with a simple wound dressing change and the patient asks you to “scrape off the dead tissue while you’re in there”; what is the best response?
a: Decline and inform the provider because debridement is not within CMA scope in most outpatient settings; the trap is attempting it as “basic wound care.”

q: In the lobby, an adult patient collapses and is unresponsive; what should the CMA do first?
a: Check responsiveness and breathing and activate EMS/clinic emergency response immediately because early activation and CPR/AED save lives; the trap is searching for the chart or moving the patient unnecessarily.

q: During intake, a 58-year-old patient says they feel “a little dizzy”; you obtain BP 82/48 and HR 122, and they look pale—what should the CMA do first?
a: Have the patient lie down with legs elevated and call for the provider/activate clinic emergency response, because these vitals suggest shock and the trap is continuing the rest of intake or walking them to another room.

q: During intake for a 62-year-old scheduled for a routine hypertension follow-up, the CMA obtains a blood pressure of 198/112 mmHg and the patient says, “I feel fine,” while reaching for their car keys to leave; what should the CMA do next?
a: Have the patient sit quietly and recheck the blood pressure using correct cuff size and technique, then immediately notify the provider of the repeated severe reading because it may require urgent evaluation; the common mistake is dismissing it as anxiety or documenting it without prompt escalation.

q: The provider asks you to place a patient in the best position for an episode of syncope-like dizziness during intake; what position should you use initially?
a: Place the patient supine with legs elevated (if tolerated) because it supports perfusion and reduces fall risk; the trap is keeping them seated upright to “get more air.”

q: A teen comes in for a sports physical; pulse oximeter reads 88% but they are talking comfortably and the finger is cold with dark nail polish—what should the CMA do first?
a: Warm the hand and reposition/replace the sensor on a clean finger and recheck before escalating, because the trap is treating the number without troubleshooting common artifact.

q: You are preparing to enter a room for a BP recheck; the prior patient had a draining wound and you notice you still have the same gloves on—what is the correct next step?
a: Remove gloves, perform hand hygiene, and don new gloves only when needed for the next task, because the trap is thinking gloves replace hand hygiene and carrying contamination room-to-room.

q: In an exam room, the sharps container is overfilled and needles are protruding from the opening—what should the CMA do first?
a: Close/secure the container and replace it per protocol (and notify the supervisor if needed) before any further sharps use, because the trap is pushing items down, which increases needlestick risk.

q: While rooming a 67-year-old for a routine visit, the CMA obtains a BP of 198/112 mm Hg; the patient denies chest pain or shortness of breath and says they “feel fine”—what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop the intake, have the patient sit quietly and recheck BP with correct cuff size/positioning, then promptly notify the provider of the severely elevated reading because it may require immediate evaluation; the common mistake is documenting it as “white coat” or continuing vitals/history first.

q: You are about to clean an exam table with visible blood droplets on the paper—what PPE and cleaning approach is most appropriate?
a: Don gloves and use an EPA-registered disinfectant with the correct wet contact time after removing visible soil, because the trap is wiping quickly with alcohol and not allowing contact time for disinfection.

q: During orthostatic vital signs, the patient becomes lightheaded after standing—what should the CMA do next?
a: Assist the patient back to a safe seated/supine position and notify the provider, because the trap is insisting they remain standing to “complete the series” despite fall risk.

q: A provider requests a sterile dressing change; the CMA opens the sterile kit and accidentally brushes the sterile field with their sleeve—what should the CMA do?
a: Stop and replace the contaminated sterile field/supplies before continuing, because the trap is “being careful from now on” after sterility has already been broken.

q: A patient hands you a used tissue with blood from a nosebleed and asks where to throw it away—what should the CMA do?
a: Direct them to discard it in a lined trash receptacle and perform hand hygiene/clean any contaminated surfaces, because the trap is placing it on counters or treating it as “regular” waste without cleaning.

q: You administer a vaccine and the patient immediately reports itching and throat tightness—what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate the clinic emergency response (call for help/911 per protocol) and prepare for anaphylaxis management while monitoring airway/breathing, because the trap is having them “sit and wait” or finishing documentation first.

q: In the lobby, a patient suddenly collapses and is unresponsive; you do not feel normal breathing—what should the CMA do first?
a: Call for help/activate EMS and start CPR while someone brings the AED, because the trap is searching for a pulse for too long instead of initiating early CPR/AED sequence.

q: While drawing up medication for an injection, you notice the vial label doesn’t match the medication listed on the order, but the dose is the same—what should the CMA do next?
a: Do not administer; set it aside and clarify with the provider/pharmacy and re-verify the medication, because the trap is focusing only on dose and ignoring the right medication/right patient safety checks.

q: You are preparing an intramuscular vaccine and the patient says they have a severe latex allergy; the syringe packaging is labeled “may contain natural rubber latex”—what is the best action?
a: Stop and obtain a latex-free alternative and alert the provider before administering, because the trap is proceeding since it’s “only the packaging,” which can still pose risk.

q: A patient is due for an injection, and you realize you forgot to ask about prior reactions until after you’ve removed the needle cap—what is the best next step?
a: Pause without giving the injection, recap using a one-hand technique only if necessary for safety, and complete the allergy/reaction screening, because the trap is injecting “since it’s already ready” and missing a contraindication.

q: A patient needs a wound dressing change; the old dressing is stuck to the wound and begins bleeding when you pull—what should the CMA do next?
a: Moisten the dressing with sterile saline to loosen it and remove gently, then report unexpected bleeding to the provider, because the trap is forcefully pulling and causing tissue trauma.

q: After a minor procedure, you notice a patient’s new bandage is rapidly saturating with blood—what is the best immediate action?
a: Apply direct pressure and elevate the site while calling the provider to assess, because the trap is adding more gauze without pressure or leaving the patient unattended.

q: A provider asks you to give 0.3 mL from a multi-dose vial; after drawing up, you notice several large air bubbles—what should the CMA do?
a: Expel the bubbles and recheck the dose at eye level before injection, because the trap is assuming bubbles “don’t matter,” which can alter dose accuracy and patient comfort.

q: A patient in a wheelchair needs an orthostatic blood pressure series ordered by the provider—what is the correct sequencing?
a: Measure BP/pulse after 5 minutes supine (or reclined), then immediately on standing, then again at 3 minutes standing, because timing affects interpretation and the trap is skipping the supine rest period.

q: An adult becomes lightheaded when standing for weight and height—what positioning should the CMA use first?
a: Assist the patient to a seated or supine position and recheck vitals as indicated, because preventing a fall is the priority and the trap is insisting the patient “push through” to finish measurements.

q: A patient’s respiration rate is documented as 10/min right after the patient sighed and held their breath during BP—what is the best action before charting?
a: Reassess respirations discreetly for a full minute while the patient is unaware, because breathing changes when observed and the trap is charting an inaccurate low rate.

q: During intake, an adult’s blood pressure reads 184/112 after walking in from the parking lot; the patient denies symptoms and asks to “just get the shot and go”—what should the CMA do first?
a: Have the patient sit quietly and recheck the BP with correct cuff size and arm positioning before rooming, because activity and technique can falsely elevate readings and the trap is documenting/acting on a single unreliable value.

q: You enter the exam room and see dried blood on the counter from a prior procedure—what should the CMA do first?
a: Don gloves and clean/disinfect the surface with an appropriate disinfectant using correct contact time, because blood requires standard precautions and the trap is wiping quickly without disinfection time.

q: While obtaining vitals, an adult patient becomes agitated and insists you tell their spouse the results; the spouse is in the hallway and the patient is not clear about permission—what should the CMA do?
a: Speak privately with the patient to confirm and document permission before sharing any information, because the trap is casually disclosing health data in the hallway without verified consent.

q: While taking vitals, you count an irregular pulse at 48 bpm in a dizzy adult who looks pale—what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop the intake, ensure the patient is seated or supine for safety, and alert the provider immediately, because symptomatic bradycardia can be urgent and the trap is finishing the rest of the vitals first.

q: During rooming, a 68-year-old reports dizziness; you obtain BP 88/54 and pulse 118 sitting, and when you ask him to stand he becomes pale and says he might faint—what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist him back to a safe position (sit or supine with legs elevated) and call for the provider/activate emergency response while rechecking vitals; this prevents a fall and addresses possible shock/orthostatic hypotension, and the common mistake is continuing the standing BP or leaving the patient alone.

q: A provider asks you to assist with a minor procedure requiring sterile technique; you accidentally touch the sterile field with your bare wrist—what should you do?
a: Speak up and replace the contaminated sterile drape/field item immediately, because sterility is broken and the trap is staying quiet to “avoid delaying” the procedure.

q: While cleaning an exam room, you find a used needle on the paper-covered table—what is the safest next step?
a: Use a mechanical method (forceps/tongs) or a scoop technique to place it into a sharps container without recapping, because preventing a needlestick is critical and the trap is picking it up by hand or recapping.

q: A patient with a persistent cough arrives unmasked and sits in a full waiting room—what should the CMA do next?
a: Offer a mask and move the patient to a separate area/room as soon as possible, because source control reduces droplet spread and the trap is waiting until the provider is ready.

q: After removing gloves, the CMA notices visible soil on hands from wound care—what is the best hand hygiene action?
a: Wash with soap and water, because visible contamination is not reliably removed by sanitizer and the trap is using alcohol rub alone.

q: During rooming, a 68-year-old patient says “I feel lightheaded,” appears pale, and their seated BP is 86/54 with a pulse of 118; what should the CMA do first before repeating the BP or continuing intake?
a: Have the patient sit or lie down safely (supine with legs elevated if tolerated), stay with them, and immediately alert the provider/activate emergency response because these vitals with symptoms suggest possible shock/syncope risk; the trap is rechecking or finishing intake first while the patient remains upright and could faint.

q: The provider orders a medication injection, but the vial concentration on hand differs from what you expected—what is the CMA’s best next step?
a: Recalculate and verify the dose/volume against the order and label (and clarify with the provider/pharmacist if mismatch), because concentration errors cause overdoses and the trap is drawing up the “usual” volume by habit.

q: Just before administering an injection, the patient states they had a severe allergic reaction to a similar medication years ago—what should the CMA do next?
a: Hold the medication and immediately notify the provider, because allergy history changes the safety plan and the trap is proceeding since “the order is already in.”

q: You are about to give an IM vaccine and realize the patient’s chart has two similar names and the DOB is not visible on the screen—what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop and verify identity using two identifiers (e.g., full name and DOB) with the patient and the chart before preparing/administering, because wrong-patient errors are preventable and the trap is relying on room number or appearance.

q: In the lobby, a patient suddenly collapses and is unresponsive—what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate emergency response (call for help/911 per clinic protocol) and start CPR once unresponsiveness and no normal breathing/pulse are confirmed, because early activation and compressions save lives and the trap is searching for paperwork or waiting for the provider.

q: During intake, a 64-year-old reports dizziness when standing; vitals show BP 86/52, HR 118, RR 22, skin cool and clammy—what should the CMA do first?
a: Have the patient lie supine with legs elevated and alert the provider immediately because these are shock/poor perfusion signs; the trap is continuing the intake or walking the patient to an exam room.

q: During wound care, the patient asks you to remove sutures “a day early” because they are uncomfortable, and the provider has not evaluated the wound—what should the CMA do?
a: Explain you cannot remove sutures without a provider order and notify the provider for assessment, because timing depends on healing and the trap is performing an unverified procedure outside instructions.

q: While obtaining vitals, a patient states they just drank a large coffee and smoked outside; the pulse is 112 and regular with no symptoms—what should the CMA do next?
a: Ask the patient to rest quietly and recheck pulse in a few minutes and document the stimulant use because recent caffeine/nicotine can elevate HR; the trap is immediately escalating as an emergency without reassessment.

q: A patient asks you to “rub the site hard” right after a vaccine because it “helps it spread”—what should the CMA do?
a: Apply gentle pressure with gauze and advise against vigorous rubbing, because rubbing can increase local irritation/bleeding and the trap is performing unnecessary manipulation.

q: A 19-year-old anxious patient’s automated BP reads 168/110 over a hoodie sleeve and they were talking and laughing—what is the best next step?
a: Recheck manually after 5 minutes of rest with the correct cuff on a bare arm and feet flat because technique errors can falsely elevate BP; the trap is documenting the first reading as “hypertension.”

q: During an emergency, the AED arrives while CPR is in progress—what should the CMA do next?
a: Turn on the AED and apply pads as instructed while minimizing interruptions in compressions, because early defibrillation for shockable rhythms improves outcomes and the trap is stopping compressions for long periods to “set up.”

q: You are changing a dressing and the old gauze is stuck to the wound bed—what is the best next step?
a: Moisten the dressing with sterile saline before removal, because dry removal can damage tissue and restart bleeding and the trap is pulling it off quickly to “get it over with.”

q: After removing gloves used for a wound dressing change, what should the CMA do next before touching the computer keyboard?
a: Perform hand hygiene immediately because gloves are not a substitute and hands can be contaminated during removal; the trap is moving directly to documentation with “clean-looking” hands.

q: In an exam room, you notice a sharps container is overfilled and needles are protruding—what is the best action?
a: Close/lock the container and replace it per facility process before further use because overfilled containers increase needlestick risk; the trap is pushing items down or continuing to use it “one more time.”

q: You are about to room a patient with active coughing and a mask in hand; several patients are in the waiting room—what should the CMA do first?
a: Provide a mask and ask the patient to put it on (and perform hand hygiene) before moving them because source control reduces transmission; the trap is taking them straight back without addressing respiratory hygiene.

q: A patient with COPD comes in for a routine visit; pulse oximetry reads 84% but the patient is speaking in full sentences and nail polish is present—what is the best action?
a: Remove nail polish/warm the hand and repeat the SpO₂ (and confirm probe placement) before notifying the provider because poor signal can give a false low; the trap is ignoring 84% or assuming it’s “normal for COPD” without verification.

q: You enter a room for a routine injection and see dried blood on the counter from the previous patient—what should you do first?
a: Put on appropriate PPE and disinfect the surface with an approved disinfectant before setting up supplies because environmental cleaning breaks the chain of infection; the trap is placing clean supplies down and “cleaning later.”

q: A provider asks you to “quickly recap that used needle” to carry it to the sharps container across the room—what should the CMA do?
a: Do not recap; engage the safety device and carry it safely to the sharps container immediately because recapping is a common cause of needlesticks; the trap is complying because it was a provider request.

q: A patient becomes pale and diaphoretic during intake and says, “I feel like I’m going to pass out”—what is the CMA’s first action?
a: Assist the patient to a safe seated/lying position and call for help because preventing a fall is the immediate safety priority; the trap is continuing questions or leaving the patient alone to “go get the nurse.”

q: During intake, a 58-year-old patient says they feel “a little dizzy,” and their vital signs show BP 86/54 mmHg with a weak rapid pulse while they are sitting upright on the exam table; what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist the patient to a supine position with legs elevated and call for the provider/activate clinic emergency response while rechecking vitals, because suspected hypotension requires immediate stabilization and escalation—do not continue routine intake or have the patient stand/walk, which can worsen syncope risk.

q: During the “rights” check for an IM antibiotic, the patient says they are allergic to penicillin and the medication name sounds similar—what should the CMA do next?
a: Hold the medication and notify the provider immediately because allergy verification is critical before administration; the trap is proceeding because “the provider ordered it” or assuming it’s unrelated.

q: A provider requests you set up a sterile field for a minor procedure; you accidentally brush the sterile drape with your sleeve—what should you do next?
a: Stop and replace the contaminated sterile drape because sterility is broken by contact with nonsterile items; the trap is ignoring it because “it barely touched.”

q: You are about to administer a subcutaneous medication when the patient suddenly says, “I’m pregnant—I forgot to mention”—what is the best action?
a: Pause the administration and immediately inform the provider because pregnancy can change medication safety/ordering decisions; the trap is administering because “it’s already prepared” and out of the CMA’s scope to judge safety.

q: You remove an old dressing and note the wound has increased redness, warmth, and purulent drainage compared with last visit—what should the CMA do next?
a: Cover with a clean dressing and promptly report the change to the provider because it suggests infection requiring provider evaluation; the trap is applying ointment or advising antibiotics, which is outside CMA scope.

q: A patient with suspected scabies needs vitals and a brief intake; what PPE is most appropriate to don first?
a: Don gloves (and a gown if contact with clothing/skin is likely) because scabies spreads by direct contact and requires contact precautions; the trap is using only a surgical mask as if it were airborne.

q: A patient is due for an IM injection and asks you to “just give it in the same sore arm as last time so I don’t have two sore arms”—what should the CMA do?
a: Assess the preferred site and choose an appropriate, non-tender site with adequate muscle mass (and rotate sites when possible) because injecting into a sore area increases pain and may affect absorption; the trap is prioritizing convenience over safe site selection.

q: After an IM vaccine, the patient stands up quickly and looks unsteady; what should the CMA do first?
a: Have the patient sit back down and observe (with fall precautions) because syncope can occur after injections and preventing injury is priority; the trap is letting them walk out because they “say they’re fine.”

q: During intake, a 67-year-old patient reports dizziness; you obtain vitals and note BP 84/52, pulse 118, and the patient looks pale—what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist the patient to a supine position with legs elevated and immediately alert the provider/activate the clinic’s emergency response because this is symptomatic hypotension suggestive of shock; the common mistake is continuing the intake or having the patient stand/walk, which increases fall risk and delays care.

q: During intake, a 58-year-old says he feels “a little dizzy,” and you obtain BP 84/52 mmHg with a weak radial pulse; what should the CMA do first?
a: Have the patient sit or lie down safely and call for the provider/activate clinic emergency response per protocol because hypotension with symptoms suggests poor perfusion; the trap is finishing the intake or sending him back to the lobby.

q: A patient becomes pale and says they feel faint immediately after standing from the exam table; what is the CMA’s best next step?
a: Assist the patient back to a seated or supine position and assess vital signs because this may be orthostatic intolerance and safety (fall prevention) is the priority; the trap is walking them to the front desk or leaving them standing.

q: In the lobby, a patient suddenly collapses and is unresponsive; you don’t see a DNR form—what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate emergency response/911 and begin CPR (send someone for the AED) because early CPR/AED saves lives and you should not delay for paperwork; the trap is searching the chart or waiting for the provider before acting.

q: While rooming a patient, you count a pulse of 48 bpm and the patient reports new lightheadedness; what should you do next?
a: Reassess vital signs (including BP) and notify the provider promptly because symptomatic bradycardia may require immediate evaluation; the trap is assuming “athlete pulse” without correlating symptoms.

q: You are obtaining respirations and the patient starts talking to you; what should the CMA do to get an accurate rate?
a: Continue counting discreetly without alerting the patient you’re measuring respirations because awareness alters breathing; the trap is restarting while openly announcing “I’m counting your breaths.”

q: A patient’s first BP is 168/104 mmHg, and they say they “ran in from the parking lot”; what is the best action before reporting it?
a: Have the patient rest quietly for 5 minutes with proper cuff size/arm position and repeat the BP because exertion and technique can falsely elevate readings; the trap is reporting a single potentially inaccurate measurement as the baseline.

q: A 72-year-old in a wheelchair needs an exam-table transfer for vitals; what is the CMA’s safest first step?
a: Lock the wheelchair and ensure the exam table is stable/at appropriate height before assisting because stabilizing equipment prevents falls; the trap is grabbing the patient’s arm to lift before securing the wheelchair.

q: A 26-year-old arrives for a routine visit, denies symptoms, and you get an oral temperature of 101.6°F (38.7°C); what is the best next step?
a: Recheck using a confirmed method (e.g., tympanic/temporal per device guidance) and report the fever to the provider with infection-control precautions because an unexpected fever changes visit planning; the trap is documenting once and proceeding as normal.

q: A provider requests a rectal temperature on an adult with diarrhea; what positioning is best for the CMA to use?
a: Place the patient in Sims’ position (left side, right knee flexed) because it provides access and comfort while maintaining safety; the trap is using prone positioning, which is less stable and less comfortable for most patients.

q: A patient is coughing in the waiting area and asks to check in at the front desk; what should the CMA do first to reduce transmission?
a: Provide a mask and separate the patient from others (as space allows) while using standard precautions because source control is the fastest way to limit droplet spread; the trap is starting paperwork first at a crowded counter.

q: The provider orders 0.5 mL of medication IM, but the prefilled syringe in your hand is labeled 1 mL; what should the CMA do before entering the room?
a: Clarify and ensure the correct dose is prepared (adjust to 0.5 mL using appropriate technique or obtain the correct syringe) because dose accuracy is a medication right; the trap is giving the whole syringe because it’s prefilled.

q: You are about to give an IM vaccine and the patient says they are “allergic to latex”; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and verify latex-free supplies (gloves, bandage, vial stopper/syringe components per product info) and notify the provider if unable to confirm because preventing an allergic reaction is a safety priority; the trap is proceeding because the allergy “isn’t medication-related.”

q: After removing gloves, you realize you touched the outside of your mask while talking to a patient; what is the best immediate action?
a: Perform hand hygiene right away because contaminated hands are a common route of self-inoculation and spread; the trap is adjusting the mask more or continuing rooming before cleaning hands.

q: While preparing a sterile dressing change, you accidentally touch the sterile gauze with your bare hand; what is the best next step?
a: Discard the contaminated gauze and replace it with a new sterile item because sterility is broken and using it increases infection risk; the trap is using it anyway because “it was just a quick touch.”

q: You enter an exam room to clean after a procedure and see a blood spill on the floor; what should the CMA do first?
a: Don appropriate PPE (gloves and, if splash risk, gown/face protection) before handling the spill because protecting yourself breaks the chain of infection; the trap is wiping it quickly with bare hands or inadequate protection.

q: A patient with a draining wound needs assistance to the restroom, and your gloves have visible drainage on them; what should you do before touching door handles or the patient’s walker?
a: Remove gloves, perform hand hygiene, and don clean gloves as needed because contaminated gloves spread pathogens to high-touch surfaces; the trap is “double-gloving” over dirty gloves or keeping the same pair on.

q: During intake, a 56-year-old reports “tight chest pressure” and looks pale; before finishing the medication list, what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the intake and alert the provider/activate emergency response per clinic protocol while keeping the patient seated and assessing airway/breathing, because chest pressure is potentially life-threatening and the trap is continuing routine questions.

q: In the lobby, a visitor collapses and is unresponsive; what should the CMA do first before retrieving the AED?
a: Confirm unresponsiveness and call for help/activate EMS (have someone call 911) because early activation speeds definitive care; the trap is leaving the person alone to search for equipment without initiating the response.

q: You are applying a pressure dressing to a small arm laceration after a lab draw and the patient reports numbness in the fingers; what should the CMA do next?
a: Loosen the dressing and reassess circulation/sensation because numbness can indicate impaired blood flow or nerve compression; the trap is leaving it tight to “stop bleeding” without checking distal perfusion.

q: A patient returns from the restroom and says they feel “itchy all over” and you notice hives and lip swelling 5 minutes after an injection; what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate emergency response (call for help/911 per clinic protocol) and assess airway/breathing because this may be anaphylaxis and is immediately life-threatening; the trap is having them sit and “wait it out” or just documenting the reaction.

q: Right before administering an injection, the patient states, “I’ve never had this shot before—what is it for?”; what should the CMA do next?
a: Pause and provide basic education within scope and/or get the provider to answer questions before administering because informed cooperation improves safety and adherence; the trap is injecting first and explaining afterward.

q: A patient’s blood pressure reads 182/110 on an automated cuff, but they’re talking comfortably and rushed in from the parking lot; what is the CMA’s best next step?
a: Recheck manually after 5 minutes of rest with correct cuff size and arm at heart level, because technique and recent activity can falsely elevate readings and the trap is immediately documenting a single questionable value as final.

q: While taking a radial pulse, you note an irregular rhythm and the rate varies; what should the CMA do next?
a: Apically count for a full 60 seconds and report the irregularity per protocol, because irregular pulses require apical confirmation and the trap is estimating for 15 seconds and missing dysrhythmia.

q: You draw up medication for an injection and realize the label on the vial is smudged and you cannot confirm the concentration; what is the best action?
a: Discard the prepared dose and obtain a clearly labeled, verified medication because you must confirm the “right medication” and “right dose”; the trap is guessing based on vial color or prior experience.

q: A patient is placed in Contact Precautions for suspected scabies; in what order should the CMA remove PPE when leaving the room?
a: Remove gloves first, then gown, then perform hand hygiene (and remove eye protection/mask if worn per situation), because gloves are most contaminated and the trap is touching your face or clothes with contaminated gloves.

q: A dizzy patient stands up from the exam table after vitals and says the room is spinning; what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist them back to a seated or supine position and ensure safety (prevent a fall) before rechecking vitals and notifying the provider, because immediate injury prevention is priority and the trap is leaving to “get help” without stabilizing them.

q: After removing gloves, the CMA’s hands look clean and the next task is to type in the EHR; what is the correct next step?
a: Perform hand hygiene immediately after glove removal, because gloves are not a substitute and contamination occurs during removal; the trap is going straight to the keyboard and spreading pathogens.

q: A child’s respiratory rate seems fast, and you’ve already placed the stethoscope on their chest; how should the CMA best obtain an accurate count?
a: Count respirations for 30–60 seconds without telling the child you’re counting, because awareness can change breathing pattern and the trap is announcing it and undercounting.

q: A provider asks you to “quickly just recap that used needle” because the sharps container is across the room; what should the CMA do?
a: Refuse to recap and instead immediately activate safety device and dispose the needle in a sharps container, because recapping is a major needlestick risk and the trap is following a convenience request that violates safety.

q: You enter an exam room and see dried blood on the counter from the prior patient; what should the CMA do before setting up supplies?
a: Don appropriate PPE and disinfect the surface with an approved disinfectant for the required contact time, because environmental cleaning breaks the chain of infection and the trap is wiping quickly without contact time.

q: During intake at an outpatient clinic, a patient says they feel “lightheaded,” and you obtain a seated BP of 86/54 with a pulse of 118; the provider is running behind and the patient asks to lie down—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Assist the patient to a safe supine position with legs elevated, stay with them, and promptly notify the provider/activate clinic emergency response as needed because symptomatic hypotension with tachycardia suggests instability; the trap is simply repeating the BP or sending them to the waiting room.

q: You are preparing for a blood glucose fingerstick on a patient with a history of hepatitis C; what infection-control approach is required?
a: Use Standard Precautions (gloves, hand hygiene, safe sharps disposal) for all patients regardless of diagnosis, because infection status doesn’t change baseline precautions and the trap is using extra precautions only when a condition is disclosed.

q: During a dressing change, the patient’s wound drainage soaks through the gauze and begins leaking; what should the CMA do next?
a: Reinforce the dressing as needed and promptly notify the provider about the amount/character of drainage, because saturation may signal bleeding or infection and the trap is removing everything repeatedly without escalation.

q: In the lobby, a patient suddenly collapses and is unresponsive; what should the CMA do first?
a: Ensure the scene is safe, check responsiveness and breathing, and have someone call 911/get the AED while you begin CPR if not breathing normally, because early CPR/AED saves lives and the trap is searching for a pulse too long before acting.

q: While preparing an injection, you realize the medication label is smudged and you cannot clearly read the concentration; what should the CMA do?
a: Discard it and obtain a clearly labeled medication (or have it verified) before drawing up, because unreadable labels create high-risk dosing errors and the trap is “guessing” based on packaging.

q: The order reads “ceftriaxone 500 mg IM,” and the vial concentration results in a volume larger than expected for one site; what is the CMA’s best next step?
a: Confirm the ordered dose and calculate volume, then follow guidance to split into appropriate sites or consult the provider/pharmacist per protocol, because excessive volume increases pain/complications and the trap is injecting the whole volume into one site without checking.

q: You are about to administer an IM vaccine, and the patient says, “I’m not sure what shot this is”; what should the CMA do next?
a: Pause and verify the medication, dose, patient identity, and provide the correct vaccine information statement/education before giving it, because informed administration and the rights of medication reduce errors and the trap is proceeding because “it’s on the schedule.”

q: A patient scheduled for an injection reports a past episode of facial swelling after the same medication; what is the CMA’s best action?
a: Hold the medication and immediately notify the provider before administering, because prior swelling suggests possible allergy and the trap is giving it anyway because “it’s ordered.”

q: While cleaning an exam table, the disinfectant label states “wet contact time 3 minutes,” but the surface dries in 30 seconds; what is the best action?
a: Reapply enough disinfectant to keep the surface wet for the full 3 minutes, because killing pathogens requires labeled contact time and the trap is assuming “wipe and dry” is adequate.

q: A patient needs a wound dressing change and the provider requests sterile technique; what is the key CMA action to maintain sterility during setup?
a: Open the sterile field without reaching over it and keep sterile items above waist and in view, because reaching over/turning away contaminates the field and the trap is treating sterile like clean technique.

q: During intake at an urgent care clinic, a 62-year-old patient says he feels “lightheaded,” and you obtain BP 82/54 with a regular pulse of 118 while he is seated; he insists he just wants to finish the paperwork—what should the medical assistant do first?
a: Stop the intake, place the patient supine with legs elevated and ensure airway/breathing are stable, then immediately alert the provider/activate emergency response and recheck vitals because symptomatic hypotension with tachycardia suggests possible shock and the common trap is continuing paperwork or walking the patient to an exam room.

q: You are rechecking a BP and the patient’s legs are dangling off the exam table while talking; what is the best correction before you repeat the reading?
a: Position the patient with back supported, feet flat on the floor, and arm supported at heart level, because poor positioning falsely elevates readings and a common trap is repeating the BP without fixing technique.

q: You attach an AED during a clinic emergency and it announces “shock advised”; what should the CMA do immediately before pressing shock?
a: Loudly state “clear,” ensure no one is touching the patient, and visually confirm the area is clear before delivering the shock, because contact can injure rescuers and the trap is shocking while staff are still providing hands-on care.

q: You enter an exam room to take vitals and notice dried blood on the reusable BP cuff from the prior patient; what is the best next step?
a: Remove the cuff from use and clean/disinfect it per manufacturer/clinic protocol before using another clean cuff, because contaminated equipment spreads infection and a common trap is wiping quickly with an alcohol pad and proceeding without proper disinfection/contact time.

q: A patient feels faint immediately after standing on the scale during check-in; what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist the patient to a chair or supine position and assess responsiveness, because fall prevention and airway/breathing/circulation come before finishing measurements and a common trap is trying to “get the weight quickly” while the patient is unstable.

q: During intake, a 62-year-old reports feeling “a little dizzy” and your first BP reading is 86/54 with a regular pulse of 96; what should the CMA do first?
a: Have the patient sit or lie down safely and immediately recheck BP (and assess for acute symptoms) before notifying the provider, because treating possible hypotension/syncope risk comes before documenting or continuing the intake and a common trap is assuming the cuff “must be wrong” and moving on.

q: While taking vitals, a 45-year-old’s BP is 182/118 and they mention a new severe headache; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the routine intake and immediately alert the provider/clinical lead while keeping the patient seated and monitored, because this may be a hypertensive emergency and a common trap is rechecking multiple times before escalating.

q: During intake, a 58-year-old reports “pressure in my chest” and looks pale; vitals show BP 88/56, pulse 122, RR 24, SpO₂ 91% on room air—what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate emergency response (call 911/alert the provider immediately) and keep the patient seated or supine while monitoring airway/breathing/circulation, because hypotension with chest pressure and low oxygen suggests a potentially life-threatening event and the trap is trying to finish the intake or recheck vitals before getting help.

q: A patient’s bandage is saturated and you’re about to change it; what is the correct sequencing for PPE and hand hygiene?
a: Perform hand hygiene, don gloves (and gown/eye protection if splash is possible), then remove the soiled dressing, because clean hands and barrier protection come before exposure and a common trap is putting on gloves without hand hygiene.

q: A patient with suspected scabies needs vitals and rooming; what infection-control approach is most appropriate in an outpatient clinic?
a: Use gloves and gown with strict hand hygiene and avoid shared equipment unless disinfected, because contact transmission is the main risk and a common trap is using only a mask while neglecting contact precautions.

q: While preparing an injection, you notice the medication vial has visible particles and is not labeled as a suspension; what should you do?
a: Do not use the vial and obtain a new vial while notifying the appropriate staff, because particles may indicate contamination or degradation and a common trap is shaking it and administering anyway.

q: You are preparing a sterile dressing change and realize you touched the center of the sterile field with an ungloved hand; what is the best action?
a: Discard the contaminated sterile setup and start over with new sterile supplies, because sterility is broken once contaminated and a common trap is “working around” the contaminated area.

q: You are about to administer an IM vaccine and the label reads 0.5 mL but the syringe you picked up is prefilled with 0.7 mL; what should you do next?
a: Stop and verify the correct dose and product with the order/packaging and your supervisor before administering, because dose discrepancies are a medication error risk and a common trap is assuming “prefilled means correct.”

q: During a throat swab, the patient gags and coughs repeatedly; what PPE should the CMA add beyond gloves?
a: Add a surgical mask and eye protection (goggles/face shield), because droplets are likely during coughing and a common trap is relying on gloves alone for splash-risk procedures.

q: You remove your gloves after wound care but still need to document on the computer in the room; what should you do next to prevent contamination?
a: Perform hand hygiene before touching the keyboard, because gloves are not a substitute for handwashing and a common trap is thinking “no visible soil” means hand hygiene can wait.

q: A patient asks you to inject their medication “a little higher” than usual because it hurts less; what is the best response by the CMA?
a: Use the approved anatomical landmark and technique for the ordered route or ask the provider to reassess the site if needed, because improper site selection risks nerve/vascular injury and a common trap is letting patient preference override safe landmarks.

q: You are rooming a patient for a pelvic exam and the provider is running behind; how should you position and drape the patient while maintaining privacy?
a: Keep the patient covered and in a comfortable position (not in lithotomy) until the provider is ready, because prolonged exposure increases discomfort and privacy risk and a common trap is positioning early to “save time.”

q: After giving a vaccine, the patient becomes pale and says they feel like they might pass out; what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist the patient to a supine position with legs elevated and stay with them while calling for help, because syncope can lead to injury and a common trap is having the patient “walk it off” or sending them to the lobby.

q: During intake at an urgent care clinic, a 58-year-old reports chest pressure and nausea; you obtain vitals showing BP 88/56, HR 118, RR 24, and the patient looks pale and sweaty—what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate emergency response (call for the provider/EMS), keep the patient seated or supine, and begin basic life support readiness while rechecking vitals as directed, because these are signs of possible shock/acute cardiac event and the common mistake is continuing routine intake or sending the patient to the waiting area.

q: In the waiting room, a visitor says “My wife is in room 3—what were her vitals, is she okay?”; what should the CMA do?
a: Politely refuse to share any information and offer to notify the patient or have the patient provide permission, because this is protected health information and a common trap is disclosing “small details” out of courtesy.

q: You draw up medication and then realize you did not verify the patient’s identity yet; what is the best next step before giving the injection?
a: Pause and confirm at least two patient identifiers and match them to the order and medication, because right patient is a core safety step and a common trap is relying on room number or familiarity.

q: During intake, a 58-year-old patient says they feel “lightheaded,” and you obtain BP 86/54 and pulse 118; what should the CMA do first?
a: Seat/lay the patient supine with legs elevated and alert the provider immediately, because these vitals suggest possible shock and the trap is continuing the intake or having them stand to recheck.

q: During wound care teaching, a patient asks if they can reuse the same gauze pad later “if it still looks clean”; what should the CMA say?
a: Instruct them to use clean, single-use dressings each time and discard used gauze, because reused materials reintroduce bacteria and a common trap is judging cleanliness by appearance alone.

q: You’re repeating a BP because the first reading was high, and the patient is talking with legs crossed; what is the best next step before rechecking?
a: Have the patient sit quietly for 5 minutes with feet flat, back supported, and arm at heart level, because poor positioning falsely elevates BP and the trap is documenting an inaccurate repeat.

q: A patient becomes dizzy when you help them from the table to standing after an exam; what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist them back to a seated or supine position and assess for injury/notify the provider as needed, because fall prevention is the priority and the trap is trying to “walk it off.”

q: You are about to enter an exam room for a patient with a draining wound; what is the correct PPE sequence before contact?
a: Perform hand hygiene then don gloves (and gown/eye protection if splash risk), because PPE selection is based on anticipated exposure and the trap is skipping hand hygiene because “gloves are on.”

q: You are preparing an IM vaccine and notice the vial label doesn’t match the order in the chart; what should you do next?
a: Stop and resolve the discrepancy by verifying the order/medication with the provider or pharmacist before drawing up, because giving the wrong product is a serious error and the trap is assuming “it’s probably the same.”

q: After removing gloves, you notice visible soil on your hands; what should you do next?
a: Wash with soap and water, because alcohol-based rub is less effective on visibly soiled hands and the trap is using sanitizer only.

q: You obtain a respiratory rate of 10/min in an adult who appears very drowsy in the exam room; what is the priority action?
a: Stay with the patient and notify the provider immediately, because low respirations with decreased alertness can signal respiratory depression and the trap is “just rechecking later.”

q: While taking vitals, you note a pulse ox of 89% on room air but the patient is speaking full sentences; what should you do next?
a: Recheck the reading (ensure warm finger/no nail polish, good waveform) and report promptly if still low, because inaccurate probe placement is common but persistent hypoxemia is urgent.

q: You remove a used needle after an injection and the sharps container is across the room; what is the safest next step?
a: Activate the safety device immediately and carry the syringe to a nearby approved sharps container without recapping, because recapping causes needlesticks and the trap is “temporary recapping to walk safely.”

q: In the hallway, a patient asks you to confirm whether their spouse was seen in the clinic today; what should the CMA do?
a: Decline and redirect them to the spouse to share information, because attendance is protected health information and the trap is thinking it’s harmless “just a yes/no.”

q: While cleaning a wound, you accidentally touch the sterile gauze to the countertop; what should you do next?
a: Discard the contaminated gauze and replace it, because any break in sterility/cleanliness can introduce pathogens and the trap is using it anyway “since it looks clean.”

q: A provider orders a wound dressing change; you set up supplies and realize sterile gauze will touch only intact skin around the wound—what technique is appropriate?
a: Use clean technique unless a sterile field is specifically required by the procedure/order, because most routine dressing changes in ambulatory care are clean and the trap is mixing sterile and nonsterile items without a plan.

q: A parent says their child “always gets the same shot” but the immunization record shows it was already given last month; what should the CMA do before administering?
a: Pause and verify the immunization history with the record/EHR and clarify with the provider, because duplicate dosing can harm and the trap is relying on memory or the parent’s request.

q: A patient begins wheezing and develops hives minutes after an injection in the clinic; what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate emergency response (get help/call 911 per protocol) and stay with the patient while preparing for CPR/AED if needed, because this may be anaphylaxis and the trap is sending them to the waiting room.

q: In the lobby, a visitor collapses and is unresponsive; what is the correct first action for the CMA?
a: Check responsiveness and breathing and call for help/activate EMS while getting the AED, because early activation and defibrillation saves lives and the trap is searching for a pulse for too long.

q: While rooming a 68-year-old for a routine follow-up, the CMA obtains vitals: BP 198/110, pulse 92, respirations 18, temp 98.4°F; the patient says they “feel fine” and asks to proceed—what should the CMA do next?
a: Recheck the BP manually after the patient rests quietly with proper cuff size and arm supported at heart level, then promptly notify the provider of the confirmed severe elevation because it may require urgent evaluation; the common trap is ignoring it because the patient is asymptomatic or charting an unverified automated reading.

q: A patient reports a history of fainting with shots and turns pale as you prepare a vaccine; what should the CMA do next?
a: Have them seated or supine before administering and monitor afterward, because positioning prevents injury from syncope and the trap is giving it standing “to be quick.”

q: While giving a subcutaneous injection, you realize you selected a 1.5-inch needle intended for IM administration; what should you do?
a: Stop before injecting and obtain the correct needle/syringe setup, because needle length affects route and absorption and the trap is proceeding once the needle is already opened.

q: During intake, a 68-year-old reports dizziness when standing; you obtain BP 92/58 and pulse 116 sitting and they look pale—what should you do first before completing the rest of the vitals?
a: Have the patient sit or lie down safely and notify the provider/lead immediately because these findings suggest possible instability; the trap is continuing the full intake or letting them walk to the scale.

q: You take an oral temperature on a patient who just drank hot coffee in the lobby; they insist they have a fever and want it recorded now—what should you do next?
a: Wait about 15 minutes (or use an alternate site per clinic protocol) and then retake because recent hot liquids skew oral temps; the trap is recording an inaccurate value to satisfy the patient.

q: A healthy 26-year-old’s automated BP reads 168/102 but they are talking and moving their arm during the reading—what is the best next step?
a: Recheck manually after 5 minutes with the correct cuff size and arm supported at heart level because motion/technique commonly causes false highs; the trap is documenting the first value as final without confirmation.

q: A patient arrives for a routine visit and says they took a “water pill” and now feels faint; their pulse is rapid and irregular on palpation—what should you do next?
a: Stop the intake, place them in a safe position, and alert the provider promptly because an irregular, symptomatic pulse needs escalation; the trap is finishing the questionnaire first or assuming anxiety.

q: During CPR in the clinic, the AED arrives and you see a medication patch on the patient’s chest; what should you do next?
a: Remove the patch with gloves, wipe the area, and then place AED pads, because patches can interfere and cause burns and the trap is placing pads directly over it.

q: While counting respirations, the patient asks, “What are you doing?” and starts breathing faster—what is the best action to get an accurate respiratory rate?
a: Continue counting discreetly while appearing to assess the pulse because awareness alters breathing; the trap is explaining in the moment and then charting the now-inaccurate rate.

q: You obtain a pediatric pulse oximeter reading of 84% but the child is kicking and the probe is on a cold finger—what is the best next step?
a: Reposition/secure the sensor, warm the extremity, ensure a good waveform, and recheck immediately because poor perfusion/motion causes false lows; the trap is ignoring a potentially critical value without verifying.

q: A patient with a history of syncope needs orthostatic vitals ordered by the provider—what is the correct sequence for obtaining them safely?
a: Measure after 5 minutes supine, then sitting, then standing with support and prompt symptom check because position changes can cause falls; the trap is starting with standing or leaving the patient unattended.

q: You are preparing to take a blood pressure on a patient with a dialysis fistula in the left arm and an IV in the right forearm from earlier—what should you do?
a: Do not use either affected arm and ask the provider for direction/alternative site (e.g., forearm cuff or thigh if trained) because compression can damage access and alter readings; the trap is “just using the IV arm quickly.”

q: You enter an exam room and see dried blood on the exam table paper from the previous patient; the next patient is waiting—what should you do first?
a: Don gloves and clean/disinfect the surface with an appropriate disinfectant and contact time before rooming the next patient because turnover must break the chain of infection; the trap is just replacing paper without disinfecting.

q: While drawing up supplies for a procedure, you realize you forgot to remove your stethoscope after examining a patient with a draining wound—what is the best next step?
a: Disinfect the stethoscope (and perform hand hygiene) before using it on anyone else because equipment is a common fomite; the trap is assuming gloves prevented contamination of shared items.

q: A patient with a frequent cough is in the waiting area without a mask and approaches the desk to check in—what should the CMA do first?
a: Provide a mask and separate them from others (spatial distancing/rooming when possible) using standard and respiratory hygiene because source control prevents spread; the trap is completing paperwork first while they remain near others.

q: You are about to put on PPE to irrigate a wound that may splash—what PPE is most appropriate?
a: Gloves, gown, and eye/face protection because splashes to mucous membranes are a key exposure route; the trap is wearing only gloves and risking eye contamination.

q: You are preparing an IM vaccine, and the patient says they had a severe allergy to a previous dose but “it was years ago”; the provider hasn’t seen them yet—what should you do next?
a: Hold the injection and immediately inform the provider because a history of severe reaction requires clinical decision-making; the trap is proceeding because the order exists or because the reaction was “in the past.”

q: A coworker asks you to recap a used needle “just this once” so they can carry it to the sharps container—what should you do?
a: Do not recap; activate the safety device and place the needle directly into a sharps container because recapping increases needlestick risk; the trap is prioritizing convenience over exposure prevention.

q: After removing your gloves, you plan to sanitize your hands but notice a visible smear of blood on your finger—what is the best action?
a: Wash with soap and water immediately because visible soil requires washing, not sanitizer alone; the trap is relying on alcohol gel when hands are visibly contaminated.

q: After an IM injection, the patient becomes pale, diaphoretic, and says they feel like they will faint—what is the best immediate action?
a: Assist them to a safe position (supine with legs elevated if tolerated) and stay with them while calling for help because vasovagal reactions can lead to falls; the trap is sending them to the lobby or leaving them alone.

q: In the exam room, a patient suddenly collapses and is unresponsive; you don’t see normal breathing—what should you do first in the outpatient clinic?
a: Activate the emergency response (call for help/911 per protocol) and start CPR while someone retrieves the AED because early CPR/AED saves lives; the trap is checking vitals or searching for a pulse for too long before starting compressions.

q: During intake, a 58-year-old reports chest pressure and looks pale; before finishing the health history, what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the intake, seat/position the patient safely and alert the provider/activate the clinic’s emergency response immediately because chest pain is potentially life-threatening and the trap is “finishing the forms/vitals first” and delaying escalation.

q: You draw up an ordered injection but the patient’s name and date of birth on the wristband do not match the chart—what should you do first?
a: Pause and re-identify the patient using two identifiers and resolve the discrepancy before giving anything because wrong-patient errors are preventable; the trap is relying on room number or verbal confirmation alone.

q: While preparing to administer an injection, you notice the medication label concentration does not match what the order in the chart states—what is the best action?
a: Stop and clarify with the provider/pharmacist/clinical lead before preparing/administering because concentration mismatches can cause dosing errors; the trap is “doing the math” and giving it anyway without verification.

q: While taking an adult’s blood pressure, the cuff is placed over a long-sleeve sweater and you get 182/96; what is the best next step?
a: Recheck BP with the correct cuff size on a bare arm after a brief rest because improper technique can falsely elevate readings; the trap is documenting/acting on an artifact value without confirmation.

q: A teen arrives for a sports physical and says they feel dizzy when standing; which patient position is best before obtaining vital signs?
a: Have the patient lie supine (or sit with support if supine not possible) before repeating vitals because safety and fall prevention come first; the trap is standing them for orthostatic vitals before stabilizing.

q: During a dressing change, the provider uses sterile supplies and asks you to open the sterile kit—what is the best technique to avoid contamination?
a: Open the outer flap away first, then side flaps, then the flap toward you, keeping your hands above waist and out of the sterile field because crossing over or reaching in contaminates; the trap is leaning over the field to “help.”

q: You record a pulse of 48 bpm in an adult who denies athletic training and appears lightheaded; what should the CMA do next?
a: Reassess the pulse for a full minute and notify the provider promptly because symptomatic bradycardia needs evaluation; the trap is assuming it’s normal or only documenting without reporting symptoms.

q: During intake in an urgent care clinic, a 58-year-old reports dizziness and you obtain BP 86/52 with a manual cuff after walking from the lobby; the patient is pale but talking—what should the CMA do next?
a: Have the patient sit or lie supine with legs elevated, recheck the BP promptly, and immediately notify the provider while staying with the patient because symptomatic hypotension can signal instability; the common trap is documenting and continuing the intake without addressing positioning and escalation first.

q: You are about to enter an exam room to remove a dressing and notice your hands are visibly soiled after cleaning a spill; what should you do next?
a: Wash with soap and water before patient contact because visibly soiled hands require washing (not just sanitizer); the trap is using alcohol rub when it won’t remove organic material effectively.

q: After removing gloves, you realize you still need to adjust the patient’s glasses and open the door; what is the correct next step?
a: Perform hand hygiene immediately after glove removal before touching anything because gloves don’t replace hand hygiene; the trap is touching “clean” items right after doffing gloves.

q: A provider requests help setting up a sterile field for a minor procedure; what is the CMA’s best practice when placing sterile packages on the field?
a: Open packages without reaching over the sterile field and keep hands above waist level because reaching over/low hands contaminate the field; the trap is “quickly” leaning across the field and breaking sterility.

q: A patient with uncontrolled coughing is checking in for a routine visit; what should the CMA do first to reduce infection spread?
a: Provide a mask and perform hand hygiene (and place them away from others) because source control interrupts transmission; the trap is rooming them first without addressing respiratory hygiene.

q: You obtain respirations immediately after telling a patient you’re going to “count their breathing,” and it reads 24; what is the best action?
a: Recount respirations discreetly (without alerting the patient) because awareness changes breathing pattern; the trap is accepting an anxiety-influenced rate as baseline.

q: You enter a room wearing gloves and the patient asks you to silence their phone; what is the best action?
a: Remove gloves, perform hand hygiene, then handle the phone (or ask the patient to do it) because personal items are contaminated surfaces and you must prevent cross-contamination; the trap is touching multiple surfaces with the same gloves.

q: Immediately after an injection, the patient becomes flushed, wheezes, and says their throat feels tight; what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate the emergency response/notify the provider STAT and stay with the patient while positioning for breathing because this suggests anaphylaxis; the trap is sending them to the waiting room or “getting water” first.

q: A patient with a known latex allergy is scheduled for an injection; what should the CMA do before preparing supplies?
a: Select latex-free gloves and equipment and verify the product packaging is latex-free because exposure can trigger a reaction; the trap is assuming “non-latex gloves alone” are enough while using latex-containing vial stoppers/supplies.

q: The provider orders a subcutaneous injection and the patient is very thin; what technique helps avoid injecting into muscle?
a: Pinch the skin and use the appropriate needle/angle (commonly 45° if minimal tissue) because proper technique ensures correct route; the trap is using a 90° angle automatically regardless of body habitus.

q: A patient is on contact precautions for suspected scabies and you must take vitals; what PPE should the CMA use at minimum?
a: Gown and gloves (plus hand hygiene) because contact precautions target skin-to-surface spread; the trap is using only gloves and contaminating clothing that then spreads organisms.

q: A patient returns after a blood draw with a growing bruise at the site and reports tenderness; what should the CMA do next?
a: Apply firm pressure and a cold compress (if available) and reassess because this is consistent with a hematoma and early compression limits bleeding; the trap is ignoring it or only offering a bandage without pressure.

q: While changing a wound dressing, you notice the outer glove touched the bed rail; what should you do to maintain asepsis?
a: Remove contaminated gloves, perform hand hygiene, and don new gloves before continuing because touching non-sterile surfaces contaminates care; the trap is continuing “carefully” with contaminated gloves.

q: You’re preparing an IM vaccine and notice the vial label doesn’t match the EHR order even though the patient says “that’s the shot I always get”; what should you do first?
a: Stop and verify the medication against the order (and clarify with the provider/pharmacist) before drawing it up because the “right medication” must be confirmed; the trap is relying on patient memory and proceeding.

q: During rooming, a 68-year-old patient says they feel “lightheaded,” then becomes pale and slumps in the chair while you are about to take blood pressure; what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist the patient to a safe position (supine with legs elevated if tolerated) and call for help/activate the clinic’s emergency response, because protecting airway/circulation and preventing a fall is the priority; a common mistake is trying to finish vital signs before stabilizing the patient.

q: During intake a 58-year-old reports dizziness; you obtain BP 84/52, HR 118, and the patient is pale but awake—what should the CMA do first?
a: Have the patient lie supine with legs elevated and call for the provider/activate clinic emergency response because these are shock-like vitals; the trap is finishing the rest of the intake or rechecking later instead of immediately supporting perfusion and escalating.

q: You are about to enter an exam room for a patient with uncontrolled coughing and you’ll be within 3 feet to take vitals; what PPE should you use first?
a: Perform hand hygiene and don a mask (and eye protection if splash risk) because droplet exposure is likely at close range; the trap is relying on gloves alone, which don’t protect mucous membranes.

q: A patient’s oral temperature is 101.9°F after drinking hot coffee in the waiting room; what is the best next step before reporting fever?
a: Wait 15–20 minutes and recheck using the correct method because recent hot liquids can falsely elevate oral readings; the trap is documenting and alerting the provider based on an inaccurate measurement.

q: While taking vitals, a 24-year-old becomes lightheaded and says they might faint; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop the procedure, assist the patient to a safe position (sit/lie down), and assess responsiveness because preventing a fall is priority; the trap is “pushing through” to finish vitals.

q: A patient’s pulse feels irregular during routine vitals, but they deny symptoms; what is the best CMA action?
a: Reassess apical pulse for a full minute and report/document the irregularity because an irregular radial pulse can be misleading; the trap is estimating for 15 seconds or ignoring it because the patient feels fine.

q: A patient arrives for a wound check and you notice visible dried blood on your last-used stethoscope diaphragm; what is the best next step before continuing care?
a: Clean and disinfect the stethoscope with an approved disinfectant because it’s a noncritical item requiring disinfection between patients; the trap is wiping with a dry tissue or proceeding because it “looks mostly clean.”

q: You find an unresponsive patient in the lobby and another staff member says they “might have just fainted”; what should the CMA do first?
a: Check responsiveness and breathing and activate emergency response/911 (and get the AED) immediately because early recognition and activation saves time in cardiac arrest; the trap is spending time searching for history or moving the patient before assessment.

q: You obtain BP 168/104 in a patient here for a refill who says they “feel normal”; what should the CMA do next?
a: Recheck in 5 minutes with correct cuff size and positioning, then notify the provider of the confirmed elevated reading because technique errors can falsely elevate BP; the trap is documenting one reading without confirmation.

q: After giving an IM injection, the patient says, “I feel itchy and my throat feels tight”; what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate emergency response, stay with the patient, and be ready to assist with epinephrine per standing orders/provider direction because this suggests anaphylaxis; the trap is having them “wait in the lobby” to see if it passes.

q: A patient is scheduled for an IM injection but states they have a severe latex allergy; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and verify that all supplies (gloves, syringe components, vial stopper, bandage) are latex-free and alert the provider if alternatives are needed because exposure can trigger anaphylaxis; the trap is proceeding with “just one bandage” that may contain latex.

q: You draw up a vaccine and then realize you did not clean the rubber stopper of a multi-dose vial; what is the best action?
a: Discard the syringe, disinfect the stopper with alcohol, and prepare a new dose because contamination risk can’t be undone once accessed; the trap is injecting anyway since the needle was “sterile.”

q: The provider orders 0.5 mL of a medication; you accidentally draw up 0.7 mL and notice before entering the room—what is the best next step?
a: Expel the excess using aseptic technique to the correct dose (or discard and redraw if sterility is compromised) because accurate dosing is part of medication safety; the trap is “rounding up” since it seems close.

q: During intake, a 54-year-old patient seated for vitals says “I’m feeling dizzy,” looks pale, and begins sliding down in the chair as you finish the blood pressure reading. What should the CMA do first?
a: Assist the patient into a safe supine position with legs elevated and stay with them while calling for the provider/clinic help, because preventing a fall and supporting perfusion is the immediate priority; a common mistake is continuing the vitals or sending the patient to the exam room unassisted.

q: You are about to administer a vaccine and the patient says they are unsure what it is for and looks hesitant; what should the CMA do next?
a: Pause and provide the Vaccine Information Statement/required education and confirm consent/understanding before giving it because informed consent is required; the trap is proceeding because the patient “showed up for the appointment.”

q: While preparing an injection, you notice the medication label doesn’t match the provider’s order in the chart; what should the CMA do first?
a: Hold the medication and clarify the discrepancy with the provider before administration because giving the wrong drug is a preventable error; the trap is assuming the pharmacy label is correct and administering anyway.

q: After removing gloves, your hands look clean and you’re heading to the next room; what should you do next?
a: Perform hand hygiene immediately because glove removal can contaminate hands; the trap is skipping hand hygiene because gloves were worn.

q: During intake in an urgent care clinic, a 52-year-old reports chest pressure and looks pale; you obtain vital signs showing BP 88/54, HR 118, RR 24, and SpO₂ 92%—what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the intake and alert the provider/activate emergency response immediately while keeping the patient seated or supine and monitoring airway/breathing/circulation, because hypotension with chest pressure is potentially life-threatening and the common trap is continuing routine vitals/history instead of escalating.

q: During intake, an adult patient sits quietly but you obtain BP 198/112 with headache and blurred vision; the provider is with another patient—what should the CMA do first?
a: Keep the patient seated, recheck BP manually after a brief rest, and immediately alert the provider/activate urgent protocol because this may be a hypertensive emergency; the trap is documenting it and letting the patient wait or sending them to the lobby.

q: During wound dressing change, the provider requests sterile technique; what should the CMA do first after setting up supplies?
a: Perform hand hygiene and don sterile gloves without contaminating them because maintaining sterility prevents introducing pathogens; the trap is touching the bedside or nonsterile packaging after gloving.

q: A patient is dizzy when standing for weight measurement; what should the CMA do to obtain an accurate weight safely?
a: Use a seated or wheelchair scale if available and ensure assistance/guarding because fall prevention outweighs convenience; the trap is having the patient “hold the wall” to stand on the scale.

q: You attach an AED to an unresponsive patient and it announces “shock advised”; what should the CMA do next?
a: Ensure everyone is clear and deliver the shock, then resume CPR immediately because minimizing pauses improves survival; the trap is rechecking for a pulse before shocking or delaying CPR after the shock.

q: A patient needs a rectal temperature due to inability to cooperate with oral/tympanic methods; what is the correct patient position to use?
a: Place the patient in Sims’ (left lateral) position because it provides safe access and comfort; the trap is using supine, which increases discomfort and risk of improper insertion.

q: A patient becomes pale and says they feel faint while standing on the scale during intake—what should the CMA do next?
a: Assist them to a safe seated or supine position and assess responsiveness/airway before continuing vitals because fall prevention and immediate safety come first; the trap is trying to “finish weight and vitals” while they’re unstable.

q: In the lobby, a patient collapses and is unresponsive; you confirm no normal breathing—what is the CMA’s first action?
a: Call for help/activate EMS and start chest compressions immediately (send someone for the AED) because early CPR is priority; the trap is searching for a pulse for too long or waiting for the provider before compressions.

q: While assisting with a sterile dressing change, you accidentally brush your gloved hand against the patient’s bedrail; what should you do next?
a: Consider the glove contaminated and replace it before touching sterile supplies because the bedrail is not sterile; the trap is continuing because “the glove still looks clean.”

q: A 6-year-old’s pulse reads 52 bpm on the automated vital sign machine but the child is alert and talking—what should the CMA do next?
a: Recheck the pulse manually (and ensure the cuff/sensor size and placement are correct) before escalating because pediatric readings are prone to device error; the trap is calling it bradycardia without confirming.

q: You are about to don PPE for irrigating a draining wound that may splash; what is the best PPE choice?
a: Wear gloves, gown, and eye/face protection because splashes can expose mucous membranes and clothing; the trap is wearing only gloves since it’s “just a quick rinse.”

q: A patient with dizziness is placed supine for an exam and then says the room is spinning when you raise the head of the table quickly—what should the CMA do best next?
a: Lower the head of the table, help them change positions slowly, and notify the provider if symptoms persist because gradual positioning prevents syncope and falls; the trap is insisting they sit up quickly to “get them ready.”

q: After removing gloves, you notice visible soil on your hands from wound drainage; what should you do next?
a: Wash hands with soap and water because visible contamination requires mechanical removal; the trap is using alcohol-based sanitizer alone when hands are visibly soiled.

q: You enter an exam room to clean after a procedure and see a used needle on the tray; what is the correct immediate action?
a: Using a one-handed technique only if needed, place the needle and syringe directly into a sharps container without recapping because recapping increases needlestick risk; the trap is recapping “to carry it safely.”

q: You are rooming a patient with a persistent cough and you have a schedule delay; what infection-control action should the CMA do first?
a: Provide the patient a surgical mask and perform hand hygiene because source control reduces droplet spread immediately; the trap is focusing first on PPE for staff while leaving the coughing patient unmasked.

q: You obtain respirations of 10/min on an adult who is chatting and not in distress; what is the best action before documenting?
