a: Assist the patient to a supine position with legs elevated and call for the provider/activate clinic emergency response as needed because this may be shock/syncope risk; the trap is continuing the intake or walking the patient to another room.

q: During intake in an urgent care clinic, a 62-year-old reports new dizziness and looks pale; you obtain vitals: BP 86/54, pulse 118, RR 22, SpO2 96%, and she says she “just needs to sit a minute”—what should the CMA do first?
a: Place the patient supine with legs elevated and immediately alert the provider/activate emergency response while staying with her, because hypotension with tachycardia suggests possible shock/syncope risk and the common mistake is having her complete paperwork or walk to an exam room before stabilizing and escalating.

q: In the waiting room, a visitor asks why a specific patient is in the clinic today—what should the CMA do?
a: Politely state you cannot share any patient information and offer to take a message because HIPAA prohibits disclosure without authorization; the trap is giving “harmless” details like confirming the patient is being seen.

q: You are rooming a patient who becomes pale and says they feel faint after standing from the chair—what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist them back to a safe seated or supine position and assess ABCs/vitals before continuing questions because preventing a fall is the immediate priority; the trap is trying to “finish intake quickly” while the patient is unstable.

q: Before entering an exam room for a cough/fever visit, the patient is not masked and is actively coughing—what is the CMA’s best first step?
a: Provide the patient a mask and perform hand hygiene before close contact because source control and standard precautions reduce transmission; the trap is putting on gloves first while leaving the patient unmasked and spreading droplets.

q: During rooming, a 62-year-old patient says they feel lightheaded; you measure BP 86/52 and pulse 118 while they are sitting upright on the exam table—what should the CMA do first?
a: Assist the patient to a supine position with legs elevated and immediately notify the provider while rechecking vitals once safe, because suspected hypotension/possible shock requires rapid positioning and escalation; the common mistake is continuing the intake or leaving the patient sitting, increasing fall risk and delaying care.

q: A patient’s BP is 178/112 on intake, they deny symptoms, and they are here for a medication refill—what should the CMA do next?
a: Recheck manually after a 5-minute rest and immediately notify the provider of persistent severe hypertension because it may require urgent evaluation; the trap is scheduling them routinely or waiting until the end of the visit to mention it.

q: While taking vitals, you note a pulse oximetry reading of 89% on a patient who is wearing dark nail polish and moving their hand—what should you do next?
a: Reassess SpO₂ by correcting technique (remove/avoid nail polish, warm and steady the finger, ensure good sensor placement) before escalating because motion/artifact can cause false lows; the trap is assuming true hypoxia without troubleshooting.

q: A 6-year-old is anxious and you measure BP with an adult cuff because it’s the closest one—what is the best action?
a: Stop and obtain the correct pediatric cuff size to repeat BP because wrong cuff size skews readings (often falsely high/low); the trap is reporting an inaccurate BP that drives unnecessary clinical decisions.

q: A provider asks you to “just recap the used needle so it’s safe for transport to the sharps container” after an injection—what should the CMA do?
a: Do not recap; activate safety device and dispose of the needle directly into a sharps container because recapping is a leading cause of needlestick injuries; the trap is following the request instead of standard sharps safety.

q: You remove gloves after cleaning up a small blood spill and your hands look clean—what should you do next?
a: Perform hand hygiene immediately because gloves are not a substitute and microscopic contamination occurs during removal; the trap is skipping hand hygiene because “I wore gloves.”

q: You prepare to administer a medication injection and notice the label is partially torn so the concentration can’t be confirmed—what should the CMA do?
a: Do not administer; obtain a properly labeled medication and confirm the correct concentration because unreadable labeling breaks medication safety rights; the trap is assuming it’s the usual concentration.

q: While cleaning an exam room after a procedure, you see a dried blood spot on the table paper and no visible wet spill—how should you handle it?
a: Wear gloves and disinfect with an EPA-registered disinfectant per label contact time because dried blood can still transmit pathogens; the trap is discarding the paper only and skipping surface disinfection.

q: You are about to perform a sterile dressing change and notice your sterile glove touches the edge of the countertop—what is the best action?
a: Stop and replace the contaminated glove (and re-establish the sterile field if needed) because sterility is broken by contact with nonsterile surfaces; the trap is continuing “carefully” to save time.

q: You are preparing an IM injection and the patient says they are allergic to latex; the only gloves available are latex—what should the CMA do next?
a: Obtain non-latex gloves (and verify non-latex supplies as needed) before proceeding because latex exposure can trigger reactions; the trap is proceeding because “it’s just for a minute.”

q: The provider orders a 0.5 mL IM vaccine and you draw up 0.7 mL by mistake—what is the best next step?
a: Discard the syringe and prepare a new dose with the correct volume because dosing errors cannot be “fixed” by guessing and can harm the patient; the trap is expelling medication back into the vial or injecting the wrong dose.

q: A patient is scheduled for an injection and asks you to “just give it in my arm through my sweater so it won’t hurt”—what is the best response?
a: Explain you must access skin and cleanse the site, and have the patient expose the area because injecting through clothing compromises asepsis and site identification; the trap is prioritizing speed or comfort over infection prevention.

q: Right before giving an ordered injection, the patient states, “I think I got that same shot yesterday at urgent care”—what should the CMA do first?
a: Pause and verify the order and immunization history with the provider/EHR before administering because duplicate dosing may be unsafe; the trap is giving it anyway because it is on today’s chart.

q: During wound care, you remove an old dressing with visible drainage—what should you do next before applying the new dressing?
a: Perform hand hygiene, don clean gloves, and clean the wound from least contaminated to most contaminated area because this limits introducing organisms; the trap is using the same gloves/tools from removal to application.

q: A patient becomes unresponsive in the waiting area and you confirm they are not breathing normally—what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate emergency response (call 911/alert team), send for the AED, and begin CPR immediately because early CPR/AED saves lives; the trap is searching for a pulse for too long or moving the patient unnecessarily.

q: A patient becomes lightheaded immediately after standing for orthostatic vitals—what is the CMA’s priority action?
a: Assist the patient back to a safe seated/lying position and recheck vitals before notifying the provider because preventing a fall comes first; trap: insisting they “finish the standing BP.”

q: While taking an adult’s BP, the cuff barely overlaps and you hear the patient say “That cuff feels too tight”—what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and select the correct cuff size then retake the BP because wrong cuff size gives inaccurate readings; trap: recording the number anyway “because it’s close.”

q: During intake a 58-year-old reports dizziness; vitals show BP 86/52, HR 118, and the patient looks pale—what should the CMA do first?
a: Seat or lay the patient supine with legs elevated and call for the provider/activate clinic emergency response because suspected hypotension/shock is immediate safety risk; trap: finishing the intake questions or sending them to the waiting room.

q: An adult has an irregular radial pulse when you measure it for 15 seconds—what should the CMA do next?
a: Count the apical pulse for a full 60 seconds (per training/policy) and report/document the irregularity because short counts miss irregular rhythms; trap: multiplying the 15-second count and moving on.

q: A patient arrives for a routine visit talking normally but breathing rapidly; RR is 28 and SpO₂ is 91% on room air—what is the best next step for the CMA?
a: Recheck SpO₂ ensuring proper probe placement and assess for acute distress while promptly notifying the provider because low oxygenation may be urgent; trap: documenting it as “anxiety” or delaying until after other vitals.

q: A patient is having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in the exam room chair—what is the CMA’s best immediate action?
a: Protect the patient from injury by easing them to the floor, clearing hazards, and timing the seizure while calling for help because safety and airway protection are priorities; the trap is restraining them or putting something in their mouth.

q: A 7-year-old is anxious and talking during a temperature reading; the oral thermometer shows 100.8°F—what should the CMA do best?
a: Confirm with a more appropriate method (e.g., tympanic/temporal per device instructions) and document method used because talking can falsely elevate an oral reading; trap: reporting a fever without verifying technique.

q: After removing gloves, you notice your hands look clean and you’re running behind—what should you do next before touching the keyboard?
a: Perform hand hygiene immediately because glove removal can contaminate hands and keyboards spread pathogens; trap: assuming gloves replace handwashing.

q: A patient with suspected influenza is coughing during triage; where should the CMA place a surgical mask in the sequence of controls?
a: Put a mask on the patient as source control right away and then don your own PPE as needed because reducing droplet spread at the source is fastest; trap: masking yourself only while the patient remains unmasked.

q: You prepare an IM vaccine and notice the vial label doesn’t match the order (similar names, different product)—what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and clarify with the provider/pharmacy or verify the order before drawing up/administering because wrong product is a serious medication error; trap: relying on “it’s probably the same one.”

q: You’re about to room a patient who says they have active vomiting and diarrhea; what infection control action is best before close contact?
a: Perform hand hygiene and don appropriate PPE (at minimum gloves, add gown/face protection if splash risk) and place the patient promptly in a room because standard precautions apply to all body fluids; trap: using only hand sanitizer after visible contamination risk.

q: You enter an exam room and see a used needle on the counter; what should the CMA do first?
a: Do not recap; use a mechanical device/forceps if needed and place it directly into a sharps container while keeping others away because preventing needlestick is the priority; trap: recapping “to make it safer” before disposal.

q: A coworker asks you to carry a tray with sterile instruments down the hall uncovered “just for a second”—what is the best response?
a: Refuse and keep the sterile items packaged/covered until point of use because exposure breaks sterility and risks infection; trap: assuming sterility is preserved if no one “touches” it.

q: A patient says they’re allergic to latex and is due for an injection—what should the CMA do before preparing supplies?
a: Verify the allergy details and select latex-free gloves/syringe components and a non-latex bandage because exposure can trigger a reaction; trap: wearing latex gloves and “just being careful.”

q: You are cleaning an exam table with disinfectant wipes; the surface looks dry after 30 seconds but the label says contact time is 2 minutes—what should you do?
a: Re-wet the surface and ensure it stays visibly wet for the full contact time because killing pathogens requires the labeled dwell time; trap: wiping dry early to speed room turnover.

q: While collecting a light blue tube for coagulation studies, the tube stops short and is only half full; what is the best next action?
a: Recollect with a properly filled light blue tube because underfilling changes the required 9:1 blood-to-citrate ratio and can falsely prolong clotting times; the trap is topping it off from another tube or submitting underfilled.

q: While preparing to administer an injection, the patient asks, “What is this shot for?” and looks unsure—what should the CMA do best?
a: Pause and provide the ordered medication name/purpose per the order and confirm the patient’s understanding/consent before giving it because informed agreement and the right patient/right medication come first; trap: giving the injection and explaining afterward.

q: During a dressing change for a simple superficial wound, the provider ordered “clean dressing change”; what technique should the CMA use?
a: Use clean technique with hand hygiene and gloves, cleaning from least contaminated (center) to most contaminated (outward) because sterile technique isn’t required unless ordered; trap: using the same gauze stroke back and forth across the wound.

q: During a morning draw you have a CMP (serum) and a CBC (EDTA) ordered on the same patient and only one venipuncture attempt planned; what tube should the CMA fill first?
a: Fill the serum tube before the EDTA tube to follow order of draw and prevent additive carryover (a common trap is drawing the lavender first, which can contaminate serum tests).

q: In the waiting area an adult suddenly collapses and is unresponsive; what should the CMA do first?
a: Verify unresponsiveness and breathing, call for help/activate EMS, and start CPR while someone retrieves the AED because early CPR/AED saves lives; trap: searching for the chart or trying to give water.

q: A provider orders PT/INR and CBC and the CMA collects the lavender EDTA tube before the light blue citrate tube; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and redraw both tests with the correct order (light blue before lavender) because additive carryover and wrong blood-to-anticoagulant ratio can invalidate results; the trap is “sending it anyway” to avoid another stick.

q: A fasting lipid panel is ordered but the patient says, “I had coffee with cream an hour ago”; what should the CMA do first?
a: Pause the draw and notify the provider/lead to reschedule or clarify instructions because non-fasting intake can alter results; the trap is proceeding and documenting “fasting” based on the order.

q: After giving a subcutaneous injection, you notice a small drop of blood at the site—what is the appropriate CMA action?
a: Apply gentle pressure with clean gauze and apply a bandage if needed, then document because minor bleeding is common and pressure prevents bruising; trap: massaging the site, which can increase tissue irritation for some meds.

q: After venipuncture, the CMA labels tubes at the nurses’ station to “keep the room moving”; what should the CMA do differently next time?
a: Label tubes immediately in the patient’s presence (at bedside/chairside) to prevent mislabeling errors; the trap is delaying labeling, which is a leading cause of specimen rejection.

q: A CMP is drawn into a gold SST tube and the CMA is busy; what is the best next step regarding tube handling before sending to the lab?
a: Gently invert the SST per manufacturer guidance and allow appropriate clotting time before centrifugation/transport because inadequate mixing or rushing can cause clots/hemolysis; the trap is shaking the tube to “mix faster.”

q: The patient’s ID band is missing and the CMA recognizes the patient from prior visits; what is the best way to verify identity before labeling tubes?
a: Use two identifiers (ask the patient to state full name and date of birth) and match to the order before labeling, because familiarity is not identification; the trap is labeling from memory or a room chart.

q: A patient reports a history of mastectomy with lymph node removal on the left and offers the left arm for blood draw; what should the CMA do?
a: Use the opposite arm (or consult the provider for an alternate site) to reduce lymphedema/infection risk; the trap is proceeding because “it’s just one stick.”

q: The CMA draws blood through a syringe and needs to transfer into evacuated tubes; what is the safest method?
a: Use a transfer device and let the vacuum fill the tubes (do not force blood through the needle) to reduce hemolysis and needlestick risk; the trap is pushing blood through a needle into tubes.

q: After a blood draw, a patient develops rapid swelling and bruising at the puncture site while the needle is still in; what is the best immediate action?
a: Remove the needle and apply firm pressure for several minutes (then ice if allowed) because this suggests a hematoma from vein leakage; the trap is continuing to probe the vein, worsening bleeding.

q: During venipuncture the patient says they feel dizzy and looks pale; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the draw, remove the tourniquet and needle, and assist the patient to a safe position (supine or head lowered) because syncope risk is immediate; the trap is trying to “finish the tube” before addressing safety.

q: A patient on anticoagulants has continued oozing after venipuncture despite a brief hold; what should the CMA do next?
a: Maintain firm pressure longer and reassess before applying a bandage, and notify the provider if bleeding persists because anticoagulation increases bleeding risk; the trap is sending the patient out with a loose bandage.

q: A patient’s antecubital veins are difficult and the CMA considers drawing from the arm with an active IV infusion; what is the best action?
a: Choose a different site/arm or consult a supervisor—avoid drawing above an active IV because dilution can alter results; the trap is drawing near the IV for convenience and assuming it “won’t matter.”

q: A POCT analyzer prints a patient result that seems inconsistent with the patient’s condition, and the CMA realizes the sample was not mixed as required; what should the CMA do next?
a: Treat the result as potentially inaccurate, recollect/retest per procedure and document the corrected action because pre-analytical handling errors can invalidate POCT; the trap is reporting the first number because it already printed.

q: The clinic runs a CLIA-waived urine pregnancy test and the control result is invalid; what should the CMA do first?
a: Do not report patient results—repeat QC per manufacturer instructions (new kit/strip, verify expiration and storage) before testing patients because invalid controls mean unreliable results; the trap is documenting “negative” based on a faint line anyway.

q: While obtaining an EKG, the machine repeatedly shows “lead off” and the RA lead is the only one reading flat; what should the CMA do next?
a: Check RA electrode contact (skin prep, dryness, snap connection, cable) and replace it if needed because a single lead issue usually indicates poor electrode connection; the trap is printing the strip anyway.

q: While preparing to run a fingerstick glucose POCT, the CMA finds the test strips expired yesterday; what is the best action?
a: Discard expired strips and obtain in-date strips before testing because expired reagents can give inaccurate readings; the trap is using them “just once” and assuming calibration will correct it.

q: The CMA places precordial leads but V1 and V2 were accidentally placed too high near the clavicle; what is the best next step before printing?
a: Reposition V1 and V2 to the 4th intercostal space at the right and left sternal borders and repeat the tracing because incorrect placement can mimic pathology; the trap is “close enough” placement to save time.

q: The CMA is performing a 12-lead EKG and notices the tracing has a jagged baseline that disappears when the patient stops talking and relaxes; what is the best correction?
a: Instruct the patient to lie still, relax muscles, and avoid talking during acquisition because muscle tremor causes artifact; the trap is immediately reapplying all electrodes without addressing motion.

q: An outpatient reports chest pressure and the provider asks for an EKG; after you obtain it, the printout shows new ST-segment elevation compared with the prior EKG in the chart; what should the CMA do next?
a: Immediately alert the provider and follow emergency protocol because this can indicate an acute event and is time-sensitive; the trap is filing it in the EHR first or attempting to interpret it to the patient.

q: A fasting lipid panel is ordered and the patient says they drank a sweetened coffee 20 minutes ago; what should the CMA do next before drawing?
a: Stop and clarify with the ordering provider or follow clinic protocol to reschedule because the specimen may be invalid; the trap is drawing anyway and producing inaccurate results.

q: During venipuncture you draw a light blue tube first because it “fills slowly,” then remember a serum tube was also ordered; what is the best action now?
a: Stop and recollect using the correct order of draw (blood cultures if ordered, then light blue after) because wrong order can contaminate additives; the trap is keeping the specimen and hoping the lab “fixes it.”

q: While drawing, the patient says “I feel dizzy” and becomes pale and sweaty; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, and assist the patient to a safe position (recline with legs elevated) because this suggests vasovagal syncope; the trap is finishing the tube “quickly” to avoid a redraw.

q: You collected a CBC in a lavender tube and set it upright on the counter while finishing charting; what should you do before sending it out?
a: Gently invert the tube the recommended number of times to mix anticoagulant and prevent clots; the trap is shaking vigorously, which can hemolyze the sample.

q: A patient’s lab order includes CBC and potassium, and you have lavender and green tubes ready; what is the best order to fill them after a red/gold tube is not needed?
a: Fill the green (heparin) before the lavender (EDTA) to prevent EDTA carryover affecting chemistry values; the trap is drawing lavender first because CBC feels “more urgent.”

q: A patient has a history of fainting with blood draws and asks to sit upright “to be brave”; what is the best action before starting?
a: Position the patient reclining or supine and ensure close observation because prevention of syncope-related falls is the priority; the trap is accommodating upright positioning without safety planning.

q: After labeling tubes at the nurses’ station, you realize two patients with the same last name are waiting and you can’t remember whose specimen is whose; what is the best next step?
a: Treat the specimens as unidentified and recollect after re-identifying the patient at the chairside because mislabeling is a critical safety event; the trap is guessing based on room number or time.

q: During venipuncture a rapidly swelling, painful area forms at the site; what should the CMA do next?
a: Immediately release the tourniquet, withdraw the needle, and apply firm pressure then a cold compress because this indicates a hematoma; the trap is continuing to draw to “get enough blood.”

q: A CLIA-waived rapid strep test kit is opened and you notice the expiration date was last month; what should the CMA do?
a: Do not use it—discard per biohazard/clinic policy and obtain an in-date kit because expired reagents can give unreliable results; the trap is using it since the control line “might still appear.”

q: While drawing a fasting lipid panel and CMP, the CMA fills the lavender EDTA tube first and then the serum (gold/tiger) tube; what should the CMA do NEXT to protect specimen accuracy?
a: Stop and recollect using the correct order of draw (serum tube before EDTA) because EDTA carryover can falsely alter chemistry results like potassium and calcium; the trap is “just relabeling” or sending it anyway since the patient is fasting.

q: After removing the needle, the patient keeps bending their elbow tightly to “make it stop bleeding”; what should the CMA instruct?
a: Ask them to keep the arm straight and apply direct pressure for several minutes to prevent hematoma; the trap is allowing elbow flexion, which can worsen bruising.

q: A patient is unable to produce enough urine for a pregnancy POCT and asks if they can add water to the cup; what should the CMA do?
a: Instruct not to dilute and offer water to drink and wait/retry because dilution can cause false-negative results; the trap is accepting adulterated specimens to save time.

q: A timed drug level is ordered for 10:00, but the patient arrives at 10:25 and already took the medication at 10:10; what should the CMA do next?
a: Document the actual medication time and draw time and notify the nurse/provider or lab instructions because timing affects interpretation; the trap is writing “10:00” to match the order.

q: A urine culture is ordered and the patient hands you a cup filled from the toilet hat without cleansing; what is the best next step?
a: Reject and recollect with clean-catch midstream instructions because contamination can cause false positives; the trap is sending it “since it’s already here.”

q: QC for the clinic’s urine dipsticks is due today, but the waiting room is full and the provider wants results quickly; what should the CMA do first?
a: Perform and document required QC before patient testing because waived tests still require QC to ensure accuracy; the trap is skipping QC to keep flow moving.

q: You perform a fingerstick glucose and the first drop is small; what is the best action for an accurate result?
a: Wipe away the first drop and use the next drop without excessive squeezing because tissue fluid can dilute the sample; the trap is “milking” the finger to get more blood.

q: You start a venipuncture for a PT/INR and the light blue tube only fills halfway before flow stops; what should you do?
a: Stop and recollect a new light blue tube to the proper fill line, because underfilling changes the blood-to-additive ratio and can invalidate results; the trap is sending it “since some blood is better than none.”

q: During an outpatient EKG, you notice the patient’s chest hair prevents the precordial electrodes from sticking; what should the CMA do to get a reliable tracing?
a: Clip hair as needed and clean/dry the skin before reapplying electrodes because poor contact causes artifact; the trap is pressing harder or repositioning randomly, which still yields poor signal.

q: During a CBC draw, you collect a light blue tube then a lavender tube, and then realize the provider also ordered a CMP; what should you do NEXT to avoid order-of-draw contamination?
a: Draw the required serum tube (red/gold) in the correct sequence before any remaining additive tubes, because drawing chemistry after EDTA can falsely elevate potassium; the trap is “just grabbing any tube” once blood flow is established.

q: You obtain an EKG but the tracing shows a thick, shaky baseline in all leads and the patient is shivering; what is the best next step?
a: Warm and relax the patient (blanket, reduce muscle tension) and repeat the EKG because muscle tremor causes artifact; the trap is assuming it’s an arrhythmia and alerting the provider before verifying artifact.

q: A patient’s EKG prints with a “leads off” message and a flat line in one lead, but the patient feels fine; what should the CMA do next?
a: Check electrode adhesion/cable connections and replace the loose electrode, then repeat the tracing because this is most consistent with equipment setup error; the trap is treating it as a cardiac emergency without confirming lead placement.

q: After drawing a lavender tube for CBC, you set it upright on the counter without mixing while you label other tubes; what should you do NEXT?
a: Gently invert the lavender tube the recommended number of times immediately, because EDTA tubes must be mixed to prevent clotting and erroneous counts; the trap is shaking vigorously (causes hemolysis) or waiting too long.

q: A fasting lipid panel and PT/INR are ordered, and you have light blue, gold, and lavender tubes ready; what is the BEST order of draw for these?
a: Fill the light blue (citrate) first, then the gold (serum), then the lavender (EDTA) if needed, because citrate tubes must be collected before additives that can alter coagulation; the trap is putting serum before coag tubes.

q: When placing limb electrodes for a 12-lead EKG, the patient has ankle edema with weeping skin; what is the best action?
a: Place electrodes on clean, dry skin higher on the limbs (avoiding broken skin) and document modified placement because intact skin contact is needed for signal quality; the trap is placing over compromised skin for “correct location.”

q: A patient’s blood draw is completed and you step out to print labels, planning to label tubes when you return; what is the BEST action?
a: Label the tubes at the patient’s side using two identifiers before leaving, because delayed labeling increases misidentification risk; the trap is relying on memory or room number.

q: After a blood draw, you notice bright red, pulsing blood entering the tube and the patient reports sharp pain; what should you do FIRST?
a: Immediately remove the needle and apply firm pressure, then report the incident, because arterial puncture or nerve involvement is a safety emergency; the trap is adjusting the needle to “see if it settles.”

q: During venipuncture, the patient says, “I feel dizzy,” becomes pale, and starts to slump; what should you do NEXT?
a: Remove the tourniquet and needle, help the patient into a safe position (recline/legs up), and call for assistance per clinic protocol, because syncope can cause falls; the trap is continuing the draw “to finish the tube.”

q: You are about to draw blood from a patient who has an IV infusing in the left forearm and no restrictions on the right; what should you do FIRST?
a: Choose the right arm for venipuncture, because drawing above an active IV can dilute the specimen and distort results; the trap is drawing from the closest visible vein.

q: During a fasting lipid panel draw, you collect light blue, then gold, then lavender and realize the light blue tube was filled only halfway; what should the CMA do next to ensure accurate results?
a: Discard the underfilled light blue tube and recollect it to the fill line with a new tube because citrate tubes require a correct blood-to-additive ratio for valid coagulation testing; the common mistake is sending an underfilled tube and “noting it” instead of recollecting.

q: During venipuncture for a fasting lipid panel and CMP, the CMA collects the lavender tube first and then the gold tube; before labeling, the provider adds a CBC and asks to use the same draw—what should the CMA do next to prevent an inaccurate result?
a: Label the tubes at the bedside and redraw using the correct order of draw (blood cultures, light blue, red/gold, green, lavender, gray) because drawing lavender (EDTA) first can contaminate the serum tube and alter chemistry results (common trap: trying to “save a stick” by keeping out-of-order tubes).

q: During a venipuncture for a CMP and CBC, the CMA fills the lavender tube first and then the light green tube and notices the green tube has visible tiny clots after gentle inversion; what should the CMA do next to best protect specimen accuracy?
a: Stop processing and redraw the specimen using the correct order of draw (light green before lavender) with proper gentle inversions because drawing EDTA first can contaminate subsequent tubes and clotted/heparinized specimens can produce inaccurate results—the common mistake is sending it anyway or trying to “mix out” clots.

q: Immediately after needle removal, a patient on anticoagulants develops a growing hematoma at the site; what should you do FIRST?
a: Apply firm direct pressure and elevate the arm, because stopping bleeding and limiting tissue damage is the priority; the trap is putting on a bandage quickly without sustained pressure.

q: A provider asks you to tell a patient they are having atrial fibrillation based on the EKG you just obtained; what is the BEST response within CMA scope?
a: Tell the patient the provider will review the results and discuss them, and promptly give the EKG to the provider, because CMAs do not diagnose or interpret for patients; the trap is sharing an interpretation to be “helpful.”

q: During a fasting lipid panel draw, the CMA fills a light blue citrate tube first and then a gold serum separator tube; what should the CMA do next to prevent an inaccurate coagulation specimen?
a: Stop and redraw using the correct order of draw (blood cultures if ordered, then light blue before serum) because drawing a citrate tube after other additives can contaminate the specimen and alter clotting results; the common mistake is trying to “fix” it by extra mixing or relabeling instead of recollecting.

q: While running an EKG, the machine displays “Lead off” and the tracing is flat in one lead; what should you do FIRST?
a: Check the patient cable connection and the specific loose electrode, then reattach/replace it, because a disconnected lead causes a non-diagnostic tracing; the trap is restarting the machine repeatedly instead of fixing the contact.

q: During a venipuncture, you draw a light blue (citrate) tube first but it only fills halfway before blood flow stops; the provider is waiting on PT/INR—what should the CMA do next?
a: Discard that underfilled citrate tube and recollect a new light blue tube that fills to the marked line before sending, because incorrect blood-to-anticoagulant ratio makes coagulation results unreliable; a common mistake is sending the partial tube “since some blood is there.”

q: You place V1 and V2 for a 12-lead EKG and the tracing suggests an unusual pattern; later you realize V1 and V2 were placed too high; what should you do NEXT?
a: Reposition V1 at the 4th intercostal space right sternal border and V2 at the 4th intercostal space left sternal border and repeat the EKG, because incorrect placement can create false abnormalities; the trap is sending it to the provider as a true change.

q: A patient hands you a urine cup for a POCT dipstick, but it has no label and multiple patients are waiting; what should you do FIRST?
a: Do not test it; verify the patient using two identifiers and label the specimen correctly in their presence, because unlabeled specimens risk serious mix-ups; the trap is assuming it’s from the last patient roomed.

q: During a waived glucometer check, the result seems inconsistent with the patient’s symptoms, and you notice the test strips expired last week; what should you do NEXT?
a: Discard expired strips, run quality control with in-date materials, and repeat the test, because expired reagents can give inaccurate results; the trap is charting the number because it “printed out.”

q: An EKG printout shows heavy baseline wander and the patient is shivering in the exam room; what is the BEST next step?
a: Warm/comfort the patient and ask them to relax and stay still before repeating the EKG, because muscle tremor creates artifact that mimics dysrhythmia; the trap is immediately escalating as an “abnormal rhythm” without checking artifact.

q: After drawing a light blue tube for PT/INR, you notice it is only half full; what is the best next action?
a: Redraw the specimen in a new light blue tube filled to the required volume because underfilling alters the blood-to-anticoagulant ratio and the trap is sending it “anyway” leading to falsely prolonged clotting times.

q: A CMP specimen arrives at the lab with visible froth and the note says it was “shaken to mix”; what is the likely best corrective action for the CMA?
a: Recollect the specimen because shaking can hemolyze blood and invalidate chemistry results; the trap is assuming any mixing method is fine as long as it’s “well mixed.”

q: You drew a lavender tube for a CBC and immediately set it upright on the counter without mixing; what should you do next?
a: Gently invert the tube the recommended number of times right away because anticoagulant tubes must be mixed to prevent microclots and the trap is shaking vigorously, which can hemolyze the specimen.

q: A provider orders blood cultures, CBC, and BMP, and the CMA has all supplies ready; what is the correct order of draw starting with the first collection?
a: Collect blood cultures first, then light blue (if ordered), then serum (red/gold), then green, then lavender, then gray because order prevents additive carryover and the trap is drawing lavender before serum and contaminating results.

q: During venipuncture for a CMP and CBC, the CMA draws the lavender-top EDTA tube first and then the serum separator tube; what should the CMA do next to protect specimen integrity and patient safety?
a: Stop and redraw both tubes in the correct order of draw (serum/SST before EDTA) using new tubes and proper mixing because EDTA carryover can falsely alter chemistry results; the common mistake is “sending it anyway” since the blood was already collected.

q: For a potassium test, the patient repeatedly pumps their fist to help you find a vein; what is the best instruction?
a: Ask the patient to relax the hand and avoid pumping because fist pumping can falsely elevate potassium and the trap is encouraging vigorous pumping to “make the vein pop.”

q: During venipuncture for a CMP and PT/INR, the patient says, “I feel hot and dizzy,” and becomes pale while the needle is still in the arm; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, activate safety, and assist the patient to a safe position (recline/legs elevated) because this is likely a vasovagal reaction and the trap is trying to “finish the tube” and risking a fall/injury.

q: While collecting a fasting lipid panel, you apply the tourniquet and the patient’s veins are difficult; two minutes pass as you search—what should you do?
a: Release the tourniquet and reapply when ready to stick because prolonged tourniquet time can hemoconcentrate results and the trap is leaving it on “until I find the vein.”

q: The clinic receives a new lot number of rapid strep tests, and patients are already waiting; what is the best next step before using the new kit?
a: Perform and document required QC for the new lot before patient testing because lot changes can alter performance, and the trap is using it immediately because it is “CLIA-waived.”

q: A CLIA-waived glucose meter displays a “QC FAIL” message at the start of clinic; what should the CMA do next?
a: Do not test patients—repeat QC per manufacturer instructions and remove the device from service if it still fails because patient results are unreliable, and the trap is running patient tests “since it’s just a screening.”

q: During a 12-lead EKG, the tracing shows a wandering baseline and the patient is shivering in a cold room; what should the CMA do first to troubleshoot?
a: Warm and reposition the patient to reduce muscle tremor artifact because shivering commonly causes baseline instability, and the trap is repeatedly reprinting without fixing the cause.

q: A patient’s first blood culture set is ordered, but the CMA cleans the site and then palpates the vein again without gloves; what is the best next action?
a: Re-clean/disinfect the site and use proper aseptic technique because re-palpation contaminates the site and can cause false-positive cultures; the trap is proceeding because “it still looks clean.”

q: After removing the needle, a hematoma begins forming at the venipuncture site; what should the CMA do next?
a: Apply firm direct pressure (longer than usual) and elevate as appropriate because continued bleeding into tissue worsens the hematoma, and the trap is placing a bandage without adequate pressure.

q: You attempt venipuncture and the patient reports a sharp, electric pain radiating down the arm; what should you do immediately?
a: Stop the procedure and remove the needle because this may indicate nerve involvement, and the trap is “repositioning” the needle and risking nerve injury.

q: You collect a urine sample for a CLIA-waived pregnancy test, but the cup is unlabeled and two patients with similar names are waiting; what should you do first?
a: Stop processing and verify identity by re-collecting/confirming with two identifiers before testing because POCT errors are often identification errors, and the trap is testing first and “fixing the label later.”

q: A patient reports they are on warfarin and asks you to “use the same arm as always,” but you see a large bruise from a recent draw on that arm; what is the best site decision?
a: Choose an alternate site/arm and avoid the bruised area because anticoagulated patients bruise/bleed more easily, and the trap is using the bruised site for convenience and causing hematoma.

q: A patient scheduled for an EKG has a hairy chest and electrodes won’t adhere; what is the best action?
a: Clip (not shave) excess hair where electrodes will be placed and clean/dry the skin because poor adhesion causes artifact, and the trap is placing electrodes over hair and accepting a poor tracing.

q: During venipuncture, the patient becomes pale and says they feel faint; what is the CMA’s best next action?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, apply pressure, and assist the patient to a safe position (supine with legs elevated if possible) because preventing syncope-related injury is the priority (trap: trying to “finish the last tube” first).

q: An EKG printout has heavy jagged artifact and you notice a lead wire is loosely connected; what should the CMA do next?
a: Reconnect/secure the lead and ensure good skin contact, then repeat the EKG because loose leads create artifact and can mimic dysrhythmias; the trap is sending the unreadable strip to the provider.

q: While preparing an outpatient EKG, the patient asks if the test can be done through their shirt for privacy; what should the CMA do?
a: Explain that electrodes must be placed on clean, dry skin on the chest and provide draping to maintain privacy because correct placement is required for accuracy, and the trap is compromising lead contact to avoid an awkward moment.

q: While drawing a light blue tube for PT/INR, the tube only fills halfway before flow stops; what should the CMA do next?
a: Discard that underfilled light blue tube and recollect with a full draw because incorrect blood-to-anticoagulant ratio makes results unreliable (trap: “topping off” from another tube is unacceptable).

q: A fasting lipid panel is ordered, and the patient says they ate breakfast an hour ago; what should the CMA do first?
a: Pause the draw and notify the provider or follow clinic protocol to reschedule because eating can invalidate the test (trap: drawing anyway and “noting it” still risks wrong clinical decisions).

q: A provider glances at a newly completed EKG and asks the CMA, “Does this show an MI?” and the patient is listening; what is the best response?
a: State you can’t interpret or diagnose, promptly give the tracing to the provider, and focus on patient reassurance because interpretation is outside CMA scope, and the trap is offering an opinion that could mislead or alarm the patient.

q: A CMA is collecting a CBC and a basic metabolic panel and has light blue, red, and lavender tubes on the tray; what is the best order of draw?
a: Draw light blue first, then red, then lavender because citrate tubes must be filled before EDTA tubes to prevent additive carryover (common trap: drawing lavender before light blue can falsely alter coag results).

q: A throat swab rapid strep test is being performed, but the patient gagged and the swab touched the tongue; what is the best next step?
a: Discard the swab and recollect properly from tonsillar pillars/posterior pharynx because saliva/tongue contact can cause false results (trap: running the test anyway to avoid repeating discomfort).

q: While preparing to draw blood, the CMA realizes the labels were printed for a different patient with a similar name; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and re-verify patient identity with two identifiers and print correct labels because mislabeling is a critical lab error (trap: crossing out the wrong name or relabeling after the draw without verification).

q: A patient’s arm is very cold and veins are hard to palpate; what is the best action before attempting venipuncture?
a: Warm the site (e.g., warm compress) and reassess because heat increases blood flow and vein dilation (trap: applying excessive tourniquet time, which increases hemoconcentration and discomfort).

q: A serum chemistry sample has visible hemolysis noted by the lab; which collection mistake is most likely and what should the CMA do next time?
a: Avoid forceful syringe transfer/shaking and allow antiseptic to dry because these can hemolyze blood; recollect using correct technique since hemolysis can falsely elevate analytes (trap: thinking hemolysis “doesn’t matter” for chemistry).

q: After venipuncture, a hematoma begins forming at the site while the tube is still filling; what should the CMA do immediately?
a: Release the tourniquet, withdraw the needle, and apply firm pressure because continued suction worsens bleeding into tissue (trap: keeping the needle in and “readjusting” to save the draw).

q: The provider orders a blood culture and a CMP; which should the CMA collect first and why?
a: Collect blood cultures first using sterile technique because they must be uncontaminated and drawn before other additives (trap: drawing chemistry tubes first increases contamination risk and invalid results).

q: After drawing a lavender tube, the CMA sets it on the counter without mixing and continues with paperwork; what should the CMA do when realizing this within a minute?
a: Gently invert the tube the recommended number of times immediately because EDTA specimens can clot if not mixed, leading to rejected CBCs (trap: shaking vigorously, which can hemolyze and alter results).

q: A urine specimen for culture is ordered, and the patient hands the CMA a cup filled from the collection hat after voiding; what should the CMA do next?
a: Explain the need for a clean-catch midstream specimen and have the patient recollect because initial-stream urine and nonsterile collection can contaminate culture (trap: accepting any urine because “it’s enough volume”).

q: During a 12-lead EKG, the right and left arm leads were accidentally reversed; what is the best next step once discovered?
a: Correct the lead placement and repeat the EKG because limb lead reversal can mimic ischemia or axis changes (trap: sending it “with a note,” risking misinterpretation and wrong treatment).

q: A provider asks the CMA to “tell me if this EKG is a STEMI”; what is the most appropriate response?
a: State that interpretation is outside the CMA scope and immediately alert the provider of any urgent symptoms/abnormal tracing concerns while ensuring the EKG is promptly delivered because CMAs obtain and relay tests, not diagnose (trap: offering an interpretation that could delay care).

q: A CMA performed a rapid influenza POCT but read the result at 25 minutes instead of the specified time window; what is the best action?
a: Repeat the test with a new kit and read within the manufacturer’s time frame because late readings can cause false results (trap: documenting the late-read result as definitive).

q: A specimen is collected for a send-out test, but the requisition is missing the ordering provider and collection time; what should the CMA do before sending it?
a: Hold the specimen and obtain the missing required information, then complete documentation because incomplete requisitions can cause rejection or misattribution (trap: sending it anyway and hoping the lab “figures it out”).

q: An outpatient EKG printout shows heavy baseline wandering, and the patient is talking and shifting; what should the CMA do first?
a: Ask the patient to lie still and relax, then repeat the EKG because motion artifact commonly causes wandering baseline (trap: immediately adjusting machine settings or interpreting it as a rhythm change).

q: A urine pregnancy test is negative, but the control line did not appear; what should the CMA do?
a: Treat it as an invalid test, repeat with a new device, and document appropriately because absent control means the test cannot be trusted (trap: reporting it as negative based on the test line alone).

q: The clinic runs a CLIA-waived glucose meter, and the QC check fails at the start of the day; what should the CMA do next?
a: Do not test patients, troubleshoot per manufacturer instructions (e.g., repeat QC with new strip/control, check expiration), and notify the supervisor if unresolved because patient results are unreliable without passing QC (trap: running patient tests “just this once”).

q: During a routine venipuncture for a fasting lipid panel and CBC, the CMA fills the lavender tube first and then the light green tube; what should the CMA do next to best protect specimen accuracy?
a: Stop and recollect using the correct order of draw (light green heparin before lavender EDTA) and label/transport properly, because drawing EDTA first can carry over anticoagulant and distort chemistry results—a common mistake is sending the specimens anyway and assuming mixing will fix it.

q: A patient becomes pale and says they feel “hot and dizzy” right after the blood draw while seated on the exam table; what should you do first?
a: Assist the patient to a safe position (lying down or head lowered), stay with them, and call for help per clinic protocol because this is likely vasovagal syncope and fall prevention is the priority, a common trap is leaving to “get water” first.

q: Immediately after removing the needle, the patient forms a rapidly enlarging bruise at the puncture site; what should you do first?
a: Apply firm direct pressure and keep the arm straight/elevated because this suggests a hematoma and prompt pressure limits bleeding, a common mistake is bending the elbow which worsens bruising.

q: You collected a lavender-top tube for a CBC but forgot to invert it and it sat upright for several minutes; what is the best next action before sending it to the lab?
a: Gently invert the tube the recommended number of times immediately and check for clots because EDTA tubes must be mixed to prevent clotting and redraws, a common trap is shaking vigorously which hemolyzes the sample.

q: While drawing a BMP, you notice the patient repeatedly pumping their fist to “help the vein”; what should you do next?
a: Ask the patient to relax the hand and avoid fist pumping because it can alter analytes (e.g., potassium) and contributes to hemolysis, a common trap is allowing vigorous pumping to continue to keep the vein prominent.

q: After applying the tourniquet and locating a vein, a phone call distracts you and the tourniquet remains on for over a minute; what is the best action before proceeding?
a: Release the tourniquet, allow a brief rest, then reapply right before the venipuncture because prolonged tourniquet time can falsely concentrate results and increase hemolysis risk, a common trap is continuing “to avoid losing the vein.”

q: During a morning draw you need a CBC, BMP, PT/INR, and a fasting glucose from the same patient; in what order should the tubes be filled to prevent additive carryover?
a: Draw light blue (citrate) first, then serum (red/gold), then green (heparin), then lavender (EDTA), then gray (fluoride) because correct order of draw prevents anticoagulants (especially EDTA) from contaminating chemistry/coag results, a common trap when grabbing lavender early.

q: You accidentally nick an artery and see bright red, pulsatile bleeding at the venipuncture site; what is the best immediate response?
a: Stop the draw and apply firm pressure for an extended time while alerting the provider/supervisor because arterial puncture requires prolonged pressure and escalation, a common trap is applying only brief pressure and sending the patient out.

q: A provider orders a blood culture and a CMP; the patient’s vein is fragile and you anticipate only one successful stick—what should you do first to protect specimen validity?
a: Collect the blood cultures first using aseptic technique before other tubes because contamination risk is highest and additive carryover from other tubes can affect culture integrity, a common mistake when “saving cultures for last.”

q: A patient needs a clean-catch urine culture but is in a hurry and asks if they can just fill the cup without cleaning; what should you do?
a: Re-teach and ensure proper cleansing and midstream technique before collection because skin flora contamination can cause false positives and unnecessary treatment, a common trap is accepting a contaminated specimen to avoid delaying the visit.

q: During venipuncture the patient reports a sharp “electric shock” pain radiating down the forearm; what should you do next?
a: Remove the needle immediately and document/report the event because this suggests nerve involvement and continuing can cause injury, a common trap is “repositioning the needle” to finish the draw.

q: You labeled tubes at the nurses’ station after leaving the room and then realize two patients with the same last name were drawn back-to-back; what is the best action?
a: Treat the specimens as potentially mislabeled, notify the lab/supervisor, and recollect with bedside labeling using two identifiers because patient ID errors are a critical safety issue, a common trap is guessing based on room number or time.

q: A specimen for a timed test (e.g., peak/trough-type timing noted on the requisition) arrives at the lab bag without collection time documented; what should you do next?
a: Contact the collector/patient immediately to obtain and document the exact collection time because timing affects interpretation and the lab may reject it, a common trap is estimating the time from when it was dropped off.

q: A urine POCT cup for pregnancy testing has been sitting on the counter for an hour before testing; what should you do next?
a: Verify the manufacturer time limits and, if exceeded, obtain a fresh specimen because delayed testing can invalidate results, a common trap is running it anyway “since it’s been covered.”

q: You notice the limb electrodes were placed on the patient’s wrists and ankles, but they are shivering and the tracing shows muscle artifact; what is the best next step?
a: Move limb electrodes to the torso (per facility protocol) and warm/relax the patient to reduce motion artifact because tremor distorts the tracing, a common trap is interpreting/printing a poor-quality strip.

q: You are collecting a throat swab for rapid strep and the patient gags, and the swab touches the inside of the cheek; what is the best next step?
a: Discard the swab and recollect without contaminating it because touching oral mucosa can give inaccurate results, a common trap is proceeding because “the swab still looks clean.”

q: While setting up a 12-lead EKG, the patient’s skin is oily from lotion and the tracings show wandering baseline; what should you do first to improve signal quality?
a: Clean and dry the skin (and lightly abrade if needed per protocol) before reapplying electrodes because poor skin contact causes artifact, a common trap is repeatedly restarting the machine without fixing electrode adhesion.

q: During a fasting lipid panel draw, you collect a light blue tube first “so it doesn’t clot,” then realize you still need a serum separator tube; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and redraw using the correct order of draw (blood cultures if ordered, then light blue, then serum/SST, then heparin, then EDTA, then glycolytic) because drawing citrate before serum can contaminate results; the trap is trying to “fix it” by just recollecting one tube from the same puncture without restarting correctly.

q: Right after starting the EKG, the machine displays “leads off” and the tracing is flat in multiple leads; what should you do next?
a: Check cable connections and ensure each electrode is firmly attached to the correct lead wire because “leads off” indicates poor connection, a common trap is replacing the entire machine before checking the simple fix.

q: A new medical assistant begins running a CLIA-waived rapid flu test but skips documenting the lot number and expiration date of the test kit; what should you do next?
a: Stop and ensure required QC documentation (lot/expiration, controls as applicable) is completed because CLIA-waived tests still require traceable QC for accuracy and audits, a common trap is thinking “waived” means no documentation.

q: At the start of the day, the glucose meter control solution result is out of range; what is the best next action before testing patients?
a: Do not test patients—troubleshoot (check strips expiration/storage, meter cleanliness, repeat control) and document QC because out-of-range controls mean results are unreliable, a common trap is testing anyway and “rechecking later.”

q: You draw blood for a CBC and CMP, but the lavender EDTA tube is underfilled; the patient wants to leave—what is the best action?
a: Explain the need for a recollect and redraw the EDTA tube to the proper fill because an underfilled anticoagulant tube alters blood-to-additive ratio and skews CBC; the trap is sending it anyway and hoping the lab “can run it.”

q: A provider orders a PT/INR and a CBC; after the draw you notice the light blue tube was not filled to the line, but the lavender was perfect—what should the CMA do?
a: Recollect the light blue tube to a full draw because citrate tubes must be filled precisely for accurate coagulation testing; the trap is assuming “close enough” is acceptable since another tube collected fine.

q: While collecting a BMP, you vigorously shake the green-top tube to “mix it faster”; what should you do to prevent an inaccurate result?
a: Gently invert the tube the required number of times per manufacturer (do not shake) because shaking can hemolyze the specimen and falsely elevate values like potassium; the trap is thinking faster mixing improves quality.

q: An EKG prints showing a heart rate of 42 with the patient reporting new lightheadedness; what should the CMA do next?
a: Immediately notify the provider and keep the patient seated/monitored because symptomatic bradycardia can be unstable and requires prompt evaluation, a common trap is filing the EKG first since the test is “complete.”

q: You collected a urine specimen for culture but realize it sat on the counter for 2 hours before transport; what is the best action?
a: Notify the lab/ordering provider and recollect if required because delayed unrefrigerated urine can allow bacterial overgrowth and invalid culture results; the trap is refrigerating it late and sending it without disclosure.

q: After drawing a potassium level, you realize you left the tourniquet on for over a minute while searching for a vein; what should the CMA do?
a: Recollect if possible and document the issue because prolonged tourniquet time can cause hemoconcentration and affect analytes; the trap is sending it without noting the pre-analytic error.

q: You are about to draw a patient on anticoagulant therapy who has persistent oozing after the first attempt; what should the CMA do next after removing the needle?
a: Apply prolonged direct pressure and reassess before bandaging because anticoagulants increase bleeding risk; the trap is placing a small adhesive bandage quickly and sending the patient out still bleeding.

q: A patient’s requisition says “2-hour postprandial glucose,” but the patient reports they ate 30 minutes ago; what should the CMA do first?
a: Clarify timing and reschedule/adjust collection per order instructions before drawing because the diagnostic value depends on correct timing; the trap is drawing now and documenting “patient ate,” which still yields a misleading result.

q: During a routine venipuncture, you draw a light blue citrate tube for PT/INR but notice it is only half full while the other tubes are filled; the patient is stable and still has good venous access—what should you do next?
a: Discard and recollect the light blue tube to the fill line before sending the specimen because citrate tubes require a precise 9:1 blood-to-additive ratio for accurate coagulation results; the common mistake is sending an underfilled tube, which can falsely prolong clotting times.

q: You labeled tubes at the nurses’ station after leaving the patient’s room because you were rushed; what should you do now?
a: Treat the specimens as potentially misidentified and follow clinic policy for recollection and incident reporting because labeling must occur in the patient’s presence to ensure two-identifier accuracy; the trap is “double-checking” the labels from memory.

q: After venipuncture for multiple tubes, blood begins pooling under the skin and the site swells; what is the CMA’s best next action?
a: Release the tourniquet, withdraw the needle, and apply firm pressure then ice as directed because this indicates a hematoma and continuing can worsen bleeding; the trap is trying to “finish the last tube” before stopping.

q: A patient becomes pale and says they feel faint during a blood draw while seated on the exam table; what should the CMA do first?
a: Remove the needle and help the patient to a safe position (supine or head-down per clinic protocol) and monitor because preventing a fall is the priority; the trap is offering water first while the needle is still in place.

q: The EKG tracing shows a wandering baseline and the patient is shivering in a cold room; what should the CMA do first?
a: Warm and reposition the patient and ask them to hold still, then repeat the tracing because muscle tremor commonly mimics artifact; the trap is assuming it’s a dysrhythmia and alerting the provider before troubleshooting.

q: An order includes a lactic acid test, and the specimen will sit until the courier arrives in 45 minutes; what should the CMA do to protect result accuracy?
a: Follow special handling (typically immediate transport on ice and prompt processing) because lactate rises in vitro if not handled correctly; the trap is treating it like a routine chemistry tube.

q: While setting up a 12-lead EKG, the patient’s chest is diaphoretic and the limb electrodes keep lifting; what is the best next step?
a: Dry/clean and gently abrade the skin as appropriate and replace electrodes securely because poor contact causes artifact; the trap is repeatedly restarting the EKG without fixing skin prep.

q: During point-of-care hemoglobin A1c testing, you realize the patient’s fingerstick sample was insufficient but the cartridge is already loaded; what should the CMA do?
a: Cancel and restart with a new cartridge and adequate specimen per manufacturer instructions because insufficient sample can yield erroneous results; the trap is adding more blood late or “topping off,” which invalidates the test.

q: While performing an EKG, you see a heart rate of 38 on the machine display and the patient reports new dizziness; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stay with the patient and immediately notify the provider/activate the clinic’s urgent response because symptomatic bradycardia can be unstable; the trap is finishing paperwork first because “the machine might be wrong.”

q: You are about to run a CLIA-waived rapid strep test, but the external control results are out of range today; what should the CMA do?
a: Do not test patient samples until the QC issue is resolved (repeat controls, check expiration/storage, and notify supervisor) because reporting results with failed QC is invalid; the trap is running the patient anyway “since it’s waived.”

q: You finish an EKG and notice the limb leads were placed on the patient’s torso over clothing for speed; what is the best action?
a: Repeat the EKG with correct lead placement on bare skin because incorrect placement can alter axis and waveforms and mislead interpretation; the trap is printing and sending it since “it still made a tracing.”

q: A coworker asks you to use yesterday’s opened glucometer control solution because “it’s still half full,” and you can’t confirm the open date; what should the CMA do?
a: Discard and use properly dated, unexpired control solution because undated/expired controls can’t verify accuracy; the trap is accepting “it looks fine” instead of ensuring traceable QC.

q: During a routine venipuncture, the CMA realizes the tourniquet has been on for over 1 minute while searching for a vein; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Release the tourniquet and allow the arm to rest before reapplying because prolonged stasis can alter results (hemoconcentration), a common mistake is proceeding anyway “to save time.”

q: While drawing an EDTA (lavender) tube for CBC, blood stops flowing and the tube only partially fills; what should the CMA do NEXT to avoid an inaccurate result?
a: Collect a new lavender tube ensuring adequate fill and gentle inversions because underfilling can alter the blood-to-additive ratio and affect CBC values, the trap is sending a short-draw EDTA anyway.

q: A provider orders a CBC, BMP, PT/INR, and type & screen; after confirming identity, what tube type should the CMA fill FIRST to follow the order of draw?
a: Draw blood culture bottles first if ordered, otherwise draw the light blue (citrate) tube first because coagulation tests are most sensitive to additive carryover, a common trap is starting with SST/green and contaminating the PT/INR.

q: Immediately after a blood draw, the patient becomes pale, sweaty, and says they feel faint while seated upright; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Assist the patient to a safe position (supine with legs elevated if possible) and monitor while calling for help per clinic protocol because this is likely vasovagal syncope, the trap is having them “walk it off” to the lobby.

q: After venipuncture, a patient develops a rapidly growing bruise and reports tightness at the site; what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Stop the draw and apply firm pressure with the arm elevated because this suggests a hematoma and continuing can worsen bleeding, the trap is “finishing the tube” before addressing the complication.

q: A CMP and potassium are ordered; the CMA notes the patient has an active IV infusing in the left arm and a saline lock in the right—what is the BEST site choice?
a: Use a site distal to and away from IV access (preferably the arm without infusion and not above the IV) because IV fluids can dilute or contaminate results, the trap is drawing from the infusion arm “since it has easy access.”

q: A fasting lipid panel and CMP are drawn; immediately after collecting, the CMA vigorously shakes the SST tube to mix—what is the BEST corrective action?
a: Redraw the specimen and document the reason because vigorous shaking can hemolyze and invalidate chemistry results, the trap is thinking “any mixing is fine” rather than gentle inversions.

q: A patient’s ID band is missing, and the label printer is down; the patient states their name and DOB correctly—what should the CMA do before drawing blood?
a: Stop and obtain a second approved identifier and a reliable labeling method (per clinic process) before collection because unlabeled/mislabeled specimens are rejected and unsafe, the trap is drawing first and “labeling later.”

q: A rapid strep test is CLIA-waived and the patient’s swab is obtained, but the kit’s external controls have not been run after opening a new lot; what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Run and document the required quality control before reporting patient results because waived tests still require QC to ensure accuracy, the trap is testing the patient immediately and “doing QC later.”

q: The CMA accidentally performs a capillary fingerstick on a cold, cyanotic fingertip for a glucose POCT; the value is unexpectedly low—what is the BEST next step?
a: Warm the hand and repeat the test on an appropriate site because poor peripheral perfusion can give falsely low capillary readings, the trap is documenting the low value as accurate without retesting.

q: During POCT glucose testing, the meter displays an error code related to expired strips; the patient is waiting—what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Discard the expired strips and retest with in-date strips (and QC if indicated) because expired reagents can produce unreliable results, the trap is repeating with the same strips hoping the error clears.

q: A urine specimen for culture was collected in a nonsterile cup and left at room temperature for 3 hours before transport; what should the CMA do?
a: Reject and recollect or ensure proper refrigeration per lab requirements because bacterial overgrowth can invalidate culture results, the trap is sending it “since it’s already collected.”

q: After attaching limb leads for an EKG, the CMA sees “lead off” and notices the right arm electrode is placed on the wrist over heavy hair; what should the CMA do?
a: Re-prep and reposition the electrode on clean, dry skin with good contact (clip hair if needed) because poor adhesion triggers lead-off and artifact, the trap is pressing “acquire” repeatedly without fixing contact.

q: A provider orders an EKG on a patient with chest pressure; the CMA notes the patient applied lotion to the chest and electrodes keep lifting—what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Clean and dry the skin (and gently abrade if needed) before reapplying electrodes because oils increase artifact and poor contact, the trap is repeatedly repositioning leads without addressing skin prep.

q: While running a 12-lead EKG, the tracing shows a wandering baseline and the patient is shivering in the cold room; what is the BEST action?
a: Warm the patient and minimize movement, then repeat the EKG because muscle tremor causes artifact that can mimic dysrhythmia, the trap is printing and handing it to the provider as-is.

q: A patient has a lab order for a timed 24-hour urine; they ask when to start because they forgot the instructions—what should the CMA tell them?
a: Instruct them to void and discard the first urine at the start time, then collect all urine for the next 24 hours including the final void at the end time because this defines the collection interval, the trap is saving the first void and shortening the timing.

q: A patient says, “I’m on blood thinners,” and after venipuncture the site keeps oozing despite a small bandage; what should the CMA do first?
a: Apply firm direct pressure longer and keep the arm extended, then reassess; the trap is using a tight tourniquet-like wrap or letting the patient bend the elbow, which can worsen bleeding/hematoma.

q: During a fasting lipid panel draw, you collect a light blue tube then realize you forgot the patient’s date of birth check and the tubes are still unlabeled on the counter; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop and re-identify the patient using two identifiers, then label the tubes in the patient’s presence immediately; labeling later is a common mislabeling trap and can invalidate results.

q: An EKG prints with a flat line in one lead but normal activity in others; the patient is talking and moving arms—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Check lead connection/placement for that specific lead and ask the patient to remain still, then repeat because a single-lead flat line is often a disconnected electrode, the trap is assuming asystole and alarming without troubleshooting.

q: While drawing blood, the CMA sees the tube is only half-filled for a sodium citrate (light blue) specimen but the draw otherwise went smoothly; what is the best action?
a: Redraw the light blue tube to the required fill line because the blood-to-anticoagulant ratio must be exact; a common mistake is sending an underfilled coag tube that yields inaccurate clotting times.

q: A throat swab for rapid influenza POCT was collected, but the test requires a nasopharyngeal swab per manufacturer instructions; what should the CMA do?
a: Do not run the test and recollect using the correct specimen type because improper collection can cause false negatives and invalid results, the trap is running it anyway “since it’s the same area.”

q: A patient with a pacemaker comes for an EKG; the CMA is unsure if pacer spikes will appear—what should the CMA do BEST?
a: Perform the EKG as ordered and document the presence of a pacemaker (and any symptoms) because CMAs obtain/record but do not interpret, the trap is delaying the test to “confirm interpretation.”

q: A provider orders PT/INR, CMP, and CBC, and the CMA has light blue, gold, and lavender tubes ready; in what order should the CMA draw them?
a: Draw light blue first, then gold, then lavender; incorrect order can cause additive carryover that alters coagulation or hematology results.

q: During venipuncture for a CBC and BMP, the CMA accidentally draws the lavender (EDTA) tube before the green heparin tube and is about to label and send both; what is the best next action?
a: Stop and redraw the BMP using a new collection set and correct order of draw because EDTA carryover can falsely elevate potassium and alter chemistry results; a common mistake is sending the specimen anyway since it “filled correctly,” which risks inaccurate lab values.

q: A urine culture is ordered, and the patient hands the CMA an unlabeled specimen cup collected in the restroom; what should the CMA do next?
a: Confirm two identifiers and label the container immediately in front of the patient, then place it in the proper transport bag; the trap is labeling at the nurses’ station, increasing mix-ups.

q: Mid-draw, the patient becomes pale and says, “I feel like I’m going to pass out”; what should the CMA do next?
a: Immediately remove the needle, activate safety, help the patient into a safe position (recline with legs elevated if possible), and notify the provider per clinic protocol; continuing the draw is a safety error.

q: After a venipuncture, a large bruise starts forming and the patient reports sharp pain at the site; what is the CMA’s best next step?
a: Stop the draw if still in progress, remove the needle, and apply firm pressure and a cold pack; the trap is “digging” for the vein, which increases hematoma and nerve injury risk.

q: During venipuncture, blood flow stops after the first tube and the CMA notices the tourniquet has been on for a prolonged time while troubleshooting; what should the CMA do next?
a: Release the tourniquet and reassess before attempting again because prolonged tourniquet time can cause hemoconcentration and inaccurate results; the trap is leaving it on while fishing for flow.

q: A patient arrives with a 24-hour urine jug at room temperature and says it sat in the car for two hours; what is the best CMA action?
a: Ask about required storage (usually refrigerated) and notify the lab/provider that storage requirements may have been violated before processing; the trap is accepting and sending without documenting compromised integrity.

q: For a CLIA-waived rapid strep test, the CMA is about to run the cartridge but notices the kit’s expiration date was last week; what should the CMA do?
a: Do not use the expired kit, obtain an in-date test, and document per QC policy; the trap is “just running it” because waived tests still require valid reagents for accurate results.

q: A fasting glucose is ordered as a point-of-care fingerstick, but the patient’s hands are visibly soiled from work; what should the CMA do first?
a: Have the patient wash hands with soap and water and dry thoroughly before the fingerstick; relying only on an alcohol swab is a common trap that can contaminate the sample and skew results.

q: The CMA draws a lavender tube for CBC and sets it upright on the counter without mixing; 10 minutes later they remember; what should the CMA do?
a: Gently invert the tube the recommended number of times as soon as possible and note if clotting is suspected; the common mistake is shaking vigorously, which hemolyzes the sample.

q: During a routine venipuncture for a CBC, CMP, and PT/INR, the CMA fills the light blue tube first but notices the tube only filled about halfway and the patient is stable; what should the CMA do NEXT to prevent an inaccurate coagulation result?
a: Discard that underfilled light blue tube and recollect a new light blue tube to the proper fill line before sending, because citrate tubes require a correct blood-to-additive ratio and a common mistake is “topping off” or submitting a short draw that can falsely prolong PT/INR.

q: After performing a waived urine dipstick, the CMA reads the results 10 minutes later while rooming the next patient; what should the CMA do?
a: Repeat the test with a new strip and read within the manufacturer’s time window; the trap is charting late-read colors, which can create false positives/negatives.

q: An EKG printout shows “LEAD OFF” and the tracing is flat in one lead; what should the CMA do first?
a: Check and reattach the indicated electrode/lead wire connection and ensure good skin contact; the trap is restarting the machine without fixing the physical connection.

q: A patient with a right-arm PICC line needs outpatient lab work, and the CMA is preparing for venipuncture; what is the best action?
a: Avoid venipuncture in the PICC arm and select the other arm or consult the nurse/provider for alternate collection; the trap is drawing near a vascular access device, increasing complication risk.

q: While running an EKG, the tracing shows a shaky baseline across multiple leads and the patient is visibly shivering; what should the CMA do next?
a: Warm and reassure the patient and minimize muscle movement, then repeat the tracing if needed; the trap is assuming it’s a cardiac rhythm problem and printing without troubleshooting artifact.

q: A provider orders a 12-lead EKG, and the CMA notices the patient’s chest is diaphoretic and lotion is present; what should the CMA do before placing electrodes?
a: Clean and dry the skin (and lightly abrade if needed) to improve electrode contact; the trap is placing electrodes over moisture/lotion, which increases artifact.

q: During EKG setup, the patient asks, “Does this mean I’m having a heart attack?”; what is the best CMA response?
a: Explain the test records the heart’s electrical activity and the provider will interpret results, then proceed promptly; the trap is giving interpretation or reassurance beyond scope.

q: After collecting a specimen for a send-out test, the CMA realizes the requisition has the correct name but the wrong medical record number; what should the CMA do next?
a: Stop processing and correct the paperwork using proper verification and facility procedure before sending; the trap is “fixing it later,” which can cause rejected specimens or misfiled results.

q: A patient on the schedule states they have a history of mastectomy with lymph node removal on the left; the CMA is preparing for venipuncture and the right arm has a visible IV from an infusion clinic; what should the CMA do next?
