a: Consult the provider for an appropriate site (often avoiding the mastectomy side and avoiding draws above/near an IV) because site selection affects lymphedema and specimen dilution; the trap is choosing the “best vein” without considering restrictions.

q: A provider orders PT/INR and the CMA collects a light blue tube that is only half full; what is the best next action?
a: Recollect the specimen ensuring the light blue tube is filled to the indicated line because underfilling changes the blood-to-anticoagulant ratio; the trap is sending it anyway and getting inaccurate coagulation results.

q: During venipuncture, blood flow stops after the first tube and the CMA considers “fishing” the needle to restart flow; what should the CMA do instead?
a: Release the tourniquet, withdraw the needle, apply pressure, and attempt a new draw at a different site because probing increases hematoma/nerve injury risk; the trap is manipulating the needle to salvage the stick.

q: A patient becomes pale and says they feel faint immediately after the needle is inserted; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, apply pressure, and position the patient safely (supine with legs elevated if possible) because syncope risk makes safety the priority; the trap is “finish quickly” to avoid wasting supplies.

q: Immediately after drawing blood cultures, the CMA realizes they labeled the bottles at the nurses’ station instead of in the room; what is the best next action?
a: Treat the specimens as mislabeled and follow the lab’s relabel/recollect process because labeling must occur in the patient’s presence to ensure identification integrity; the trap is adding the label later because you “know it’s theirs.”

q: After removing the needle, the CMA sees rapid swelling at the puncture site; what is the best immediate action?
a: Apply firm pressure and elevate the arm, then document/notify per protocol because this suggests a hematoma and needs prompt control; the trap is placing a bandage only and letting the patient leave.

q: During an outpatient phlebotomy, you draw a light blue (citrate) tube first but it only fills halfway because blood flow stops; the patient is stable and the provider needs PT/INR—what should the CMA do next?
a: Discard the underfilled light blue tube and redraw a new light blue tube that fills to the marked line because citrate tubes require the correct blood-to-additive ratio for accurate coagulation results, and the common mistake is sending an underfilled tube that can falsely prolong clotting times.

q: A fasting glucose is ordered and the patient’s tube sits on the counter for an hour before processing; what should the CMA do next?
a: Follow lab protocol for delayed processing (often recollect or ensure appropriate glycolysis inhibitor tube/handling) because glucose can drop if not handled correctly; the trap is assuming refrigeration alone fixes pre-analytic error.

q: After a fingerstick, the CMA strongly “milks” the finger to fill the microcollection device; what is the best correction for next time?
a: Use gentle pressure and wipe away the first drop rather than forcefully squeezing because excessive milking causes hemolysis and tissue-fluid contamination; the trap is thinking more pressure equals a better sample.

q: While obtaining an EKG, the machine displays “leads off” and the patient is anxious, asking if something is wrong with their heart; what should the CMA do next?
a: Reassure the patient it’s a contact issue, check cable connections/electrode adherence, and restart once corrected because this is usually equipment/patient interface—not a diagnosis; the trap is alarming the patient or discussing interpretation.

q: A capillary fingerstick is planned for POCT hemoglobin, and the patient’s hands are cold; what should the CMA do before puncture?
a: Warm the hand/finger and ensure good circulation before puncture because poor perfusion leads to inadequate/hemolyzed samples; the trap is squeezing hard to force blood, which dilutes with tissue fluid.

q: An EKG tracing shows a wandering baseline and the patient is shivering in the room; what should the CMA do first?
a: Address the patient’s comfort (provide warmth, have them relax/keep still) and then repeat the EKG because muscle tremor mimics artifact; the trap is interpreting it as an arrhythmia and escalating before troubleshooting.

q: The provider orders a clean-catch urine, and the patient asks if they can collect it after wiping once quickly; what should the CMA do next?
a: Re-educate on proper clean-catch steps (cleanse appropriately, start stream, collect midstream without touching inside of cup) because poor technique contaminates culture results; the trap is rushing collection to keep clinic flow moving.

q: While drawing blood for a CMP and CBC, the CMA fills the lavender tube first and then the light green tube; what should the CMA do next to protect specimen accuracy?
a: Label and send the specimens but notify the provider/lab that the order of draw was incorrect and a redraw may be needed, because EDTA carryover from lavender can falsely alter chemistry results (common mistake is trying to “fix” it by pouring blood into another tube or ignoring the error).

q: A urine culture is ordered and the patient hands the CMA a specimen cup filled to the brim with unlabeled urine; what should the CMA do first?
a: Verify patient identity and label the specimen immediately in the patient’s presence (then assess if recollection is needed for sterile technique) because unlabeled specimens risk misidentification; the trap is sending it “since it’s fresh.”

q: During a fasting lipid fingerstick POCT, the CMA’s first drop of blood touches the patient’s skin and then the test strip while the patient asks to “just run it anyway”; what should the CMA do next?
a: Discard that strip, wipe away the first drop, obtain a new drop, and retest with a new strip because contaminated/hemolyzed first-drop samples can cause inaccurate results, and the common mistake is trying to “save” the test after the strip has been contaminated.

q: The CMA opens a new box of test strips for a CLIA-waived strep test and plans to start testing immediately; what should the CMA do first?
a: Perform and document required QC for the new lot (and verify expiration/storage) before patient testing because lot changes can affect accuracy; the trap is assuming waived testing never needs QC.

q: While drawing a fasting lipid panel, you notice the tourniquet has been on for over 1 minute because you were searching for a vein; what should you do FIRST?
a: Release the tourniquet and allow circulation to normalize before reapplying because prolonged tourniquet time can falsely elevate analytes; the trap is proceeding to draw “quickly” anyway.

q: During a venipuncture, blood flow slows and the patient’s fist is repeatedly pumping; what should the CMA do NEXT to obtain an accurate sample?
a: Ask the patient to relax the hand and release fist-pumping because it can hemoconcentrate and alter results; the trap is encouraging pumping, which can worsen accuracy and flow.

q: A provider orders a CBC, BMP, and PT/INR on a patient, and you have to draw all specimens in one venipuncture; what tube should you fill first?
a: Draw the light blue citrate tube first because coagulation testing is most sensitive to additive carryover; a common trap is starting with serum or EDTA and contaminating the PT/INR.

q: After completing a CLIA-waived urine dipstick, the CMA documents results but forgets to record the reagent strip lot number and expiration; what is the best next action?
a: Add the missing QC/lot documentation per protocol as soon as identified because traceability is required for quality audits and result validity; the trap is thinking only the numeric result matters and QC details are optional.

q: In POCT glucose testing, the control solution result is out of the acceptable range but the patient is waiting; what should the CMA do next?
a: Do not report patient results, troubleshoot per manufacturer instructions (check strip lot/expiration, storage, meter cleaning, rerun controls) and repeat QC before testing because out-of-range controls invalidate results; the trap is “running the patient anyway” to save time.

q: You collected a lavender-top tube for CBC but forgot to invert it and it clots in the lab; what is the BEST corrective action?
a: Redraw the specimen because a clotted EDTA sample is unusable for CBC; the trap is trying to “shake it” later, which can’t undo clotting and may hemolyze.

q: A provider asks the CMA if the EKG “looks like atrial fibrillation” and whether to start treatment; what is the appropriate response?
a: State you cannot interpret or recommend treatment, and promptly give the tracing to the provider while reporting any urgent symptoms observed because interpretation/prescribing is outside CMA scope; the trap is offering a diagnosis based on pattern recognition.

q: You labeled tubes after leaving the exam room because you were interrupted, and now you’re not 100% sure which patient they belong to; what is the BEST action?
a: Treat the specimens as unlabeled/mislabeled and recollect with bedside labeling because patient ID errors are high-risk; the trap is “guessing” based on room number or appearance.

q: After venipuncture, a patient develops a rapidly enlarging bruise at the site while you’re still holding gauze; what should you do NEXT?
a: Apply firm direct pressure for several minutes and elevate the arm because this suggests a hematoma; the trap is using a tight wrap briefly and letting them leave too soon.

q: Immediately after you remove the needle, the patient says they feel lightheaded and looks pale; what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Stop the procedure, have the patient sit or lie back, and ensure airway/breathing while applying pressure to the site because syncope is a safety emergency; the trap is sending them to the waiting room “to rest.”

q: You collected a serum tube for a chemistry test and immediately place it in the centrifuge without waiting; what is the BEST next step?
a: Stop and allow the specimen to clot fully before centrifugation (per tube requirements) because spinning too soon can cause fibrin and inaccurate results; the trap is rushing to meet pickup time.

q: A patient has an IV infusing in the left forearm and the only good vein you see is just above the IV site; what is the BEST action?
a: Use the other arm or a site away from the IV because draws above an infusion risk dilution/contamination of results; the trap is drawing “above the IV” to avoid the catheter.

q: You are asked to draw blood cultures and a CMP from the same patient in clinic; after identifying the patient, what is your NEXT priority before the culture draw?
a: Perform antiseptic skin prep with appropriate contact time and avoid repalpating the site because contamination causes false-positive cultures; the trap is touching the site after cleaning.

q: A patient’s fasting glucose was ordered, but the patient admits they drank a sweet coffee on the way in; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Inform the provider or follow clinic protocol to reschedule/clarify the order because the result will be unreliable; the trap is drawing anyway and documenting “non-fasting” without notifying.

q: You are drawing blood and notice bright red blood spurting into the tube and increasing pain at the site; what should you do FIRST?
a: Stop the draw and withdraw the needle, then apply firm pressure because arterial puncture is possible and needs prompt control; the trap is “finishing the tubes” to avoid a redraw.

q: While preparing for an EKG, you find a thick layer of chest hair where V1–V3 should be placed and prior EKGs were unreadable; what should you do NEXT?
a: Clip (not shave) small areas for electrode contact as allowed and clean/dry the skin because poor adhesion causes artifact; the trap is pressing harder on electrodes without improving contact.

q: You are about to run a CLIA-waived glucometer test, and the meter displays a message that QC is overdue; what should you do FIRST?
a: Perform the required quality control checks before testing the patient because QC verifies accuracy and compliance; the trap is testing first “since it’s just screening.”

q: You placed the limb leads for an EKG over the patient’s wrists and ankles, but the patient is tremoring and the signal is poor; what adjustment is BEST?
a: Move limb electrodes to the upper arms and thighs (maintaining right/left placement) to reduce motion artifact; the trap is swapping lead locations, which can create misleading tracings.

q: During a 12-lead EKG, the tracing shows thick, irregular baseline “fuzz” in all leads while the patient is talking and moving; what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Instruct the patient to lie still and not talk, then repeat the tracing because muscle artifact is the most common cause; the trap is immediately repositioning all electrodes without addressing motion.

q: You draw blood into an additive tube but vigorously shake it to “mix it faster”; what should you do to prevent this error in the future?
a: Gently invert the tube the recommended number of times because shaking causes hemolysis and can invalidate results; the trap is thinking more force equals better mixing.

q: A coworker asks you to use last month’s opened control solution for a waived rapid strep test because “it still looks fine”; what is the BEST response?
a: Do not use expired/open-date–expired controls and obtain in-date controls because QC materials have stability limits that affect validity; the trap is relying on appearance instead of dates/documentation.

q: A patient’s EKG has a wandering baseline, and you notice the patient is shivering in a cold exam room; what is the BEST action NEXT?
a: Warm the patient (blanket, adjust room temp) and repeat the EKG because shivering creates artifact; the trap is interpreting it as a rhythm problem and alarming the patient.

q: During a point-of-care urine pregnancy test, the control line does not appear; what is the BEST action?
a: Consider the test invalid, repeat with a new device, and follow QC/troubleshooting because no control line means the result cannot be reported; the trap is documenting it as “negative.”

q: You need to collect a blood culture and a CMP from the same venipuncture; what should the CMA do first to reduce contamination risk?
a: Collect blood cultures first using strict antisepsis, then proceed with other tubes; the trap is drawing chemistry tubes first, which raises contamination risk and can invalidate cultures.

q: A patient has a mastectomy with lymph node removal on the left and a dialysis fistula on the right; where should the CMA plan to collect blood?
a: Notify the provider and follow facility protocol for an alternative site (often hand/forearm with approval) because both arms are contraindicated; the trap is choosing the “less bad” arm without escalation.

q: You’re drawing blood and the patient says they feel “hot and dizzy” and becomes pale while you’re filling the last tube; what is the CMA’s best next action?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, apply pressure, and assist the patient to a safe position (recline/legs elevated) while calling for help per clinic protocol; the trap is trying to “finish the tube” which increases fainting/injury risk.

q: During a fasting lipid panel draw, you collect a light blue tube first and realize the provider also ordered a CBC; what should you do next to ensure correct order of draw?
a: Collect the CBC in a lavender tube next, then document the order of draw was followed after the blue; the trap is switching to a serum tube “because it’s common” instead of continuing correctly to prevent additive carryover.

q: You attempt venipuncture and blood flow stops after 2 mL in the first tube; what is the best action to troubleshoot without compromising the specimen?
a: Gently adjust the needle angle/reposition slightly and ensure the tube is fully seated, then continue if flow returns; the trap is “digging” aggressively or removing/reinserting the needle, which increases hemolysis and injury.

q: After drawing a potassium level, you vigorously shake the green-top tube to mix it quickly before sending it out; what is the most appropriate corrective action?
a: Recollect the specimen because vigorous shaking can hemolyze blood and falsely elevate potassium; the trap is thinking “more mixing is better” instead of gentle inversion.

q: At the bedside you notice two unlabeled tubes on your tray after a venipuncture and the patient has already left the room; what should you do?
a: Discard the specimens and recollect with correct patient ID and immediate labeling because unlabeled specimens are not acceptable; the trap is labeling later from memory, which is a serious patient-safety error.

q: While collecting a urine specimen for culture, the patient hands you a cup without a label and says, “It’s mine, I’m the only one here”; what should you do next?
a: Verify the patient using two identifiers and label the specimen in the patient’s presence before accepting it; the trap is labeling at the desk, which increases misidentification.

q: You’re preparing to draw coagulation studies (PT/INR) and notice the light blue tube is only half-filled after collection; what is the best next step?
a: Recollect to the correct fill line because blue-top tubes require a precise blood-to-additive ratio for accurate results; the trap is “sending it anyway” since the sample looks adequate.

q: You are performing a CLIA-waived rapid strep test and the control line fails to appear; what is the CMA’s best action?
a: Treat it as an invalid test, repeat with a new device per manufacturer instructions, and do not report results; the trap is reporting “negative” just because the test line is absent.

q: You print an EKG that shows a wandering baseline and the patient is shivering in a cold room; what is the best next step before repeating the EKG?
a: Warm the patient/offer a blanket and have them relax and remain still, then repeat the EKG because muscle tremor mimics artifact; the trap is assuming it’s a true rhythm problem and escalating without troubleshooting.

q: During a glucose fingerstick POCT, you realize you used an expired test strip after obtaining the reading; what should you do next?
a: Repeat the test with in-date strips and document the issue per QC policy because expired strips can give inaccurate results; the trap is charting the first value because “it seems reasonable.”

q: A patient’s arm develops rapid swelling and pain at the venipuncture site during blood draw; what should you do first?
a: Stop the draw immediately, remove the needle, and apply firm pressure and a cold compress as appropriate while reporting per protocol; the trap is continuing to fill tubes, which worsens a hematoma.

q: During venipuncture for a lipid panel (serum) and CBC, the CMA accidentally fills the lavender tube first and then the gold-top tube; the patient is stable and both tubes are labeled at the bedside—what should the CMA do next?
a: Notify the provider/lab and redraw using the correct order of draw (gold/serum before lavender/EDTA) because EDTA carryover can falsely alter serum analytes; the common mistake is sending the specimen anyway, which risks inaccurate results and repeat testing later.

q: A provider orders a timed drug level and the patient arrives 45 minutes late; what should the CMA do next before drawing?
a: Confirm the collection time requirements with the ordering provider/lab and document the actual collection time because timing affects interpretation; the trap is drawing immediately without clarification and letting the result be misread.

q: On a busy morning, you are asked to run POCT A1c even though the daily quality control has not been documented; what should you do first?
a: Perform and document QC (or verify it was completed) before testing patient samples because results are not reportable without required QC; the trap is skipping QC to “save time.”

q: A provider orders PT/INR, CMP, and CBC; the CMA has light blue, red/gold, and lavender tubes ready—what is the correct order of draw?
a: Draw light blue first, then red/gold, then lavender, because coagulation tests must be collected before tubes with additives that can contaminate and the trap is drawing lavender first and falsely altering PT/INR.

q: During venipuncture for a CBC and CMP, you enter the vein and see blood flow, but the lavender-top tube only fills halfway before flow stops; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Remove the partially filled tube and try a new tube or reposition the needle while maintaining sterility, because EDTA tubes require a full draw-to-additive ratio and the common trap is sending a short EDTA tube that can clot or give inaccurate results.

q: Immediately after filling each blood tube, what is the CMA’s BEST action before setting it in the rack?
a: Gently invert each additive tube the recommended number of times (do not shake) to mix anticoagulant/additive, because inadequate mixing causes microclots/invalid results and the trap is shaking, which can hemolyze the specimen.

q: You are about to collect a throat swab for a rapid influenza test, and the patient coughs directly toward you; what should you do immediately to protect yourself and specimen integrity?
a: Pause and don appropriate PPE (at least a mask/eye protection per precautions) and then recollect using proper technique because droplet exposure risk is high; the trap is proceeding without PPE to “get it over with.”

q: After completing an EKG, you realize the limb leads were placed on the torso to “make it faster,” but the provider requested a diagnostic 12-lead; what should you do next?
a: Repeat the EKG with correct limb placement because torso placement can alter waveforms and interpretation; the trap is sending a potentially non-diagnostic tracing to the provider.

q: A patient reports chest pressure while you are preparing the EKG; what should the CMA do first?
a: Immediately alert the provider/activate the clinic’s emergency response while obtaining the EKG as directed because symptoms suggest a potentially emergent condition; the trap is finishing setup silently and delaying escalation.

q: During a routine venipuncture, the CMA draws a light blue sodium citrate tube for PT/INR but the vacuum stops early and the tube is only about half full; the next patient is waiting and the provider wants the result quickly—what should the CMA do NEXT to ensure an accurate test?
a: Discard the underfilled light blue tube and recollect a new citrate tube filled to the indicated line because citrate tests require the correct blood-to-additive ratio; a common mistake is sending a short-draw anyway or “topping off” the tube, which can falsely prolong clotting results.

q: You collected blood for a fasting lipid panel and labeled the tubes at the counter after leaving the room; what should you do now?
a: Stop and recollect using proper bedside labeling with two patient identifiers, because labeling away from the patient risks misidentification and the trap is “fixing” it later by guessing based on room number.

q: A urine culture is ordered, and the patient hands you a specimen cup filled to the brim from a non-sterile cup they used at home; what should the CMA do?
a: Request a new clean-catch midstream specimen using the sterile container and provide instructions, because culture requires sterile technique and the trap is accepting the sample since “there’s enough urine.”

q: You have a urine specimen for pregnancy testing and it has been sitting at room temperature for over 2 hours without a preservative; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Follow lab policy for stability—typically recollect or confirm acceptability with the lab before testing—because delayed, improperly stored specimens can give unreliable results and the trap is running it anyway “to save time.”

q: During venipuncture for a BMP and a CBC, the CMA accidentally fills the lavender EDTA tube first and then the light green heparin tube; the patient is stable and the blood is not yet sent—what should the CMA do next to best protect test accuracy?
a: Discard both tubes and recollect using the correct order of draw (light green heparin before lavender EDTA) because EDTA carryover can falsely alter chemistry results (e.g., potassium/calcium), and “just relabeling or sending anyway” is a common mistake that risks inaccurate provider decisions.

q: After removing the needle, you notice rapid swelling and bruising at the site; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Apply firm pressure and then a cold compress, elevate the extremity, and document/notify as appropriate because this indicates a hematoma and the trap is immediately applying heat, which can worsen bleeding early.

q: A patient becomes pale and says they feel faint during venipuncture; what is the CMA’s NEXT best action?
a: Remove the needle, apply pressure, assist the patient to a safe position (supine with legs elevated if possible), and alert the clinical team because preventing a fall is the priority and the trap is leaving the patient seated while you “get water.”

q: While drawing blood, the patient suddenly reports tingling down the forearm and sharp, shooting pain; what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Immediately stop the draw and remove the needle, apply pressure, and notify the provider per protocol because this suggests nerve involvement and the trap is continuing to “finish the tube” despite neurologic symptoms.

q: The provider orders a 12-lead EKG; the patient has a hairy chest and diaphoretic skin, and electrodes keep lifting—what should the CMA do to improve lead adherence?
a: Dry the skin and prep by clipping hair or using skin prep/abrasion as allowed, then apply new electrodes, because poor contact causes artifact and the trap is pressing harder on failing electrodes instead of re-prepping.

q: While recording an EKG, the baseline wanders and the tracing is jagged; the patient is shivering and talking—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Instruct the patient to remain still and warm them (blanket, adjust room temp) before repeating, because muscle tremor/movement causes artifact and the trap is troubleshooting cables first when the patient is clearly moving.

q: During a 12-lead EKG, you realize you accidentally swapped the right and left arm leads; what should the CMA do?
a: Correct the lead placement and repeat the EKG, clearly labeling the accurate tracing, because limb-lead reversal can mimic pathology and the trap is sending the incorrect tracing to the provider without repeating.

q: While performing an EKG, the machine shows heavy 60-cycle interference; the patient is still and electrodes are secure—what is the BEST next troubleshooting step?
a: Ensure the machine is properly grounded/unplug nearby electrical devices and move cables away from power cords, because electrical interference commonly causes this artifact and the trap is repeatedly reapplying electrodes without addressing the environment.

q: A patient asks you to explain what their abnormal EKG “means” after you complete the test; what is the CMA’s BEST response?
a: Tell the patient the provider will review and interpret the EKG and you will ensure it’s given to them promptly, because interpretation is not within CMA scope and the trap is offering reassurance or a diagnosis based on the tracing.

q: The EKG prints with a “leads off” message and flat lines in multiple leads; what is the CMA’s NEXT step?
a: Check that each lead wire is snapped to the correct electrode and that electrodes are firmly attached to prepped skin, because most “asystole-like” readings are connection errors and the trap is documenting it as a real rhythm change.

q: A provider orders a CBC, but the specimen arrives at the lab in a lavender-top tube with visible clots; what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Arrange recollection and document the rejection reason, because clotted EDTA specimens yield invalid counts and the trap is asking the lab to “run it anyway” and risking inaccurate clinical decisions.

q: During a rapid strep POCT, you realize you started the timer late and can’t confirm the read time window; what should the CMA do?
a: Discard the test and repeat with a new cassette/sample following exact timing, because reading outside the time window can cause false results and the trap is “estimating” the time and documenting a result anyway.

q: You perform a CLIA-waived fingerstick glucose test and the meter displays a QC failure message; the patient is waiting—what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Do not report a patient result; run QC per manufacturer instructions (or replace strips/meter as indicated) and repeat testing only after QC passes, because invalid QC means results are unreliable and the trap is retesting the patient immediately to “see if it works.”

q: A new shipment of urine dipsticks arrives; what is the CMA’s BEST action before using them on patients?
a: Verify expiration date, storage requirements, and perform required quality control with control materials per manufacturer/clinic policy, because new lots can perform differently and the trap is using them immediately because they’re “factory sealed.”

q: A provider orders PT/INR and CBC, and the CMA has already drawn the lavender tube first; what is the best action?
a: Notify the supervisor/ordering provider and recollect with a new venipuncture using the correct order (light blue before lavender) because EDTA contamination can falsely prolong coag tests; the trap is sending it anyway “since blood is blood.”

q: During a routine draw, the patient says, “I feel dizzy,” becomes pale, and slumps in the chair; what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle safely, and assist the patient to a safe position (legs elevated if possible) because vasovagal syncope can lead to injury; the trap is trying to “finish the tube” before helping.

q: While preparing for venipuncture, the CMA cleanses the site and then palpates again with an ungloved finger to “confirm the vein”; what should the CMA do?
a: Re-cleanse the site and avoid re-palpating the prepped area (or palpate with a clean gloved finger before final cleanse) because recontamination increases infection risk; the trap is proceeding without re-cleaning.

q: Immediately after filling an EDTA (lavender) tube, the CMA sets it upright without mixing; what is the best next step?
a: Gently invert the tube the recommended number of times right away to mix additive and prevent clotting; the trap is shaking vigorously, which can hemolyze the specimen.

q: During a fasting CMP draw, the CMA collects a light blue tube, then a lavender, then realizes a gold SST was also ordered; what should the CMA do next before drawing the SST?
a: Stop and recollect the tubes in the correct order of draw (light blue then SST/gold then lavender) because incorrect order can cause additive carryover and inaccurate results; a common trap is “just adding the missed tube at the end.”

q: A patient’s requisition and labels are printed, but the patient steps away to the restroom before labeling; when should the CMA label the tubes?
a: Label the tubes in the patient’s presence immediately after collection using two identifiers because labeling later increases misidentification risk; the trap is labeling at the nurses’ station “to save time.”

q: After venipuncture, the CMA notices a rapidly swelling, painful site at the puncture area; what is the best immediate action?
a: Release the tourniquet, withdraw the needle, and apply firm pressure because this suggests a hematoma/infiltration; the trap is continuing to draw or massaging the area.

q: The CMA draws a light blue coag tube that is only half full; what should the CMA do?
a: Recollect a new light blue tube filled to the required line because coag testing requires a precise blood-to-anticoagulant ratio; the trap is topping it off from another tube or submitting it underfilled.

q: During a 12-lead EKG, the tracing shows consistent wandering baseline in all leads while the patient is shivering; what should the CMA do next?
a: Warm/comfort the patient and minimize muscle movement, then repeat the EKG because muscle tremor causes artifact; the trap is printing and sending the noisy strip as diagnostic.

q: A patient arrives for an outpatient EKG, and the CMA notices the skin is diaphoretic and covered with lotion; what should the CMA do before applying electrodes?
a: Clean and dry the skin (and lightly abrade if needed) to improve electrode contact because moisture/oils cause artifact; the trap is placing electrodes immediately and blaming the machine for “bad tracing.”

q: The CMA must collect a urine culture specimen and the patient hands in a cup filled to the top but says it was not midstream; what should the CMA do?
a: Request a new clean-catch midstream specimen with proper instructions because contamination can cause false-positive culture results; the trap is accepting it because “there’s plenty of urine.”

q: After placing limb leads, the CMA sees lead II is inverted and the printout flags “lead reversal suspected”; what is the best next step?
a: Verify correct limb lead placement and reconnect leads, then repeat the EKG because lead reversal can mimic abnormal rhythms/axis; the trap is documenting it as a true cardiac change.

q: A patient reports chest pressure and shortness of breath while the CMA is setting up the EKG; what should the CMA do first?
a: Activate the clinic’s emergency response (alert provider/911 per protocol) and obtain vitals while preparing for immediate EKG because symptoms may indicate acute coronary syndrome; the trap is completing routine registration before escalating.

q: A patient on anticoagulants has persistent oozing after the draw despite brief pressure; what should the CMA do next?
a: Maintain firm pressure longer and apply a pressure dressing, and notify the provider per clinic protocol because bleeding risk is higher; the trap is sending the patient out with only a small bandage.

q: A CMP specimen in an SST is left on the counter for an hour after spinning, and the serum is still sitting on the cells; what is the best action?
a: Separate/aliquot the serum per protocol (or recollect if stability is exceeded) because prolonged contact with cells can change analytes like potassium and glucose; the trap is sending it unseparated because it was centrifuged.

q: During a draw, blood stops flowing after initially filling part of the tube; the patient’s arm is bent and the tourniquet has been on for over a minute; what should the CMA do next?
a: Ask the patient to straighten the arm and release/reapply the tourniquet as needed because prolonged tourniquet time and arm position can impede flow and alter results; the trap is repeatedly probing with the needle.

q: The CMA opens a new box of glucose test strips and is busy, so plans to run QC “later”; what is the best action?
a: Run quality control per manufacturer/clinic policy before patient testing because new lots can produce inaccurate results without verification; the trap is assuming new strips are automatically reliable.

q: The provider asks the CMA whether an EKG shows “ST elevation” and if the patient is having an MI; what is the appropriate response?
a: State that interpreting EKGs is outside the CMA scope and promptly relay the tracing and symptoms to the provider because diagnosis must be made by a licensed clinician; the trap is offering an interpretation to “be helpful.”

q: After filling a light blue citrate tube for PT/INR, the CMA notices it is only about 70% full; what should the CMA do next?
a: Recollect a properly filled light blue tube, because citrate tubes require the correct blood-to-additive ratio and “sending it anyway” can falsely prolong clotting results.

q: A CLIA-waived rapid strep test is negative, but the internal control line did not appear; what should the CMA do next?
a: Treat the test as invalid, repeat with a new kit/sample per instructions and QC requirements, and notify the provider if still invalid because controls verify accuracy; the trap is reporting “negative” based on the test line alone.

q: During venipuncture the CMA accidentally palpates the cleansed site again after applying alcohol; what is the best next step?
a: Clean the site again and allow it to dry before sticking, because re-touching contaminates the site and proceeding anyway is a common mistake that increases infection risk.

q: A provider orders PT/INR, CBC, and a BMP to be drawn at the same visit; what is the correct order of draw for these tubes?
a: Draw light blue first, then lavender, then green (or gold/SST if used for chemistry), because incorrect order can cause additive carryover (a common trap is drawing lavender before light blue, affecting coag results).

q: A patient’s fingerstick glucose on POCT reads 38 mg/dL, but the patient looks well and says they just washed hands after using hand lotion; what should the CMA do next?
a: Recheck using proper technique (clean, dry finger; consider a different site) and immediately notify the provider of critical results per protocol because contamination can skew readings but hypoglycemia is time-sensitive; the trap is dismissing the value as “machine error” without confirmation or escalation.

q: A fasting CMP is ordered and the CMA prepares to draw blood; which action must the CMA do first before applying the tourniquet if the patient has the same first and last name as another patient on the schedule?
a: Verify identity using two identifiers (e.g., full name and DOB) against the order and wristband if present, because misidentification is a major lab error and “confirming by room number or face” is a common trap.

q: During a fasting lipid panel and CMP draw, you fill a light blue tube first because it was closest, then remember the order of draw; what should you do NEXT before sending the specimens to the lab?
a: Discard the incorrectly collected light blue tube and redraw using the correct order of draw (blood culture if ordered, then light blue before serum/SST) because drawing after other tubes can contaminate the citrate tube and alter coagulation results; a common mistake is keeping it and “noting it,” which doesn’t fix the pre-analytical error.

q: After venipuncture, the CMA notices continued oozing at the site and the patient reports taking a blood thinner; what should the CMA do next?
a: Maintain firm pressure longer and apply a pressure dressing as needed, because anticoagulants increase bleeding risk and “a quick bandage” can lead to re-bleeding/hematoma.

q: A patient is on a “no needle” preference but agrees to testing; the first venipuncture attempt misses and a hematoma starts forming; what should the CMA do first?
a: Release the tourniquet, withdraw the needle, and apply firm pressure immediately, because continuing the draw worsens the hematoma (trap: trying to “fish” for the vein).

q: A patient is collecting a clean-catch urine sample but asks if they can fill the cup to the top “to make sure there’s enough”; what should the CMA instruct?
a: Collect midstream urine to the indicated fill line and avoid touching the inside of the cup, because overfilling/contamination can affect culture results (trap: “more is always better”).

q: A provider orders a basic metabolic panel and a lactate; the CMA draws both but then places the lactate tube in the regular pickup bin; what is the best corrective action?
a: Follow special handling—typically keep lactate on ice and send promptly per lab protocol—because improper transport alters results and “all tubes can wait for routine pickup” is a common error.

q: The CMA collects a CBC in a lavender tube and sets it on the counter to label later; what is the best next step?
a: Label the tube immediately at the patient’s side with required identifiers, because delayed labeling risks mislabeling (trap: labeling at the nurses’ station).

q: While drawing blood, the patient says they feel dizzy and looks pale; what is the CMA’s best immediate action?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, help the patient to a safe position (recline or supine) and monitor, because preventing a fall is priority and “finishing the tube first” is unsafe.

q: A urine culture is ordered but the patient hands the CMA an unlabeled specimen cup from the restroom; what should the CMA do first?
a: Confirm the specimen belongs to the patient using two identifiers and label it immediately in their presence, because accepting an unlabeled specimen without verification is a major identification trap.

q: The EKG printout shows excessive interference and the CMA notices a lead wire is loose at the electrode; what is the best next action?
a: Reattach/replace the electrode and secure the lead, then repeat the EKG, because poor contact creates artifact and “sending a noisy strip to the provider” delays care.

q: After completing an EKG, the CMA sees ST-segment elevation on the machine’s interpretive message; what should the CMA do next?
a: Immediately notify the provider/activate clinic urgent response per protocol and document the time, because CMAs don’t interpret/diagnose but must escalate potential acute findings (trap: filing the result for later review).

q: A patient scheduled for routine labs reports a history of mastectomy with lymph node removal on the right side; what is the best site selection?
a: Avoid venipuncture in the affected-side arm and use the other arm if possible, because lymph removal increases lymphedema/infection risk and “it’s fine if the vein looks good” is a common trap.

q: Immediately after drawing an SST (gold) tube, the CMA shakes it vigorously to mix; what is the best next step?
a: Gently invert the tube the recommended number of times (do not shake) and recollect if hemolysis is suspected, because shaking can hemolyze and distort chemistry results (trap: treating tubes like “mix by shaking”).

q: During daily QC for a point-of-care glucometer, the reading is out of the acceptable control range; what is the best next action before testing patients?
a: Do not use the meter for patient testing; repeat QC and troubleshoot (strip lot, expiration, cleaning, calibration) and notify the supervisor per protocol, because using a failed-QC device can produce unsafe patient results (trap: “it’s only slightly off”).

q: A patient with chest discomfort is placed for an EKG and the CMA notes the limb electrodes were placed on the wrists/ankles over heavy lotion; what is the best correction before recording?
a: Clean/dry the skin and place electrodes on appropriate sites (often distal limbs or torso per protocol) with good contact, because lotion reduces adhesion/conduction and “pressing harder” won’t fix poor signal.

q: While performing a 12-lead EKG, the tracing shows a wandering baseline and the patient is shivering in a cold room; what should the CMA do next?
a: Warm and relax the patient (blanket, reduce shivering) and ensure they are still before repeating, because muscle tremor causes artifact (trap: immediately reprinting without fixing the cause).

q: A CLIA-waived rapid strep test is running and the control line fails to appear; what should the CMA do next?
a: Treat the test as invalid, repeat with a new device/specimen as appropriate, and follow QC/troubleshooting steps, because reporting a result without a valid control is a common safety error.

q: You verify a patient’s identity and notice the lab requisition has no date of birth and the patient’s name is common; what should you do next before drawing blood?
a: Stop and resolve the order by confirming two identifiers with the patient and the ordering source/EHR before collecting, because drawing on an incomplete/ambiguous order risks wrong-patient results (trap: “I’ll just label carefully after the draw”).

q: You must collect blood cultures, PT/INR (light blue), CMP (serum), and CBC (lavender); what order of draw should you use?
a: Blood cultures first, then light blue, then serum tube, then lavender, because order of draw prevents additive carryover that can alter coagulation and hematology results (trap: drawing lavender before coag).

q: You are collecting a basic metabolic panel and the patient has a tight tourniquet on for over a minute while you search for a vein; what is the best action?
a: Release the tourniquet and reapply only when ready to puncture, because prolonged tourniquet time can hemoconcentrate and skew results (trap: leaving it on “to keep the vein up”).

q: A patient becomes pale and says “I’m going to faint” during the draw while seated on the exam table; what should the CMA do first?
a: Remove the tourniquet and needle and assist the patient to a safe position (recline/legs elevated) and call for help per clinic protocol, because preventing a fall is the priority (trap: trying to “finish the tube quickly”).

q: After filling a lavender-top tube for a CBC, you notice the blood looks “stringy” and may clot; what should you do immediately?
a: Gently invert the tube the recommended number of times right away, because EDTA must mix promptly to prevent clots that can invalidate the CBC (trap: shaking vigorously, which causes hemolysis).

q: During a routine venipuncture, blood flow stops after you’ve partially filled the first tube and the patient is calm; what is the best next step?
a: Gently adjust the needle angle or reposition the bevel and ask the patient to relax the fist without pumping, because minor needle position issues are common and pumping can hemolyze the sample (trap: immediately switching sites without trying a safe adjustment).

q: After a venipuncture, the site begins swelling and bruising while the tube is still filling; what should you do next?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, and apply firm pressure with elevation, because this indicates a developing hematoma and continuing worsens bleeding (trap: just tightening the tourniquet or continuing to fill tubes).

q: You drew a serum tube and forgot to label it at the bedside; you’re now at the lab counter with two unlabelled tubes and one patient in the room; what should you do?
a: Treat the specimen as unlabeled and follow clinic policy (typically discard and recollect with bedside labeling), because you cannot ensure correct patient identification after leaving the bedside (trap: guessing based on memory or room number).

q: A provider orders a fasting lipid panel but the patient mentions they ate breakfast an hour ago; what should the CMA do next?
a: Do not collect the specimen yet; notify the provider and reschedule or obtain instructions, because collecting a non-fasting sample may produce misleading results (trap: drawing anyway and “noting it later”).

q: An outpatient EKG prints with “leads off” and you notice the limb electrodes were placed on the patient’s lower legs over socks; what is the best next step?
a: Re-prep skin and place electrodes on clean, dry skin (no clothing) in correct limb positions, because poor contact causes lead-off alarms and inaccurate tracings (trap: hitting “print” again without fixing contact).

q: When removing the needle safety cap before venipuncture, the needle touches the countertop; what should you do?
a: Discard the needle and replace with a new sterile needle, because contamination increases infection risk and cannot be corrected by wiping (trap: cleaning it with an alcohol pad and proceeding).

q: You’re about to collect a specimen for a therapeutic drug level and the patient says they took the medication “just now in the car”; what should you do next?
a: Pause and clarify timing requirements on the order (peak vs trough) and notify the provider if timing is incorrect before drawing, because timing errors can lead to wrong clinical decisions (trap: drawing immediately without verifying timing).

q: For a capillary fingerstick glucose on an adult, the patient’s hands are cold and you get a poor blood drop; what is the best next step?
a: Warm the hand and allow it to hang down briefly before reattempting, because warming improves capillary flow and reduces the need for excessive squeezing (trap: “milking” the finger, which can dilute the sample with tissue fluid).

q: While collecting a urine specimen for culture, the patient hands you a cup that is filled to the brim with no lid and says it’s “clean catch”; what should you do?
a: Reject and recollect with correct instructions and a secure lid, because contamination and leakage compromise culture accuracy and safety (trap: accepting it to avoid “inconveniencing” the patient).

q: A patient’s PT/INR sample in a light-blue tube is only half full after the draw; what is the best action?
a: Recollect the specimen to ensure the tube is filled to the required line, because incorrect blood-to-anticoagulant ratio can falsely prolong or shorten results (trap: sending it “since there’s some blood”).

q: During a 12-lead EKG, the tracing shows a jagged baseline and the patient is shivering in a cold room; what should you do first to troubleshoot?
a: Warm the patient and reduce muscle movement (blanket, relax arms, ensure comfortable position) before repeating, because muscle tremor artifact mimics rhythm problems (trap: moving leads randomly without addressing the cause).

q: During a fasting lipid panel draw, you collect a light blue tube first because it “fills fastest,” then notice the requisition also includes a CMP in a serum tube; what is the best immediate action?
a: Stop and redraw using the correct order of draw (blood cultures if ordered, then light blue, then serum, then heparin, then EDTA, then glycolytic) because drawing blue before serum can contaminate additives and alter results, and the trap is thinking order only matters when multiple sites are used.

q: A provider asks you to perform a rapid strep test, but the kit’s external control documentation shows QC was not run for the new lot number; what should you do first?
a: Run and document the required QC before testing patient samples, because CLIA-waived tests still require QC to ensure valid results (trap: testing the patient first to “save time”).

q: While filling a light blue (citrate) tube for PT/INR, the tube stops short and is only half full; what should the CMA do next?
a: Discard and recollect a new light blue tube to the fill line because coag tests require a strict 9:1 blood-to-additive ratio, and the trap is “topping off” or sending an underfilled tube.

q: Your glucometer displays an error code during a busy clinic session and you’re unsure what it means; what is the best next step?
a: Stop patient testing and follow the device troubleshooting steps (manual/posted guide) and notify the supervisor if unresolved, because using a malfunctioning device risks incorrect results and unsafe decisions (trap: borrowing a reading from another patient’s device or guessing).

q: You obtain an EKG on a patient with chest pressure and the machine interpretation flags “possible acute MI”; what should the CMA do next?
a: Immediately notify the provider/activate the clinic’s urgent response while keeping the patient monitored and at rest, because CMAs don’t interpret/diagnose but must escalate critical alerts promptly (trap: trying to “confirm” by re-reading the strip yourself).

q: You successfully draw blood from an antecubital vein but notice a rapidly growing, painful swelling at the site; what is the best next action?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, apply firm pressure and then a cold compress, and document/notify per protocol because this indicates a hematoma from blood leaking into tissue, and the trap is continuing to draw or massaging the area.

q: After venipuncture, a patient says, “I’m going to faint,” becomes pale, and slumps in the chair; what should you do first?
a: Remove the tourniquet and needle, activate safety, and place the patient supine with legs elevated while calling for assistance because preventing injury and maintaining perfusion is priority, and the trap is trying to finish labeling or get “one more tube” first.

q: After running a CLIA-waived urine pregnancy test, the control line is absent but the test line is faintly present; what should you do next?
a: Treat the result as invalid and repeat with a new test per manufacturer instructions (and escalate if still invalid), because a missing control line means the test did not function properly (trap: reporting “positive” based on the faint test line).

q: You need a urine culture specimen and the patient hands you a cup filled from the first part of the stream; what should you do next?
a: Request a new clean-catch midstream specimen with proper perineal cleansing instructions because first-stream urine increases contamination, and the trap is accepting it because the container is sterile.

q: A patient’s requisition shows “CBC and HbA1c” and you have lavender and gray tubes available; which tube should be drawn first if both are needed and no other tubes are ordered?
a: Draw the lavender (EDTA) before the gray (fluoride/oxalate) because EDTA tubes come earlier than glycolytic inhibitor tubes in the order of draw, and the trap is choosing gray first because it’s “more urgent for glucose.”

q: While drawing blood for a CMP and CBC, the CMA fills the lavender tube first and then the gold serum tube; what should the CMA do NEXT to best protect specimen integrity?
a: Stop the draw and recollect using the correct order of draw (gold before lavender) because drawing EDTA first can carry over anticoagulant and falsely alter chemistry results; the common trap is sending the miscollected tubes anyway hoping the lab will “fix it.”

q: A provider orders an EKG on a patient with chest discomfort in the clinic; the patient is anxious and talking, and the tracing shows jagged baseline; what should the CMA do first to reduce artifact?
a: Instruct the patient to lie still, relax arms/legs, and avoid talking during acquisition because muscle tremor causes artifact, and the trap is immediately reapplying electrodes without addressing patient movement.

q: You have one successful venipuncture and need multiple tubes; what is the correct action regarding mixing the tubes?
a: Gently invert each additive tube the recommended number of times immediately after it is removed from the holder because this prevents clotting/hemolysis, and the trap is shaking vigorously or waiting until all tubes are collected.

q: A CMP specimen in a serum separator tube was just drawn and must be sent to the lab; what is the best handling step before transport?
a: Allow the specimen to clot (per lab timeframe) and then centrifuge if required before sending because premature spinning or transport can affect serum quality, and the trap is immediately centrifuging or leaving it unprocessed too long.

q: After collecting a CBC in a lavender tube, you realize you labeled it at the workstation using the schedule rather than at the bedside; what is the best action?
a: Do not send the specimen; recollect and label in the patient’s presence using two identifiers because mislabeling is a critical safety error, and the trap is “fixing” it by crossing out or adding a sticker later.

q: During a draw from a hand vein, the patient reports burning pain and you see blanching around the site; what should you do next?
a: Stop the draw and remove the needle, then apply pressure and assess/notify because this suggests infiltration/extravasation, and the trap is adjusting the needle deeper to “get flow back.”

q: You are running a CLIA-waived rapid strep test and the control line does not appear; what should you do next?
a: Treat the test as invalid, repeat with a new device and verify kit storage/expiration, documenting QC as required because missing control means the result can’t be trusted, and the trap is reporting it as negative.

q: You place precordial leads quickly and the EKG shows abnormal R-wave progression; the patient’s chest is sweaty; what is the best next action?
a: Re-prep the skin (dry/shave if needed) and verify correct V1–V6 placement landmarks before repeating because misplacement and poor adhesion can mimic pathology, and the trap is assuming it’s a true cardiac abnormality and interpreting it.

q: An EKG prints with a wandering baseline that worsens when the patient’s feet touch a metal chair rung; what should you do next?
a: Ensure proper grounding by having the patient not contact metal and confirm cables are intact/away from power cords, then repeat because electrical interference can cause baseline wander, and the trap is blaming the patient’s heart rhythm.

q: A patient’s rapid influenza test is negative but they have high fever and the provider asks you to document the POCT; what is the most appropriate documentation?
a: Record the test name, specimen type, result, date/time, operator ID (if required), and lot/expiration/QC per clinic protocol because POCT must be traceable for quality compliance, and the trap is charting only “flu negative” without test details.

q: A walk-in asks you to “tell me if my EKG is normal” after you perform it for the provider; what is the correct response?
a: Tell the patient the provider will review and discuss results and promptly give the tracing to the provider because interpretation is not in CMA scope, and the trap is offering reassurance based on appearance.

q: While performing a 12-lead EKG, the machine displays “LEAD OFF” and the printout is missing a lead; what is the best next action?
a: Check the indicated lead wire connection and electrode adhesion/skin prep, then repeat the EKG because a disconnected/poorly adherent electrode causes missing leads, and the trap is printing and filing an incomplete tracing.

q: Your glucose meter displays an error code immediately after you insert the strip and apply blood; what should you do next?
a: Repeat the test with a new strip and ensure adequate sample and proper strip insertion, then run controls if errors persist because device/strip issues can cause false readings, and the trap is documenting the failed number as a real value.

q: During venipuncture for a CBC and a CMP, the CMA accidentally fills the lavender-top tube first and then the serum (gold/SST) tube; what should the CMA do next to protect specimen integrity?
a: Stop and redraw the specimens using the correct order of draw (serum tube before lavender) because EDTA carryover can falsely alter chemistry results; the common trap is sending the tubes anyway and hoping the lab “fixes it,” which risks inaccurate patient care.

q: A patient’s requisition says “fasting lipid panel,” but at the chair they mention they drank a sweetened coffee an hour ago; what should you do next?
a: Pause the draw and notify the ordering provider or follow clinic protocol to reschedule/clarify, because non-fasting can alter results (trap: drawing anyway and “noting it” can still lead to wrong clinical decisions).

q: During venipuncture the patient says “I’m going to faint” and becomes pale and diaphoretic; what is your best immediate action?
a: Stop the draw, remove the needle, activate safety, and assist the patient to a safe position (supine with legs elevated if possible) while calling for help per protocol, because preventing injury is priority (trap: continuing to “finish the tube” risks syncope and falls).

q: You complete a blood draw, then realize you labeled the tubes at the nurses’ station using the schedule instead of at the patient’s side; what should you do?
a: Treat the specimens as unlabeled/mislabeled and follow policy for recollection with correct bedside labeling after verifying two identifiers, because identification errors are a major patient-safety risk (trap: guessing based on time or room number).

q: While drawing blood, the patient reports sharp tingling down the forearm and into the hand; what is the best action?
a: Immediately discontinue the draw and remove the needle, because this suggests possible nerve involvement and continuing can cause injury (trap: “repositioning the needle” after nerve pain increases risk).

q: You apply the tourniquet and struggle to find a vein; 2 minutes have passed and the patient’s fist is pumping—what should you do first?
a: Release the tourniquet and allow the arm to rest before trying again, because prolonged stasis and fist pumping can falsely elevate analytes and increase hemolysis (trap: “just one more try” with the tourniquet on).

q: While collecting a BMP in a green-top tube, you forget to invert it and it sits upright for 5 minutes before labeling; what is the best next step?
a: Gently invert the tube the required number of times immediately and document if needed, because proper mixing prevents microclots and inaccurate results (trap: shaking vigorously causes hemolysis and redraws).

q: During a routine venipuncture for CBC and CMP, the CMA draws the lavender tube first and then a green tube; what should the CMA do next before sending specimens to the lab?
a: Redraw the specimens using the correct order of draw (green before lavender) because drawing EDTA before a chemistry tube can contaminate the sample and falsely alter results; the common trap is sending “acceptable-looking” tubes anyway, which risks inaccurate lab values.

q: A provider orders a CBC, BMP, PT/INR, and lipid panel, and you are drawing with evacuated tubes; what order of draw should you use to avoid additive carryover?
a: Draw light blue (citrate) first, then SST/gold (serum) for lipids/BMP if serum is used, then green (heparin) if applicable, then lavender (EDTA) for CBC; this prevents anticoagulant contamination (common trap: drawing lavender before blue can falsely prolong coag tests).

q: During EKG placement, the patient has oily skin and the electrodes keep lifting; what is the best action before restarting the EKG?
a: Clean and dry the skin (and gently abrade if allowed) then replace electrodes, because poor adhesion increases artifact and misreads (trap: adding tape over a poorly prepped electrode often still fails).

q: A patient becomes short of breath and dizzy while you are obtaining an EKG for chest discomfort; what should you do first?
a: Stop the procedure and immediately alert the provider/activate emergency response per clinic protocol while keeping the patient safe, because worsening symptoms may indicate an acute event beyond CMA scope (trap: trying to “finish the EKG first” delays care).

q: You collect blood into an SST tube for a chemistry test, and the centrifuge is available immediately; what should you do before spinning?
a: Allow the SST to clot fully per manufacturer/lab guidance before centrifuging, because spinning too soon can create fibrin strands and instrument errors (trap: rushing to centrifuge to “save time”).

q: A urine culture specimen arrives at the lab counter without the time of collection noted; the patient has already left—what is the best next step?
a: Hold the specimen and notify the supervisor/provider to determine acceptability per lab policy, because missing collection time can invalidate culture handling and result interpretation (trap: backdating or estimating the time is falsification).

q: While performing a fingerstick, you milk the finger to get more blood and the result seems unexpectedly low; what is the best corrective action?
a: Repeat the test with a new strip after obtaining a free-flowing drop without excessive squeezing, because tissue fluid contamination skews results (trap: documenting the suspicious value without retesting can lead to wrong treatment).

q: The EKG prints with a calibration mark that is not the standard 10 mm/mV; what should you do next before handing it to the provider?
a: Correct the calibration/standardization setting and repeat the EKG, because improper calibration can misrepresent voltage and lead to misinterpretation (trap: assuming the provider will “just know” it’s off).

q: A provider requests a capillary fingerstick glucose, but the patient’s hands are cold and visibly bluish; what should you do first?
a: Warm the hand (e.g., warm compress) and ensure good circulation before puncture, because poor perfusion can give inaccurate low readings (trap: squeezing hard to obtain blood dilutes with tissue fluid).

q: You are setting up a 12-lead EKG and the tracing shows wandering baseline and muscle artifact; the patient is talking and shivering—what should you do next?
a: Re-educate the patient to lie still and relax, warm them if needed, and ensure electrodes have good skin contact, because motion/tremor commonly causes artifact (trap: immediately reprinting without addressing the cause).

q: At opening, the glucometer’s quality control fails at Level 2, but patient testing is scheduled in 5 minutes; what should you do next?
a: Stop patient testing and troubleshoot (new strip vial, check expiration, clean meter, rerun QC) and escalate if it still fails, because QC must pass before reporting results (trap: running patients “just this once” is unsafe and noncompliant).

q: While drawing a CBC and BMP, you accidentally collect the lavender tube first and then the light green tube; what should you do NEXT before sending specimens to the lab?
a: Stop and redraw using the correct order of draw because additive carryover from EDTA can falsely alter chemistry results, and the trap is “it’s fine if the tubes are labeled correctly.”

q: During a routine venipuncture for CBC and CMP, you accidentally collect the lavender-top EDTA tube before the light green-top heparin tube, and you notice the lavender tube was filled and gently inverted; what should you do next to best protect specimen accuracy?
a: Stop and recollect using a new venipuncture with the correct order of draw (light green before lavender), because drawing EDTA first can contaminate subsequent tubes and alter chemistry results; the common trap is sending the samples anyway since the tubes look properly filled and mixed.

q: You are performing a CLIA-waived rapid strep test and the control line does not appear; what is the best next step?
a: Do not report the result, repeat the test with a new device and verify storage/expiration, because a failed control indicates an invalid test (trap: reporting based on a faint test area without a control).

q: A patient asks you to tell them what their abnormal lab value “means” while you’re processing the specimen; what is the best response?
a: Tell them you can’t interpret results but you will ensure the provider receives them and can discuss meaning and next steps, because CMAs must stay within scope and avoid diagnosing (trap: explaining “it means you have…” can cause harm and liability).

q: You draw a light blue tube for PT/INR but it fills only halfway because blood flow stops; what should you do NEXT?
a: Discard it and recollect a fully filled tube because the blood-to-anticoagulant ratio must be correct, and the trap is sending it anyway “since some blood is present.”

q: A patient is dehydrated and you consider drawing from an IV arm that is currently infusing normal saline; what should you do BEST?
a: Choose a different site/arm because IV fluids dilute and alter results, and the trap is drawing “below the IV” without proper clearance and documentation.

q: A provider orders PT/INR and CMP, and you have only one venipuncture attempt to minimize patient anxiety; what is the BEST tube sequence to collect?
a: Collect the light blue tube first, then the serum tube (red/gold), then the light green tube because coagulation testing is most sensitive to contamination and the trap is putting serum before citrate “to fill others first.”

q: You collected a throat swab for a rapid strep but the courier is delayed and it will sit at room temperature for hours; what should you do BEST?
a: Follow the test’s specimen handling requirements (e.g., place in appropriate transport medium and store as directed or recollect if stability is exceeded) because viability/stability affects accuracy, and the trap is “sending it whenever it leaves.”

q: During venipuncture, the patient reports sharp tingling down the forearm and you feel resistance; what should you do FIRST?
a: Immediately stop the draw and remove the needle, then apply pressure because this may indicate nerve involvement, and the trap is continuing “just to finish the tube.”

q: After venipuncture, a patient develops a rapidly swelling, painful lump at the site; what should you do NEXT?
a: Stop the draw (if still in progress), remove the needle, and apply firm pressure with a cold pack because this indicates hematoma, and the trap is applying heat immediately or “just bandaging and moving on.”

q: After collecting several tubes, you notice the tourniquet has been on for over 2 minutes while you searched for a vein; what is the BEST action?
a: Release the tourniquet and allow time before reapplying because prolonged stasis can hemoconcentrate and skew results, and the trap is leaving it on “so you don’t lose the vein.”

q: You collect a potassium level and shake the tube vigorously to mix it before it clots; what is the most appropriate corrective step?
a: Recollect the specimen and gently invert per tube requirements because vigorous shaking can hemolyze and falsely elevate potassium, and the trap is thinking “more mixing is better.”

q: A urine culture is ordered, and the patient hands you a sample collected in a nonsterile cup from home without instructions; what is the BEST next step?
a: Request a new specimen using a sterile container and provide clean-catch instructions because nonsterile collection compromises culture results, and the trap is accepting it “since urine is urine.”

q: While labeling tubes, you realize you forgot to confirm the patient’s date of birth and only used the name on the chart; what should you do FIRST?
a: Verify two identifiers with the patient and label in their presence (or discard and recollect if identity can’t be confirmed) because misidentification is a major lab error, and the trap is “asking the front desk later.”

q: During a venipuncture for a CMP and CBC, the CMA draws the lavender tube first and then the gold serum tube; before labeling, the provider adds an order for PT/INR—what should the CMA do NEXT to ensure valid results?
a: Stop and recollect using the correct order of draw starting with a light blue citrate tube (then serum, then lavender) and label at the bedside; drawing EDTA before coag/serum can contaminate specimens and falsely alter results, and a common mistake is trying to “add on” PT/INR from the wrong tube or continuing the draw sequence anyway.

q: A CLIA-waived urine pregnancy test shows no control line; what is the BEST action?
a: Treat it as an invalid test and repeat with a new device/sample per procedure because no control means results can’t be trusted, and the trap is reporting it as negative.

q: You perform a fingerstick glucose and the first drop of blood is used directly on the strip after the patient’s hands were just sanitized with alcohol; what should you do NEXT?
a: Repeat the test after the finger is fully dry and wipe away the first drop because alcohol/first drop can dilute or contaminate the sample, and the trap is trusting the number because it “looks reasonable.”

q: You place EKG limb electrodes on the wrists and ankles of a shivering patient, and the tracing has heavy baseline artifact; what should you do NEXT?
a: Reduce muscle tremor and improve electrode contact (warm/cover patient, have them relax, prep skin and reposition electrodes if needed) because tremor commonly causes artifact, and the trap is repeatedly re-running without fixing the cause.

q: At the start of the day, the POCT glucometer fails QC but patient testing is already scheduled; what should you do BEST?
a: Do not run patient tests, troubleshoot per manufacturer (new strips, control solution, cleaning, recalibration) and notify the supervisor/provider if unresolved because QC failure invalidates results, and the trap is testing anyway “to avoid delaying the clinic.”

q: A patient complains of chest pressure while you are about to start an ordered EKG for “palpitations,” and they look sweaty and anxious; what should you do FIRST?
a: Alert the provider immediately and initiate the clinic’s emergency response while obtaining the EKG as directed because symptoms may indicate an acute event and the trap is prioritizing “finish the test before telling anyone.”

q: You are setting up a 12-lead EKG and notice the patient’s chest is oily with lotion; what is the BEST next step before applying precordial leads?
a: Clean and dry the skin (and lightly abrade if needed) to improve adhesion and signal quality because poor contact creates artifact, and the trap is pressing harder on electrodes and assuming the machine is broken.

q: During a venipuncture, the patient becomes pale and says they feel faint; what should you do FIRST?
a: Stop the procedure and assist the patient into a safe position (seated with head down or supine) because syncope risk is immediate, and the trap is trying to “finish the last tube quickly.”

q: After completing an EKG, the machine prints “AC interference,” and you see the patient’s phone charging cable near the leads; what should you do NEXT?
a: Remove/relocate potential electrical sources and ensure leads are secure, then repeat the tracing because electrical interference can distort readings, and the trap is sending the strip “since it printed.”

q: A patient at the front desk speaks loudly about having an STI and asks you to confirm their diagnosis in front of others—what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Move the conversation to a private area and speak quietly using neutral language, because continuing at the desk risks an incidental disclosure even if the patient started the conversation.

q: While rooming a patient, you realize the provider documented the wrong medication dose in yesterday’s note and the patient is worried—what is the CMA’s BEST next action?
a: Notify the provider and follow the clinic’s amendment process rather than editing the provider’s note yourself, because altering another user’s documentation can be considered falsification.

q: You are drawing blood for PT/INR (light blue) and a lipid panel (serum) using a butterfly set, and you accidentally fill the serum tube first—what is the best next step?
a: Discard that collection and redraw using the correct order of draw (blood culture if ordered, then light blue before serum) because drawing serum first can contaminate the citrate tube and falsely alter coag results; a common trap is keeping the blue tube “since it filled,” but the error affects test accuracy.

q: A minor arrives alone for a sports physical and hands you a signed consent “from mom” on notebook paper—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Confirm legal consent per state/clinic policy (e.g., parent/guardian present or verified consent) before proceeding, because accepting informal notes without verification is a common consent error.

q: You entered a vaccine lot number in the EHR and then notice one digit is wrong—what is the BEST way to correct it?
a: Follow the EHR’s correction/addendum function with date/time and reason, because deleting or overwriting the original entry can compromise the legal integrity of the record.

q: A patient’s spouse calls asking for the patient’s lab results and says, “I’m on the HIPAA form somewhere,” but you don’t see a release in the EHR—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Verify whether a valid authorization is on file before discussing any results and, if not, decline and offer to have the patient call back, because assuming a spouse has access is a common HIPAA breach.

q: A patient asks you to email their visit summary to a work email “because it’s easier”—what should the CMA do?
a: Use the approved patient portal or secure release process and confirm the patient’s preferred secure method, because standard email is often unsecured and can violate HIPAA.

q: During a venipuncture for a CMP and CBC, the patient says “I feel hot and dizzy,” becomes pale, and starts sliding down the chair while the tourniquet is still on—what should the CMA do first?
a: Stop the draw by releasing the tourniquet and removing the needle, then assist the patient to a safe position and alert the provider per clinic protocol because preventing injury from syncope is the priority; a common trap is trying to “finish the tube” before addressing the patient’s reaction.

q: An insurance claim is denied for “invalid diagnosis code,” and the patient calls upset—what should the CMA do NEXT within scope?
a: Route the issue to the billing/coding workflow to review coding/coverage and inform the patient you will follow up, because a CMA should not guess codes or promise coverage.

q: A walk-in patient demands to be seen immediately for a “refill” and becomes angry when told there are no openings—what is the CMA’s BEST response?
a: Use calm, respectful communication and assess for urgent symptoms that require escalation while offering the next available appointment or provider message, because dismissing without screening can miss an emergency.

q: During documentation, you notice you charted vitals under the wrong patient with a similar name—what should the CMA do NEXT?
a: Immediately alert a supervisor/manager and follow the EHR’s misfiled documentation correction process for both charts, because simply re-entering in the correct chart without addressing the erroneous entry leaves a dangerous record.

q: A patient requests a copy of their entire medical record at check-out—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Provide the clinic’s records release process (authorization form, identity verification, and timeframe) rather than printing immediately, because records requests must follow legal release procedures and minimum necessary standards.

q: A provider asks you to “just backdate” a note to match the visit date because they forgot to sign it—what is the CMA’s BEST action?
a: Refuse to backdate and advise using the correct late-entry process with the actual entry date/time, because backdating is falsification even if the content is accurate.

q: A patient says they never received a portal message about abnormal results and asks you over the phone what they were—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Verify identity and then follow the clinic protocol for communicating results (often provider review and documented communication) rather than improvising, because giving results without authorization/documentation is a common legal and safety trap.

q: You receive a phone call from someone claiming to be a patient asking, “What time is my appointment and what is it for?”—what should the CMA do FIRST?
a: Verify identity using approved identifiers before sharing any details, because confirming the visit reason to an unverified caller can disclose protected information.

q: You are scheduling a follow-up for a patient who needs a referral to cardiology and asks, “Can you just book it for me anywhere?”—what is the CMA’s BEST next step?
a: Confirm the patient’s insurance requirements (in-network, prior authorization, referral form) and follow the referral process before scheduling, because booking without verifying can lead to denied coverage and delays.

q: While rooming a patient, you notice yesterday’s progress note in the EHR has your name on it but you did not write it; what should you do first?
a: Notify your supervisor/office manager and the provider immediately and follow policy to correct the author/attestation because misattribution is a legal documentation error; the trap is “just editing it” yourself, which can worsen audit risk.
