a: Notify the provider and connect the patient with available resources (samples/discount programs/community assistance per clinic process) because financial barriers require coordinated support; the trap is telling the patient to “just take it as prescribed” without addressing access.

q: A patient brings a friend to interpret during discharge education, but you notice the friend answers for the patient and minimizes the patient’s questions. What should the CMA do?
a: Request a qualified interpreter and direct questions to the patient with teach-back because accuracy and patient autonomy are required; the trap is accepting informal interpretation that may distort instructions.

q: The provider orders a mammogram and a 6‑month follow-up visit; the patient says they “don’t want to think about it” and starts gathering belongings. What should the CMA do next?
a: Offer to schedule both before they leave and provide clear written next-step instructions, emphasizing the importance of timely screening, because immediate scheduling improves adherence; the trap is letting an avoidant patient leave without a plan.

q: You are updating a recall list and see a patient overdue for a diabetic eye exam; the chart shows no documented outside report. What should the CMA do next?
a: Contact the patient to confirm whether the exam occurred and, if so, request the report with proper release process/document the outreach because care coordination depends on documented completion; the trap is assuming it was done because the patient “usually goes yearly.”

q: After an ED visit, a patient calls saying the hospital told them to “follow up with your PCP,” but they’re unsure when or what records are needed. What should the CMA do next?
a: Schedule the follow-up per discharge timeframe and help obtain the ED summary/testing reports per clinic process because continuity of care requires documentation; the trap is scheduling without ensuring records will be available.

q: A patient is discharged with “return in 2 weeks” instructions, but later calls saying they forgot what symptoms should prompt earlier return. What should the CMA do next?
a: Review the provider’s written return precautions with the patient in clear language, confirm understanding with teach-back, and document the education because reinforcement prevents delayed care; the trap is telling them to “read the paperwork” without verifying comprehension.

q: A patient with a new glucometer demonstrates testing but wipes the finger with an alcohol pad and immediately lances while the skin is still wet. What should the CMA do next?
a: Re-teach to let the site dry completely before lancing and have the patient re-demonstrate using teach-back because wet alcohol can cause stinging and inaccurate readings; the trap is praising the demo without correcting technique.

q: A patient with limited English nods during discharge instructions and the adult child answers for them; what should the CMA do first?
a: Offer a qualified medical interpreter and address the patient directly, because accurate understanding and consent depend on the patient’s communication and the trap is relying on family to interpret.

q: A patient is leaving after new inhaler teaching and says, “Yeah, I get it,” while looking confused; what is the best action for the CMA?
a: Use teach-back by asking the patient to show and explain how they will use it at home, because teach-back verifies understanding and the trap is accepting a yes/no confirmation.

q: At checkout, a patient says, “I’ll schedule my blood pressure follow-up later,” but the provider note states “return in 2 weeks”; what should the CMA do next?
a: Schedule the follow-up appointment before the patient leaves and provide the date/time in writing, because closing the loop reduces no-shows and the common trap is assuming the patient will call later.

q: A patient declines a recommended vaccine and says, “My culture doesn’t do that,” then becomes quiet. What should the CMA do next?
a: Respond respectfully, ask permission to share information, provide culturally sensitive education in plain language, and use teach-back to confirm understanding because trust and comprehension affect adherence; the trap is arguing or dismissing the concern.

q: A specialist office calls asking for the patient’s last visit note and labs, but you realize the referral order was placed without the patient’s correct phone number on file. What should the CMA do first?
a: Verify and update the patient’s contact information in the EHR and send the required referral documentation through approved channels because incorrect demographics commonly derail referrals; the trap is sending records without fixing contact data.

q: A patient missed a diabetes follow-up appointment and says, “I forgot,” when called; what is the best CMA response?
a: Reschedule the appointment and document the outreach and outcome, because continuity of care requires documented follow-up and the trap is only noting it as a no-show without attempting to re-engage the patient.

q: A clinic’s recall report shows a patient is overdue for colorectal cancer screening; the patient calls asking if it’s “really necessary”; what should the CMA do best?
a: Reinforce the provider’s preventive screening recommendation and help schedule or route a message per protocol, because the CMA supports adherence without diagnosing and the trap is giving personal risk estimates or discouraging screening.

q: A provider orders a cardiology referral and the patient asks, “So am I supposed to call them or will they call me?”; what should the CMA do next?
a: Explain the referral process clearly (who will schedule, expected timeframe, and what the patient should do if not contacted) and provide written next steps, because unclear handoffs lead to failed referrals and the trap is giving vague reassurance.

q: A patient’s lab result is flagged critical in the EHR, but the patient’s voicemail greeting does not identify them; what should the CMA do first?
a: Notify the provider immediately and follow the clinic’s critical-result workflow while making a privacy-compliant contact attempt (no detailed voicemail), because timely escalation is required and the trap is leaving results on voicemail.

q: During discharge teaching, a patient says they will “double up” on a medication if they miss a dose to “catch up”; what should the CMA do best?
a: Reinforce that the patient should follow the prescribed directions and contact the clinic/pharmacy for missed-dose instructions, because doubling doses can be unsafe and the trap is offering medication-specific dosing changes outside CMA scope.

q: A referral is delayed because the specialist requires insurance preauthorization; what is the CMA’s most appropriate action?
a: Route the referral to the designated staff/workqueue for authorization and document the status for tracking, because preauthorization is an administrative step that must be coordinated and the trap is telling the patient the appointment is confirmed before approval.

q: After a visit, a patient calls and says they lost their written instructions and are unsure when to return; what should the CMA do first?
a: Verify the patient’s identity, then restate the provider’s return precautions and follow-up timing and resend instructions as allowed, because safety depends on clear return guidance and the trap is giving advice without confirming identity.

q: While processing a specialist referral, the patient states they cannot afford the visit and may skip it; what should the CMA do best?
a: Notify the provider/team and connect the patient with appropriate financial assistance or community resources per clinic process, because addressing barriers improves follow-through and the trap is pressuring the patient without offering options.
